Rolling Resistance
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** OEEET722 - HYBRID AND ELECTRIC VEHICLES > - **Module:** Module 1 > - **Topic:** Rolling Resistance # 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal KTU 2024 Definition > [!IMPORTANT] > **Rolling Resistance (Fr)** is the force resisting the motion of a body (typically a pneumatic tire) when it rolls on a surface. It is generated primarily due to the **non-symmetric distribution of the normal reaction force** at the tire–road contact patch, which is caused by the viscoelastic hysteresis of the tire material and the energy dissipated during the continuous deformation and recovery cycle of the tire as it rolls. In the context of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles (HEVs/EVs), rolling resistance is one of the three primary forces opposing vehicle motion at steady-state cruising (the other two being **aerodynamic drag** and **climbing resistance**). Since EVs have no engine idling losses, reducing rolling resistance is critical to extending the **driving range** per charge — a key performance parameter of any KTU 2024 Scheme HEV design problem. The rolling resistance is modeled as: $$F_r = \mu_r \cdot W = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot \cos(\theta)$$ where $\mu_r$ (or $C_{rr}$) is the **dimensionless coefficient of rolling resistance** and $W = mg\cos(\theta)$ is the normal load on the tire. ## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition > [!NOTE] > **Real-world analogy:** Imagine pushing a **deflated rubber ball** across a rough floor versus pushing a **hard steel ball** of the same weight. The rubber ball continually flattens at the contact patch, "drags," and slowly recovers its shape — you feel a constant resistance. The steel ball barely deforms, so it rolls smoothly. The "dragging" feeling you sense on the soft ball is exactly **rolling resistance** — energy is being wasted as heat inside the rubber every fraction of a second. For a pneumatic tire, the contact patch on the **leading edge** of the rolling tire compresses more (storing energy), while the **trailing edge** recovers (but cannot give back all the energy due to internal molecular friction of the rubber — called **hysteresis**). This creates an asymmetric pressure distribution, leading to a net retarding moment. ## 1.3 Standard Reference Values (KTU Frequently Tested) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Typical Coefficient of Rolling Resistance ($C_{rr}$) — for KTU numerical problems:** | Vehicle / Surface | $C_{rr}$ (Dimensionless) | |---|---| | Car tire on concrete/asphalt | **0.010 – 0.015** | | Truck tire on asphalt | **0.006 – 0.012** | | Bicycle tire on asphalt | **0.004 – 0.008** | | Railroad steel wheel on steel rail | **0.0001 – 0.0020** | | Low Rolling Resistance (LRR) EV tire | **0.005 – 0.008** | The standard value used in most KTU textbook problems: **$C_{rr} = 0.015$** for a passenger car on asphalt. # 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 Physics of Rolling Resistance — Step-by-Step Logic **Step 1 — The Contact Patch is NOT a Point:** Unlike the idealized "knife-edge" contact of a rigid wheel in classical mechanics, a pneumatic tire flattens over a finite contact area (typically 150–250 cm² for a passenger car tire) when loaded. **Step 2 — Viscoelastic Deformation:** The rubber compound is **viscoelastic** — it behaves partly like a spring (elastic) and partly like a viscous fluid (energy-dissipating). When the tire enters the contact zone, it must do **work to deform**, but when it leaves, it recovers **less energy** than was put in. The difference is dissipated as heat in the tire. **Step 3 — Asymmetric Pressure Distribution:** Because of this hysteresis, the **vertical reaction force is shifted forward** in the direction of wheel rotation. The resultant normal force $N$ effectively acts at a small distance $a$ ahead of the geometric center of the contact patch. **Step 4 — The Retarding Moment:** This forward shift creates a moment $N \cdot a$ about the wheel center, which the propulsion torque must overcome. Equating the propulsion force at the axle to the moment arm of the wheel radius $r$ gives us the rolling resistance force. **Step 5 — The Coefficient Emerges:** The ratio $\frac{a}{r}$ is found to be approximately **constant** for a given tire–surface–speed combination, and is defined as the **coefficient of rolling resistance**: $$C_{rr} = \frac{a}{r}$$ ## 2.2 Key Factors Affecting Rolling Resistance - **Tire Inflation Pressure** — Higher pressure reduces contact patch area and deformation → **lower $C_{rr}$**. - **Tire Material & Tread Design** — Softer compounds have more hysteresis → **higher $C_{rr}$**. - **Vehicle Speed** — At low/moderate speeds, $C_{rr}$ is roughly constant. Above ~100 km/h, it rises approximately linearly with speed due to standing wave and aerodynamic effects. - **Surface Roughness / Hardness** — Softer road surfaces deform more → **higher $C_{rr}$**. - **Temperature** — Hysteresis losses vary with tire temperature (an optimum exists). - **Wheel Diameter** — Larger diameter reduces the deformation per unit arc length → **lower $C_{rr}$**. ## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet > [!NOTE] > **All formulas you will need for KTU Module 1 problems on Rolling Resistance:** | # | Formula | Description | Units | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | $F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g$ | Rolling resistance force on level road | **N** | | 2 | $F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot \cos(\theta)$ | Rolling resistance on a slope of angle $\theta$ | **N** | | 3 | $F_r = N \cdot \frac{a}{r}$ | Force from the offset-of-normal-force model | **N** | | 4 | $C_{rr} = \dfrac{a}{r}$ | Definition of coefficient of rolling resistance | dimensionless | | 5 | $P_r = F_r \cdot v = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot v$ | Power lost to rolling resistance at speed $v$ | **W (J/s)** | | 6 | $E_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot d$ | Energy lost over distance $d$ | **J** | | 7 | $a = C_{rr} \cdot r$ | Forward shift of resultant normal force | **m** | > **Where:** > - $m$ = vehicle mass (kg) > - $g$ = 9.81 m/s² (gravitational acceleration) > - $v$ = vehicle speed (m/s) > - $r$ = effective tire radius (m) > - $a$ = offset of the normal reaction (m) > - $\theta$ = road gradient angle > - $N$ = normal load on the wheel (N) ## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility In modern **EV and HEV design**, rolling resistance directly determines the **battery energy consumed per kilometer**. A reduction in $C_{rr}$ from 0.015 to 0.008 (achievable with LRR tires) can extend the driving range of a typical EV by approximately **5–8%**, which is significant for the KTU Module 1 design-analysis questions on range extension strategies. # 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Derivation #1: Rolling Resistance from the Offset-of-Normal-Force Model This is the **most important derivation** for KTU Module 1 and is a frequent 7-mark question in board exams. ### Setup Consider a driven wheel of radius $r$ rolling at constant velocity on a horizontal surface. The contact patch length is $\ell$, and the resultant vertical reaction $N$ acts at a distance $a$ ahead of the geometric center of the contact patch (i.e., in the direction of rolling). **Free-Body Diagram Notation:** - $F_r$ = tractive (propulsion) force applied at the axle in the rolling direction - $N$ = normal reaction from the ground - $W = mg$ = weight of the wheel-load - $F_x$ = horizontal friction force at the ground (neglected for pure rolling) - $a$ = horizontal offset of $N$ from the wheel center (forward) ### Step-by-Step Derivation **Step 1 — Force equilibrium in the vertical direction:** The vertical forces must balance, so the normal reaction equals the weight on the wheel: $$\sum F_y = 0 \implies N - W = 0$$ $$N = W = mg$$ **Step 2 — Moment equilibrium about the wheel center:** The wheel rolls at constant angular velocity, so the net moment about the wheel center is zero. The propulsion force $F_r$ acts at the axle (no moment arm from $F_r$ itself for translational motion) and the normal force $N$ is offset by distance $a$ forward, creating a retarding moment $N \cdot a$ about the center. $$\sum M_{\text{center}} = 0$$ $$F_r \cdot r - N \cdot a = 0$$ > *Explanation: $F_r$ applied at the axle produces a forward rolling torque $F_r \cdot r$ about the contact patch. The offset normal $N$ acting at distance $a$ ahead of center produces an opposing moment $N \cdot a$. For steady rolling, these must balance.* **Step 3 — Solve for $F_r$:** $$F_r \cdot r = N \cdot a$$ $$F_r = \frac{N \cdot a}{r}$$ **Step 4 — Substitute $N = W = mg$:** $$F_r = \frac{a}{r} \cdot W = \frac{a}{r} \cdot mg$$ **Step 5 — Define the coefficient of rolling resistance:** Define the dimensionless ratio: $$C_{rr} \equiv \frac{a}{r}$$ **Step 6 — Final compact form:** $$\boxed{F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g}$$ > **For a road inclined at angle $\theta$**, the normal component of weight is $W \cos(\theta) = mg \cos(\theta)$, so: $$F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot \cos(\theta)$$ --- ## 3.2 Derivation #2: Power and Energy Lost to Rolling Resistance ### Setup A vehicle of mass $m$ travels at constant speed $v$ (m/s) on a level road. The rolling resistance force is $F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g$. ### Step-by-Step Derivation **Step 1 — Definition of power:** Power is the rate at which the traction system does work against $F_r$: $$P_r = F_r \cdot v$$ **Step 2 — Substitute the rolling resistance force:** $$P_r = (C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g) \cdot v$$ **Step 3 — Result (in Watts, if SI units are used):** $$\boxed{P_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot v \quad \text{[W]}}$$ **Step 4 — Energy lost over a distance $d$:** Since $P_r = \dfrac{dE_r}{dt}$ and $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$: $$\frac{dE_r}{dx} = \frac{P_r}{v} = F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g$$ Integrating over distance $d$: $$\boxed{E_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot d \quad \text{[J]}}$$ > **Engineering Insight:** Notice that rolling resistance losses are **independent of speed** (the *force* is constant) — but the *power* dissipated grows linearly with speed. This is why **aerodynamic drag** (which grows as $v^3$ in power) dominates at high speeds, but **rolling resistance** dominates in city driving cycles (low to medium speeds) — a critical point in EV/HEV range calculations. --- ## 3.3 Analytical Worked Example (KTU Board Style) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Problem:** A 1500 kg passenger EV travels at a constant 20 m/s on a level road. The coefficient of rolling resistance is 0.012, and the coefficient of aerodynamic drag is 0.30 with a frontal area of 2.2 m². Air density is 1.2 kg/m³. Find: > (a) The rolling resistance force. > (b) The power required to overcome rolling resistance. > (c) The total tractive power if the rolling + aerodynamic + climbing losses are all active on a 3% upgrade. **Solution:** **(a) Rolling resistance force:** $$F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g = 0.012 \times 1500 \times 9.81$$ $$F_r = 176.58 \text{ N}$$ **(b) Power to overcome rolling resistance:** $$P_r = F_r \cdot v = 176.58 \times 20$$ $$P_r = 3531.6 \text{ W} \approx 3.53 \text{ kW}$$ **(c) Total tractive power on 3% upgrade:** Climbing force: $F_c = mg \sin(\theta)$, where $\sin(\theta) \approx 0.03$ for a 3% grade. $$F_c = 1500 \times 9.81 \times 0.03 = 441.45 \text{ N}$$ Aerodynamic drag force: $F_a = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho C_d A v^2$ $$F_a = 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 0.30 \times 2.2 \times (20)^2 = 158.4 \text{ N}$$ Total tractive force: $$F_t = F_r + F_a + F_c = 176.58 + 158.4 + 441.45 = 776.43 \text{ N}$$ Total tractive power: $$P_t = F_t \cdot v = 776.43 \times 20 = 15528.6 \text{ W} \approx 15.53 \text{ kW}$$ # 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Free-Body Diagram of a Rolling Wheel (Mermaid Block-Level) ```mermaid flowchart LR nodeA["WEIGHT W = m g
Acts downward at wheel center"] nodeB["NORMAL FORCE N

from geometric center of contact"] nodeC["ROLLING RESISTANCE FORCE F r
Acts at axle, opposes motion"] nodeD["WHEEL CENTER
Radius = r"] nodeE["CONTACT PATCH
Length = ell
Center of pressure shifted forward"] nodeF["PROPULSION TORQUE T
Applied at axle by motor"] nodeA --> nodeD nodeB --> nodeE nodeD --> nodeC nodeE --> nodeD nodeF --> nodeD subgraph MOMENT_BALANCE nodeM["MOMENT EQUILIBRIUM
F r times r = N times a
C rr = a divided by r"] end nodeM --- nodeD nodeM --- nodeE ``` ## 4.2 Block Diagram — Factors Influencing Rolling Resistance ```mermaid flowchart TD nodeA["ROLLING RESISTANCE FORCE F r"] --> nodeB["Total Vehicle Resistance"] nodeC["Tire Inflation Pressure"] --> nodeA nodeD["Tire Material and Tread"] --> nodeA nodeE["Vehicle Speed v"] --> nodeA nodeF["Road Surface Hardness"] --> nodeA nodeG["Wheel Diameter 2 r"] --> nodeA nodeH["Ambient Temperature"] --> nodeA nodeI["Vehicle Mass m"] --> nodeA nodeJ["Road Gradient theta"] --> nodeA nodeB --> nodeK["Tractive Power Required
P = F r times v"] nodeK --> nodeL["EV Battery Energy Consumption

Compression phase
Energy STORED in rubber"] --> nodeB["HIGH PRESSURE ZONE
at the leading edge
of contact patch"] nodeB --> nodeC["RESULTANT NORMAL FORCE N

M = N times a
about wheel center"] nodeD --> nodeE["FORCE F r REQUIRED AT AXLE

Recovery phase
Energy RETURNED less than stored"] --> nodeB nodeG["HYSTERESIS LOSS
Energy dissipated as heat
inside the rubber compound"] --> nodeF ``` > [!NOTE] > **Reading the diagram:** The pressure-distribution block diagram illustrates *why* the resultant normal force is offset by a small distance $a$ in the direction of rolling. The energy lost to **hysteresis** is the root physical cause — not surface friction, as is often mistakenly assumed by students. # 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Q1. **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Paper Q1]** > Define the term **coefficient of rolling resistance**. List any **four factors** that affect it. **Model Answer:** The coefficient of rolling resistance ($C_{rr}$) is defined as the ratio of the rolling resistance force to the normal load on the wheel: $$C_{rr} = \frac{F_r}{N} = \frac{a}{r}$$ where $a$ is the forward offset of the normal reaction in the contact patch and $r$ is the effective wheel radius. It is **dimensionless** and typically ranges from 0.001 (railroad) to 0.015 (car tire on asphalt). **Four factors affecting $C_{rr}$:** 1. Tire inflation pressure (lower pressure → higher $C_{rr}$) 2. Tire material / compound (more viscoelastic → higher $C_{rr}$) 3. Road surface hardness (softer road → higher $C_{rr}$) 4. Vehicle speed (increases at high speeds due to standing-wave effects) --- ### Q2. **[KTU University Exam – Jun 2024, Model Paper Q2]** > Differentiate between **rolling resistance** and **aerodynamic drag** in terms of their dependence on vehicle speed. **Model Answer:** | Parameter | Rolling Resistance $F_r$ | Aerodynamic Drag $F_a$ | |---|---|---| | Force dependence on speed | **Independent** of speed | $\propto v^2$ | | Power dependence on speed | $P_r \propto v$ | $P_a \propto v^3$ | | Dominant regime | City / low-speed driving | Highway / high-speed driving | | Primary cause | Tire viscoelastic hysteresis | Air turbulence around vehicle body | At low speeds, **rolling resistance** dominates the total tractive demand. At high speeds (typically above 60–80 km/h for an EV), **aerodynamic drag** becomes the dominant term. --- ## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each) — Module Internal Choice ### **Question A** (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Paper Q8]** > **(a)** Derive an expression for the **rolling resistance force** experienced by a pneumatic tire rolling on a level road, starting from the offset-of-normal-force model. Clearly define the **coefficient of rolling resistance** and state its typical value for a passenger car. **(7 Marks)** > > **(b)** An electric vehicle of mass **1800 kg** (including battery and passengers) is cruising at a constant speed of **90 km/h** on a level road. The coefficient of rolling resistance is **0.013**, the coefficient of aerodynamic drag is **0.28**, the frontal area is **2.4 m²**, and air density is **1.225 kg/m³**. Calculate: > - (i) The rolling resistance force > - (ii) The aerodynamic drag force > - (iii) The total tractive power required at the wheels **(7 Marks)** #### Model Solution **Part (a) — Derivation:** Refer to **Section 3.1** above for the complete step-by-step derivation. Summary of result: $$\boxed{F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g, \quad \text{where } C_{rr} = \frac{a}{r}}$$ Typical value for a passenger car on asphalt: **$C_{rr} \approx 0.010$ to $0.015$** (use $C_{rr} = 0.015$ as standard). **Part (b) — Numerical Solution:** **Given:** $m = 1800$ kg, $v = 90$ km/h $= 25$ m/s, $C_{rr} = 0.013$, $C_d = 0.28$, $A = 2.4$ m², $\rho = 1.225$ kg/m³, $g = 9.81$ m/s². **(i) Rolling resistance force:** $$F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g = 0.013 \times 1800 \times 9.81$$ $$F_r = 229.55 \text{ N} \approx 230 \text{ N}$$ **(ii) Aerodynamic drag force:** $$F_a = \frac{1}{2} \rho C_d A v^2$$ $$F_a = 0.5 \times 1.225 \times 0.28 \times 2.4 \times (25)^2$$ $$F_a = 0.5 \times 1.225 \times 0.28 \times 2.4 \times 625$$ $$F_a = 257.25 \text{ N} \approx 257.3 \text{ N}$$ **(iii) Total tractive power at the wheels:** Total tractive force (level road, no grade): $$F_t = F_r + F_a = 229.55 + 257.25 = 486.8 \text{ N}$$ Total tractive power: $$P_t = F_t \cdot v = 486.8 \times 25$$ $$\boxed{P_t = 12170 \text{ W} \approx 12.17 \text{ kW}}$$ --- ### **Question B (Alternative Choice)** (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam – Jun 2024, Model Paper Q9]** > **(a)** Explain with a neat sketch the **physical origin of rolling resistance** in a pneumatic tire. Discuss the role of **hysteresis** in its generation. **(7 Marks)** > > **(b)** A 1200 kg hybrid vehicle climbs a uniform slope of **5%** at a constant speed of **54 km/h**. The coefficient of rolling resistance is **0.010**, and $g = 9.81$ m/s². Calculate: > - (i) The rolling resistance force > - (ii) The climbing (grade) resistance force > - (iii) The power required to overcome **only the rolling and climbing resistance** combined **(7 Marks)** #### Model Solution **Part (a) — Physical Origin:** Refer to **Sections 1.2 and 4.3** above. Key points to mention in the answer: - A pneumatic tire is **viscoelastic** (combination of viscous and elastic behavior). - As the tire enters the contact zone, the rubber **deforms and stores elastic energy** ($E_{\text{stored}}$). - As the tire leaves the contact zone, the rubber **recovers and releases less energy** ($E_{\text{recovered}}$). - The difference $\Delta E = E_{\text{stored}} - E_{\text{recovered}}$ is the **hysteresis loss**, dissipated as **heat** within the rubber compound. - This asymmetric energy storage–release cycle causes the resultant normal force to be **shifted forward by a small distance $a$** in the direction of rolling, creating a net retarding moment. - The retarding moment must be continuously overcome by the propulsion force → this is the **rolling resistance**. **Part (b) — Numerical Solution:** **Given:** $m = 1200$ kg, slope $= 5\% \implies \tan(\theta) = 0.05$, $v = 54$ km/h $= 15$ m/s, $C_{rr} = 0.010$, $g = 9.81$ m/s². **Step 1 — Slope angle:** For small angles, $\theta = \arctan(0.05) = 2.86°$. Approximate (acceptable for KTU 2024): $\sin(\theta) \approx \tan(\theta) = 0.05$, $\cos(\theta) \approx 0.9987 \approx 1$. **(i) Rolling resistance force (on a slope):** $$F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot \cos(\theta)$$ $$F_r = 0.010 \times 1200 \times 9.81 \times \cos(2.86°)$$ $$F_r = 0.010 \times 1200 \times 9.81 \times 0.9987$$ $$F_r = 117.56 \text{ N} \approx 117.6 \text{ N}$$ **(ii) Climbing (grade) resistance force:** $$F_c = m \cdot g \cdot \sin(\theta) = 1200 \times 9.81 \times \sin(2.86°)$$ $$F_c = 1200 \times 9.81 \times 0.0499$$ $$F_c = 587.3 \text{ N} \approx 587.4 \text{ N}$$ > *Equivalently, using $\sin(\theta) \approx \tan(\theta) = 0.05$:* $F_c = 1200 \times 9.81 \times 0.05 = 588.6$ N (very close — both are accepted). **(iii) Combined power (rolling + climbing only):** $$F_{\text{combined}} = F_r + F_c = 117.56 + 587.3 = 704.86 \text{ N}$$ $$P_{\text{combined}} = F_{\text{combined}} \cdot v = 704.86 \times 15$$ $$\boxed{P_{\text{combined}} = 10572.9 \text{ W} \approx 10.57 \text{ kW}}$$ --- > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:** > > 1. **Unit conversion trap:** A common 1–2 mark loss happens when students forget to convert km/h to m/s when computing power ($P = F \cdot v$). Always check: $v$ in m/s for power in Watts. > 2. **Slope formula trap:** On a slope, students often incorrectly use $F_r = C_{rr} \cdot mg$ instead of $C_{rr} \cdot mg \cos(\theta)$. The normal load on a slope is **reduced** by the factor $\cos(\theta)$ — remember to include it. > 3. **Defining $C_{rr}$:** Examiners **deduct marks** if the student writes $C_{rr} = F_r / F_a$ or any other wrong ratio. The correct definition is $C_{rr} = a / r = F_r / N$. > 4. **Speed dependence:** Some students wrongly state that rolling resistance "increases with $v^2$" like aerodynamic drag. Rolling resistance force is **independent of speed** (at low–moderate $v$); only its *power* is linear in $v$. > 5. **Hysteresis vs Friction:** Rolling resistance is **NOT** due to surface friction between tire and road (the contact patch is essentially stationary — pure rolling). It is due to **internal material hysteresis**. Examiners check this distinction. --- ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!NOTE] > **Rapid Revision Checklist — Rolling Resistance (KTU Module 1):** > > - ✅ **Definition:** Rolling resistance is the retarding force due to **viscoelastic hysteresis** in the tire. > - ✅ **Master Formula:** $F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g$ (level) ; $F_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot \cos(\theta)$ (slope). > - ✅ **Coefficient Definition:** $C_{rr} = a / r$ (dimensionless, typically 0.005–0.015 for cars). > - ✅ **Power:** $P_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot v$ (linear in $v$). > - ✅ **Energy:** $E_r = C_{rr} \cdot m \cdot g \cdot d$ (linear in distance $d$). > - ✅ **Key Insight:** Rolling resistance force is **speed-independent**; aerodynamic drag is $\propto v^2$ (power $\propto v^3$). > - ✅ **Low Rolling Resistance (LRR) tires** can extend EV range by 5–8% — high-yield KTU 2024 application point. > - ✅ **Higher inflation pressure** → smaller contact patch → lower $C_{rr}$. > - ✅ **Larger wheel diameter** → smaller deformation per revolution → lower $C_{rr}$. > - ✅ **Hysteresis** is the root cause, NOT surface friction. > - ✅ **Standard value used in KTU problems:** $C_{rr} = 0.015$ unless otherwise stated.

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** OEEET722 - HYBRID AND ELECTRIC VEHICLES > - **Module:** Module 1 > - **Topic:** Grading Resistance # ⚙️ MODULE 1 — VEHICLE DYNAMICS FUNDAMENTALS ## Topic: Grading Resistance > [!NOTE] > **Syllabus Anchor (KTU 2024 — OEEET722):** *Vehicle dynamics fundamentals — Tractive effort, total tractive resistance, grading resistance, rolling resistance, aerodynamic drag, inertia, and vehicle performance characteristics for conventional, hybrid, and electric powertrains.* --- ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU Board Standard) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Grading Resistance (F_g):** The component of a vehicle's gravitational weight that acts **parallel to the road surface** in the direction opposing the vehicle's motion when the vehicle traverses a slope (incline or decline). It represents the additional force the powertrain must overcome (on an upgrade) or the force the brakes must absorb (on a downgrade) due to road gradient. Mathematically, for a vehicle of gross mass $M$ (kg) moving on a road of slope angle $\alpha$: $$F_g = M \cdot g \cdot \sin(\alpha)$$ where $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$ is the **acceleration due to gravity** and $\alpha$ is the **angle of inclination** of the road with respect to the horizontal. --- ### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — "The Hill-Climb Intuition" Imagine you are pushing a loaded shopping trolley up the ramp of a parking garage. The ramp is tilted by some angle. You can feel a force pulling the trolley *backward* (down the slope) — that is **gravity's parallel component** trying to roll the trolley back down. To keep it moving up, you must push *harder* than you would on flat ground. The extra push you need is exactly the **Grading Resistance**. Similarly, in an EV or HEV, when the driver presses the accelerator on a hill, the motor must supply additional torque to defeat this gravity component. This extra force requirement: - **Reduces range** in Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs). - **Increases fuel consumption** in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEVs). - **Demands higher peak motor torque** during design. > [!NOTE] > **Physical Constants Used Throughout This Note:** > - Gravitational acceleration: $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$ > - Small-angle approximation valid for $\alpha \le 10°$ (typical road grade $\le 10\%$) > - Standard road-grade convention: *positive grade = upgrade* --- ### 1.3 Role of Grading Resistance in the Total Tractive Equation (Big Picture) In the canonical KTU vehicle-dynamics model, the **Tractive Effort (F_t)** required at the wheels must balance the **Total Resistance (F_R)**: $$F_t = F_R = F_{rr} + F_{ad} + F_g + F_i + F_{j}$$ Where: | Symbol | Resistance Term | |:------:|:----------------| | $F_{rr}$ | Rolling Resistance | | $F_{ad}$ | Aerodynamic Drag | | $F_g$ | **Grading Resistance** (this topic) | | $F_i$ | Inertia (Mass × Acceleration) | | $F_j$ | Rotational inertia of drivetrain components | **Grading Resistance is the only term that depends on road geometry** — all others depend on speed, vehicle mass, or aerodynamic shape. ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Force Decomposition on an Inclined Plane When a vehicle of mass $M$ rests on a road inclined at angle $\alpha$, its weight $W = M \cdot g$ acts **vertically downward** through the center of gravity. This weight vector can be resolved into two orthogonal components relative to the road surface: **Step 1 — Identify the weight vector.** The weight vector $W = M g$ points straight down toward the Earth's center. **Step 2 — Resolve into slope-parallel and slope-perpendicular components.** - Component **parallel to slope** (pointing down the incline): $W \cdot \sin(\alpha) = M g \sin(\alpha)$ - Component **perpendicular to slope** (pressing into the road): $W \cdot \cos(\alpha) = M g \cos(\alpha)$ **Step 3 — Define grading resistance.** The slope-parallel component that opposes forward motion (during an upgrade) is defined as the **Grading Resistance**: $$F_g = M \cdot g \cdot \sin(\alpha)$$ **Step 4 — Recognize the perpendicular component's role.** The perpendicular component $M g \cos(\alpha)$ reduces the **normal reaction force** $N$ on the tires, which in turn reduces rolling resistance (since $F_{rr} = \mu_r \cdot N$). On very steep grades, this becomes a significant secondary effect. --- ### 2.2 Percentage Grade vs. Angle of Inclination Civil engineers and road-design codes specify gradients as **percentage grade (% grade)** rather than degrees. The conversion is: $$\text{Grade (\%)} = \frac{\text{Vertical Rise}}{\text{Horizontal Run}} \times 100 = 100 \cdot \tan(\alpha)$$ Inverting for the angle: $$\alpha = \arctan\left(\frac{\text{Grade (\%)}}{100}\right)$$ For small angles ($\alpha \le 10°$, i.e., grade $\le 17.6\%$), the following approximations hold: $$\sin(\alpha) \approx \tan(\alpha) \approx \alpha_{\text{rad}} = \frac{\pi \alpha_{\text{deg}}}{180}$$ This yields the **most-used KTU engineering formula**: $$\boxed{F_g \approx M \cdot g \cdot \tan(\alpha) \approx M \cdot g \cdot \frac{\text{Grade (\%)}}{100} = 0.01 \cdot M \cdot g \cdot (\text{Grade \%})}$$ --- ### 2.3 Sign Convention (KTU Convention) | Scenario | Sign of $F_g$ | Physical Meaning | |:---------|:-------------:|:-----------------| | **Upgrade** (positive grade) | $F_g > 0$ | Opposes motion; motor must overcome | | **Downgrade** (negative grade) | $F_g < 0$ | Assists motion; brakes must dissipate energy | | **Level road** (0% grade) | $F_g = 0$ | No contribution | > [!IMPORTANT] > In the KTU model, **all resistances are summed as positive magnitudes in the direction opposing motion**, while $F_g$ may be either added (upgrade) or subtracted (downgrade) depending on slope sign. --- ### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet > [!NOTE] > **Master these expressions — they appear in nearly every Part-B vehicle-dynamics problem on KTU exams.** | # | Formula | Description | Typical Units | |:-:|:--------|:------------|:--------------| | 1 | $F_g = M g \sin(\alpha)$ | **Exact** grading resistance | N | | 2 | $F_g \approx M g \tan(\alpha)$ | Small-angle approximation (KTU preferred) | N | | 3 | $F_g = 0.01 \cdot M g \cdot (\%G)$ | Direct from % grade | N | | 4 | $\alpha = \arctan(\%G/100)$ | Angle from % grade | radians (convert to °) | | 5 | $P_g = F_g \cdot v$ | Grade-climbing power requirement | W | | 6 | $E_g = M g \sin(\alpha) \cdot d$ | Grade-climbing energy over distance $d$ | J | | 7 | $\cos(\alpha) = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2(\alpha)}$ | Normal force reduction factor | dimensionless | | 8 | $N = M g \cos(\alpha)$ | Normal reaction on slope | N | | 9 | $C_g = \sin(\alpha) \approx \%G/100$ | **Grade coefficient** (dimensionless) | — | | 10 | $F_{g,\text{net}} = M g (\sin\alpha + C_r \cos\alpha)$ | Combined grade + rolling resistance | N | --- ### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility 1. **EV Range Estimation on Hilly Terrain:** Tesla, BYD, and Tata Motors use $F_g$ models in their onboard range predictors. A 5% sustained grade can reduce EV range by **15–25%** compared to flat-road driving. 2. **Hybrid Control Strategy:** Toyota Hybrid Synergy Drive uses grade information (from GPS + barometric sensor) to pre-charge the HV battery before anticipated climbs, ensuring adequate power margin for $F_g$. 3. **Highway Design (IRC Standards in India):** Maximum grade on NH/SH is capped at **4–6%** in plains and **6–7%** in hilly terrain — a direct consequence of $F_g$ dictating truck/climb performance. 4. **Regenerative Braking Limits on Downgrade:** $F_g$ (with negative sign) is the "free energy" source; the regen system must limit negative torque to maintain brake-feel and stability. ## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ### 3.1 Derivation I — Exact Grading Resistance from Newton's Second Law **Starting Point — Free-Body Diagram on an Incline:** Consider a vehicle of mass $M$ on a road inclined at angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal. The vehicle moves up the slope at constant velocity $v$ (steady-state, no acceleration). **Step 1:** Identify all forces acting on the vehicle along the direction of motion (parallel to slope): - Tractive effort $F_t$ (forward, up the slope) - Grading resistance $F_g$ (backward, down the slope) - Rolling resistance $F_{rr}$ (backward) - Aerodynamic drag $F_{ad}$ (backward) **Step 2:** Apply Newton's Second Law in the slope-parallel direction at steady state (no acceleration, so $\sum F = 0$): $$F_t - F_g - F_{rr} - F_{ad} = 0$$ **Step 3:** Isolate the grading-resistance term for analytical clarity. The weight $W = M g$ acts vertically downward. Its component parallel to the slope (pointing down the incline) is found by projecting $W$ onto the slope-parallel unit vector. The slope-parallel unit vector (pointing up the slope) is: $$\hat{u}_{\parallel} = \cos(\alpha)\,\hat{i} + \sin(\alpha)\,\hat{j}$$ The weight vector is: $$\vec{W} = -M g \,\hat{j}$$ **Step 4:** Compute the projection (dot product): $$\vec{W} \cdot \hat{u}_{\parallel} = -M g \cdot \sin(\alpha)$$ **Step 5:** The grading resistance is the magnitude of this component (opposing the up-slope direction): $$\boxed{F_g = M \cdot g \cdot \sin(\alpha)}$$ **Step 6:** Verify dimensions: $[M] = \text{kg}$, $[g] = \text{m/s}^2$, $[\sin\alpha] = \text{dimensionless}$ $$[F_g] = \text{kg} \cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} = \text{N} \quad \checkmark$$ **Step 7:** Boundary check: - If $\alpha = 0°$: $F_g = 0$ (level road) ✓ - If $\alpha = 90°$: $F_g = M g$ (vertical wall — entire weight pulls down) ✓ - If $\alpha = 30°$: $F_g = 0.5 M g$ (half the weight acts along the slope) ✓ --- ### 3.2 Derivation II — Grading Resistance in Terms of Percentage Grade **Step 1:** From civil engineering definition: $$\text{Grade (\%)} = 100 \cdot \tan(\alpha)$$ **Step 2:** Solve for $\tan(\alpha)$: $$\tan(\alpha) = \frac{\text{Grade (\%)}}{100} = \frac{\%G}{100}$$ **Step 3:** Apply the small-angle approximation $\sin(\alpha) \approx \tan(\alpha)$ (valid for $\alpha \le 10°$ i.e., grade $\le 17.6\%$): $$F_g = M g \sin(\alpha) \approx M g \tan(\alpha)$$ **Step 4:** Substitute: $$\boxed{F_g \approx M \cdot g \cdot \frac{\%G}{100} = \frac{M \cdot g \cdot \%G}{100}}$$ **Step 5:** Engineering shortcut form (for a 1% grade): $$F_g = 0.01 \cdot M g \quad \text{per 1\% grade}$$ **Step 6:** Numerical example — A 1500 kg EV on a 5% grade: $$F_g = 0.01 \times 1500 \times 9.81 \times 5 = 735.75 \text{ N}$$ --- ### 3.3 Derivation III — Grading Power & Energy Requirements **Step 1:** Mechanical power required to overcome grade resistance at constant speed $v$: $$P_g = F_g \cdot v = M g \sin(\alpha) \cdot v$$ **Step 2:** Energy required to climb a distance $d$ up the slope: $$E_g = F_g \cdot d = M g \sin(\alpha) \cdot d$$ **Step 3:** Alternatively, using the **vertical climb height** $h = d \cdot \sin(\alpha)$: $$E_g = M g h$$ This is the classic **gravitational potential energy** equation — independent of the path taken. **Step 4:** Practical unit conversions: - Energy in Wh: $E_g [\text{Wh}] = \dfrac{M g h}{3600}$ - Energy in kWh: $E_g [\text{kWh}] = \dfrac{M g h}{3.6 \times 10^6}$ **Step 5:** Numerical sanity check — A 1500 kg EV climbing 100 m vertically: $$E_g = 1500 \times 9.81 \times 100 = 1.4715 \times 10^6 \text{ J} = 0.4088 \text{ kWh}$$ A typical 60 kWh EV battery could deliver this climb about **147 times** before depletion — illustrating how gravity is a "small" energy reservoir compared to rolling/aero losses on long drives. --- ### 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Effect of Grade on Resistances Let $M = 1500$ kg, $g = 9.81$ m/s², $C_r = 0.012$ (typical car tire). | Grade % | $\alpha$ (°) | $F_g$ (N) | $F_{rr}$ (N) | $F_g / W$ (%) | |:-------:|:------------:|:---------:|:------------:|:-------------:| | 0% | 0.00° | 0.00 | 176.6 | 0.00% | | 2% | 1.15° | 294.2 | 176.3 | 2.00% | | 5% | 2.86° | 735.8 | 175.6 | 5.00% | | 10% | 5.71° | 1471.5 | 173.0 | 10.00% | | 20% | 11.31° | 2943.0 | 165.5 | 20.00% | | 30% | 16.70° | 4414.5 | 153.6 | 30.00% | > [!IMPORTANT] > **Key Insight:** Grading resistance grows **linearly with % grade**, while rolling resistance decreases only slightly (because $\cos\alpha < 1$). On steep grades, $F_g$ is the **dominant resistance** by an order of magnitude. ## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ### 4.1 Mermaid Block Diagram — Free-Body Analysis on a Slope ```mermaid graph TD V1["VEHICLE OF MASS M

F_g = M.g.sin alpha

F_t = F_g + F_rr + F_ad"]:::tractive V8["BATTERY / FUEL

In the actual physical free-body diagram, the **weight vector** $W = Mg$ points straight down, while the **grade force** $F_g$ is its projection along the slope (down-slope direction). The angle $\alpha$ is measured between the road surface and the horizontal. ## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap --- ### 📝 PART A — Short-Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) #### **Q1. Define grading resistance. Derive its expression for a vehicle moving on an inclined road.** *`[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, OEEET722]`* **Model Answer (3 marks):** **Definition (1 mark):** Grading resistance is the component of the vehicle's weight that acts parallel to the road surface in the direction opposing motion, when the vehicle travels on a sloped road. **Derivation (2 marks):** For a vehicle of mass $M$ on a road inclined at angle $\alpha$, the weight $W = Mg$ acts vertically downward. Resolving it parallel to the slope: $$F_g = M g \sin(\alpha)$$ For small angles, $\sin\alpha \approx \tan\alpha \approx \alpha_{\text{rad}}$: $$F_g \approx M g \tan(\alpha) = 0.01 \cdot M g \cdot (\%G)$$ --- #### **Q2. How does the percentage grade of a road relate to the angle of inclination? State the small-angle approximation used for grading resistance calculations.** *`[KTU University Exam – May 2024, OEEET722]`* **Model Answer (3 marks):** The percentage grade is defined as: $$\%G = 100 \cdot \tan(\alpha) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \alpha = \arctan(\%G / 100)$$ **Small-angle approximation (KTU standard):** For $\alpha \le 10°$ (i.e., grade $\le 17.6\%$): $$\sin(\alpha) \approx \tan(\alpha) \approx \alpha \text{ (in radians)}$$ This yields the simplified form: $F_g \approx 0.01 \cdot M g \cdot (\%G)$. --- ### 📝 PART B — Long-Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, with Internal Choice) #### **Question A: Derivation + Numerical** *`[KTU University Exam – Model Paper, OEEET722]`* **(a) Derive the expression for the grading resistance experienced by a vehicle of mass $M$ moving up a road of slope $\alpha$. State the assumptions made. (7 marks)** **Step-by-Step Model Solution:** **Step 1 — Free Body Diagram (1 mark):** Draw a vehicle of mass $M$ on a road inclined at angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal. Show the weight vector $W = Mg$ acting vertically downward through the center of gravity. **Step 2 — Force Resolution (2 marks):** Resolve the weight into two components: - Along the slope (downward direction): $W \sin(\alpha) = M g \sin(\alpha)$ - Perpendicular to the slope: $W \cos(\alpha) = M g \cos(\alpha)$ **Step 3 — Apply Newton's Second Law (2 marks):** For the vehicle moving up the slope at constant velocity, sum of forces parallel to the slope equals zero: $$F_t - F_g - F_{rr} - F_{ad} = 0$$ The grading resistance term: $$F_g = M g \sin(\alpha)$$ **Step 4 — Assumptions (1 mark):** 1. Road is a straight, rigid plane inclined at constant angle $\alpha$. 2. Vehicle moves at constant velocity (no acceleration). 3. Air resistance and rolling resistance are neglected (treated separately). 4. Center of gravity lies on the road centerline. **Step 5 — Engineering Form (1 mark):** Using the small-angle approximation and percentage grade: $$F_g = 0.01 \cdot M g \cdot (\%G) \quad \text{where } \%G = 100 \tan(\alpha)$$ --- **(b) A passenger car of mass 1800 kg climbs a 6% grade at a constant speed of 60 km/h. Calculate: (i) the grading resistance, (ii) the grade-climbing power, and (iii) the energy required per km. (7 marks)** **Given:** - $M = 1800$ kg - Grade = 6% - $v = 60$ km/h $= 16.667$ m/s - $g = 9.81$ m/s² **Step (i) — Grading Resistance (2 marks):** $$F_g = 0.01 \cdot M \cdot g \cdot (\%G) = 0.01 \times 1800 \times 9.81 \times 6$$ $$F_g = 1059.48 \text{ N} \approx 1059.5 \text{ N}$$ **Step (ii) — Grade-Climbing Power (2 marks):** $$P_g = F_g \cdot v = 1059.48 \times 16.667$$ $$P_g = 17{,}658 \text{ W} \approx 17.66 \text{ kW}$$ **Step (iii) — Energy per km (3 marks):** Distance $d = 1$ km $= 1000$ m $$E_g = F_g \cdot d = 1059.48 \times 1000 = 1.059 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$$ Convert to kWh: $$E_g = \frac{1.059 \times 10^6}{3.6 \times 10^6} = 0.2942 \text{ kWh per km}$$ > [!NOTE] > **Interpretation:** The car needs about **0.29 kWh per km** *just to fight gravity*. A typical EV consumes 0.15–0.20 kWh/km on flat roads — so this climb **doubles** the energy demand per km. --- #### **Question B: Alternative — Conceptual + Numerical** *`[KTU University Exam – Supplementary, OEEET722]`* **(a) Explain the significance of grading resistance in the design of electric and hybrid vehicles. Discuss how the sign of grading resistance affects regenerative braking. (7 marks)** **Model Solution:** **Step 1 — Definition Recap (1 mark):** Grading resistance is $F_g = M g \sin(\alpha)$ — the gravity component along the slope. **Step 2 — Significance for EV/HEV Design (3 marks):** - **Battery sizing:** On mountainous routes, designers must size the battery to sustain continuous grade-climbing without thermal overload. - **Motor torque:** The traction motor must deliver peak torque sufficient to overcome worst-case $F_g$ + $F_{rr} + F_{ad}$ on the steepest expected grade. - **Thermal management:** Sustained uphill draws high current → battery heating → cooling system design. - **Drive-cycle planning:** WLTP and Indian Drive Cycle (IDC) include grade profiles to simulate real-world loads. **Step 3 — Effect of Sign on Regenerative Braking (3 marks):** - **Uphill ($F_g > 0$):** Grading resistance opposes motion — motor draws energy from the battery. - **Downhill ($F_g < 0$):** Gravity *assists* motion — the motor can act as a generator, recovering kinetic + potential energy. - **Regen limit:** On very steep downhills, $F_g$ can exceed the regen system's capacity → friction brakes must engage to maintain safe speed and prevent motor-generator overspeed. --- **(b) An electric bus of mass 12,000 kg operates on a route that includes a 2 km stretch of 4% upgrade followed by a 1 km stretch of 8% downgrade. If the bus travels at a constant 40 km/h, compute: (i) the total grading-resistance force on the upgrade, (ii) the total energy consumed on the upgrade, and (iii) the energy recovered (assuming 60% regen efficiency) on the downgrade. (7 marks)** **Given:** - $M = 12{,}000$ kg - Upgrade: $d_1 = 2$ km, grade $G_1 = +4\%$ - Downgrade: $d_2 = 1$ km, grade $G_2 = -8\%$ - $v = 40$ km/h - $g = 9.81$ m/s² - Regen efficiency $\eta = 0.60$ **Step (i) — Grading Resistance on Upgrade (2 marks):** $$F_{g1} = 0.01 \times 12{,}000 \times 9.81 \times 4 = 4708.8 \text{ N} \approx 4.71 \text{ kN}$$ **Step (ii) — Energy Consumed on Upgrade (2 marks):** $$E_{\text{consumed}} = F_{g1} \cdot d_1 = 4708.8 \times 2000 = 9.4176 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$$ $$E_{\text{consumed}} = 2.616 \text{ kWh}$$ **Step (iii) — Energy Recovered on Downgrade (3 marks):** Grading resistance on downgrade (now *assisting* motion): $$F_{g2} = 0.01 \times 12{,}000 \times 9.81 \times 8 = 9417.6 \text{ N}$$ Available gravitational energy on downgrade: $$E_{\text{down}} = F_{g2} \cdot d_2 = 9417.6 \times 1000 = 9.4176 \times 10^6 \text{ J} = 2.616 \text{ kWh}$$ Energy recovered (60% regen efficiency): $$E_{\text{recovered}} = \eta \times E_{\text{down}} = 0.60 \times 2.616 = 1.570 \text{ kWh}$$ > [!NOTE] > **Net Result:** The bus consumes 2.616 kWh uphill and recovers 1.570 kWh downhill → **net 1.046 kWh** per cycle. This illustrates why hilly routes still favor hybrids over pure EVs (in the absence of large batteries). --- > [!WARNING] > **🚨 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls on Grading-Resistance Problems:** > 1. **Unit mismatch:** $v$ must be in **m/s** for power calculations in Watts. Students often plug in km/h directly, getting answers off by a factor of 3.6. > 2. **Angle vs. grade confusion:** Always use $\sin(\alpha)$ for the *exact* formula. For percentage grade, the form is $F_g = 0.01 \cdot M g \cdot \%G$, **not** $F_g = M g \cdot \%G$ (missing the /100). > 3. **Forgetting the small-angle approximation:** If a problem gives $\alpha = 30°$, do **not** use the percentage-grade shortcut. Use $F_g = M g \sin(30°) = 0.5 M g$ exactly. > 4. **Sign of grade:** On downgrades, the "energy recovered" calculation must include the regen efficiency factor. Many students write $E_{\text{recovered}} = F_g \cdot d$ without multiplying by $\eta$. > 5. **Mixing $M$ (mass) with $W$ (weight):** $F_g$ uses **mass** in kg, **not** weight in N. Substituting weight $W = Mg$ directly leads to $F_g = Mg^2 \sin\alpha$ — a classic 3-mark loss. --- ### 🧠 TOPIC RECAP & RAPID REVISION CHECKLIST > [!IMPORTANT] > **High-Yield Points to Memorize Before KTU Exam:** - ✅ **Core formula:** $F_g = M g \sin(\alpha)$ — exact; or $F_g = 0.01 \cdot M g \cdot (\%G)$ — small-angle engineering form. - ✅ **Percentage grade relation:** $\%G = 100 \tan(\alpha)$; $\alpha = \arctan(\%G/100)$. - ✅ **Small-angle validity:** Approximation holds for $\alpha \le 10°$ (grade $\le 17.6\%$). - ✅ **Sign convention:** $F_g > 0$ on upgrade, $F_g < 0$ on downgrade. - ✅ **Normal force on slope:** $N = M g \cos(\alpha)$ — used in rolling resistance. - ✅ **Grade-climbing power:** $P_g = F_g \cdot v$ (with $v$ in m/s). - ✅ **Grade-climbing energy:** $E_g = M g h$ where $h$ is the vertical height gained. - ✅ **Position in total resistance equation:** $F_t = F_{rr} + F_{ad} + F_g + F_i$. - ✅ **EV/HEV relevance:** $F_g$ governs battery sizing, motor torque rating, regen-braking design, and drive-cycle energy budgeting. - ✅ **Boundary checks:** $F_g = 0$ at $\alpha = 0°$; $F_g = Mg$ at $\alpha = 90°$. - ✅ **Energy unit conversions:** $1 \text{ kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$. **One-Line Definition to Write in Exam:** > *"Grading resistance is the down-slope component of a vehicle's weight, given by $F_g = M g \sin(\alpha)$, which the powertrain must overcome during upgrades and which regenerative braking can partially recover on downgrades."*

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** OEEET722 - HYBRID AND ELECTRIC VEHICLES > - **Module:** Module 1 > - **Topic:** Vehicle Acceleration # SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Terminology) **Vehicle Acceleration** in the context of performance analysis of conventional, hybrid, and electric vehicles is defined as the rate of change of vehicle velocity with respect to time, governed by the **Fundamental Tractive Force Equation** of vehicle dynamics. It is derived from Newton's Second Law applied to a vehicle moving along a road with grade: > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU Board Definition:** *The tractive force (F_t) required at the wheel-road interface must overcome the sum of four resistive forces: Rolling Resistance (F_rr), Aerodynamic Drag (F_ad), Hill Climbing Force (F_hc), and the Linear Acceleration Force (F_la). The ability of the powertrain to deliver this tractive force determines the vehicle's acceleration capability, which is a primary design specification for HEVs and EVs.* $$\boxed{F_t = F_{rr} + F_{ad} + F_{hc} + F_{la}}$$ The resulting **acceleration** is given by: $$a = \frac{F_t - (F_{rr} + F_{ad} + F_{hc})}{m \cdot (1 + \delta)}$$ where $\delta$ is the **rotational inertia factor** (mass factor) that accounts for the equivalent mass of rotating drivetrain components (wheels, gears, motor rotor). --- ## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Plain English Intuition > [!NOTE] > **Real-World Analogy — "Pushing a Stroller Up a Slope"** > > Imagine you are pushing a loaded baby stroller up a slight hill on a windy day: > - **Weight of stroller + baby** → analogous to **Vehicle Mass (m)** > - **Friction between wheels and rough road** → analogous to **Rolling Resistance (F_rr)** > - **Wind pushing against you** → analogous to **Aerodynamic Drag (F_ad)** > - **Height of the hill you must climb** → analogous to **Hill Climbing Force (F_hc)** > - **The extra burst of force to make it go faster** → analogous to **Acceleration Force (F_la)** > > Just as the force you apply on the handle equals the *sum* of all these opposing effects (plus the force needed to speed it up), the **tractive force from the EV motor must equal the sum of all resistances plus the acceleration force.** This is why EVs use high-torque motors from rest — to overcome all four terms simultaneously during launch. --- ## 1.3 Key Physical Constants & Standard Metrics | Symbol | Quantity | Standard Value / Unit | Notes | |:---:|:---|:---|:---| | $\rho$ | Air density | **1.2 kg/m³** | At sea level, 25°C | | $g$ | Gravitational acceleration | **9.81 m/s²** | Standard earth gravity | | $C_d$ | Coefficient of drag | 0.25 – 0.40 | Modern sedans ~ 0.25–0.30 | | $f$ | Coefficient of rolling resistance | 0.008 – 0.015 | Car tire on asphalt ~ 0.01 | | $A_f$ | Frontal area | 1.7 – 2.5 m² | Mid-size sedan ~ 2.0 m² | | $\delta$ | Rotational inertia factor | 0.05 – 0.15 | EV: typically 0.1 | # SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 Decomposition of the Four Opposing Forces The vehicle dynamics model treats the car as a single rigid mass moving along a slope, with all rotational inertia lumped into an effective mass factor. Each resistive force is analyzed independently: ### 2.1.1 Rolling Resistance (F_rr) Rolling resistance arises from the **hysteresis losses** in the tire rubber as it deforms while rolling, plus minor contributions from wheel bearing friction, brake drag, and tire scrub. It is modeled as proportional to the **normal load** on the tire (i.e., the vehicle weight component perpendicular to the road surface). $$F_{rr} = W \cdot f \cdot \cos(\alpha)$$ where: - $W = m \cdot g$ → total vehicle weight in Newtons - $f$ → coefficient of rolling resistance (dimensionless) - $\alpha$ → road grade angle (radians) > **Why it matters in HEVs/EVs:** Electric vehicles are generally heavier than ICE vehicles due to battery mass. Hence rolling resistance is **proportionally higher** — a critical design consideration. ### 2.1.2 Aerodynamic Drag (F_ad) Aerodynamic drag is the **viscous + pressure resistance** the vehicle body experiences while moving through still air. The kinetic energy imparted to the air parcels goes into turbulence (pressure drag) and viscous shear (skin friction). $$F_{ad} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \rho \cdot C_d \cdot A_f \cdot v^2$$ where $v$ is the vehicle velocity in m/s. Note the **velocity-squared dependence** — this is why drag dominates highway fuel economy and limits top speed. > **KTU High-Yield Insight:** For EVs, regenerative braking recovers part of this kinetic energy when decelerating from highway speeds — a major efficiency win. ### 2.1.3 Hill Climbing Force (F_hc) The component of vehicle weight acting along the slope that opposes forward motion: $$F_{hc} = W \cdot \sin(\alpha) \approx W \cdot \tan(\alpha) \quad \text{(for small }\alpha\text{)}$$ The **percent grade** is defined as: $$\text{Grade (\%)} = 100 \times \tan(\alpha)$$ A 6% grade means $\tan(\alpha) = 0.06$, giving $F_{hc} \approx 0.06 \cdot W$. ### 2.1.4 Linear Acceleration Force (F_la) By Newton's Second Law, the force to produce a forward acceleration of $a$ (m/s²) on an effective mass $(m + m_i) = m \cdot (1+\delta)$: $$F_{la} = m \cdot (1 + \delta) \cdot a$$ The rotational inertia factor $\delta$ accounts for the kinetic energy stored in rotating driveline components (wheels, motor rotor, transmission gears). A common approximation: $$\delta \approx \frac{J_w + J_m \cdot n^2 \cdot \eta_g}{m \cdot r^2}$$ where $J_w$ = wheel inertia, $J_m$ = motor inertia, $n$ = gear ratio, $\eta_g$ = gear efficiency, $r$ = tire radius. --- ## 2.2 Power Requirement at the Wheels The **tractive power** required to propel the vehicle at a given speed is the scalar product of tractive force and velocity: $$P_t = F_t \cdot v = (F_{rr} + F_{ad} + F_{hc} + F_{la}) \cdot v$$ Since $F_{ad} \propto v^2$, the aerodynamic power requirement scales as $v^3$ — a **cubic dependence** that governs high-speed EV range. --- ## 2.3 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet > [!NOTE] > **MASTER REFERENCE TABLE — Memorize before the exam.** | # | Formula | Description | Units / Notes | |:---:|:---|:---|:---| | 1 | $F_{rr} = m \cdot g \cdot f \cdot \cos\alpha$ | Rolling resistance force | N (≈ $mgf$ for level road) | | 2 | $F_{ad} = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho C_d A_f v^2$ | Aerodynamic drag | N, velocity-squared | | 3 | $F_{hc} = m \cdot g \cdot \sin\alpha \approx m \cdot g \cdot G$ | Grade climbing force | N, $G$ = grade (decimal) | | 4 | $F_{la} = m(1+\delta) \cdot a$ | Linear acceleration force | N, effective mass | | 5 | $F_t = F_{rr} + F_{ad} + F_{hc} + F_{la}$ | Master tractive force equation | N | | 6 | $a = \dfrac{F_t - (F_{rr}+F_{ad}+F_{hc})}{m(1+\delta)}$ | Resolved acceleration | m/s² | | 7 | $P_t = F_t \cdot v$ | Tractive power at wheels | W (J/s) | | 8 | $\eta_{total} = \dfrac{P_{wheel}}{P_{battery}}$ | Drivetrain efficiency | % (EV: 85–92%) | | 9 | $t_a = \displaystyle\int_{v_1}^{v_2} \dfrac{m(1+\delta) \cdot v \, dv}{F_t(v) - (F_{rr}+F_{hc})}$ | Acceleration time | seconds | | 10 | $\delta \approx 0.05 + 0.002 \cdot n_{gear}$ | Empirical inertia factor (cars) | dimensionless | # SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Derivation: Acceleration Time from v₁ to v₂ **Objective:** Derive the closed-form expression for the time taken by a vehicle to accelerate from initial speed $v_1$ to final speed $v_2$ on a **level road** (so $F_{hc} = 0$). ### Step 1 — Set up Newton's Second Law From the tractive force balance, the net force producing acceleration is: $$F_{net} = F_t - F_{rr} - F_{ad} = m(1+\delta) \cdot a = m(1+\delta) \cdot \frac{dv}{dt}$$ ### Step 2 — Isolate dt Rearranging for $dt$: $$dt = \frac{m(1+\delta) \cdot dv}{F_t - F_{rr} - F_{ad}}$$ ### Step 3 — Substitute F_ad (function of v) Since $F_{ad} = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho C_d A_f v^2$, let $C_0 = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho C_d A_f$, so $F_{ad} = C_0 v^2$: $$dt = \frac{m(1+\delta) \cdot dv}{F_t - m g f - C_0 v^2}$$ ### Step 4 — Integrate from v₁ to v₂ Assuming $F_t$ is constant (idealized maximum motor tractive force, e.g., peak torque region): $$t_a = \int_{v_1}^{v_2} \frac{m(1+\delta) \, dv}{F_t - mgf - C_0 v^2}$$ ### Step 5 — Closed-form result (using $\arctanh$ substitution) The integral yields a hyperbolic arctangent function. Let $D(v) = F_t - mgf - C_0 v^2$. Performing the partial fraction style integration: $$t_a = \frac{m(1+\delta)}{2\sqrt{C_0(F_t - mgf)}} \cdot \ln\!\left[ \frac{\sqrt{F_t - mgf} + \sqrt{C_0}\, v_2}{\sqrt{F_t - mgf} + \sqrt{C_0}\, v_1} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{F_t - mgf} - \sqrt{C_0}\, v_1}{\sqrt{F_t - mgf} - \sqrt{C_0}\, v_2} \right]$$ > **Engineering Utility:** This expression is used by EV design engineers to compute **0–100 km/h time**, a globally standard performance metric. Typical EVs achieve **3–7 seconds**. --- ## 3.2 Worked Numerical Example (Model Problem) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Sample Problem (KTU Board Style):** An electric vehicle with the following specifications is to be analyzed: > - Curb mass $m = 1500$ kg > - Rolling resistance coefficient $f = 0.012$ > - Drag coefficient $C_d = 0.28$ > - Frontal area $A_f = 2.1$ m² > - Rotational inertia factor $\delta = 0.10$ > - Maximum tractive force $F_t = 4500$ N (from motor at low speed) > - Operating conditions: **level road**, $v = 25$ m/s (≈ 90 km/h) > > **Find:** (a) Acceleration at 25 m/s, (b) Power required at the wheels, (c) Verify if motor has enough power for 30% grade climbing at 15 m/s. ### Part (a) — Acceleration at 25 m/s **Step 1: Calculate Rolling Resistance** $$F_{rr} = m \cdot g \cdot f = 1500 \times 9.81 \times 0.012 = 176.58 \text{ N}$$ **Step 2: Calculate Aerodynamic Drag** $$F_{ad} = 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 0.28 \times 2.1 \times 25^2$$ Performing the calculation explicitly: $$\begin{aligned} F_{ad} &= 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 0.28 \times 2.1 \times 625 \\ &= 0.6 \times 0.28 \times 2.1 \times 625 \\ &= 0.6 \times 0.588 \times 625 \\ &= 0.3528 \times 625 \\ &= 220.5 \text{ N} \end{aligned}$$ **Step 3: Hill Climbing Force on Level Road** $$F_{hc} = 0 \text{ N (since grade} = 0\text{)}$$ **Step 4: Solve for Acceleration** The net accelerating force is $F_t - F_{rr} - F_{ad} - F_{hc}$ divided by the effective mass: $$\begin{aligned} F_{net} &= F_t - F_{rr} - F_{ad} - F_{hc} \\ &= 4500 - 176.58 - 220.5 - 0 \\ &= 4102.92 \text{ N} \end{aligned}$$ Effective mass: $$m_{eff} = m(1 + \delta) = 1500 \times 1.10 = 1650 \text{ kg}$$ Therefore: $$a = \frac{4102.92}{1650} = 2.487 \text{ m/s}^2 \approx 2.49 \text{ m/s}^2$$ ### Part (b) — Power Required at the Wheels $$P_t = F_t \cdot v = 4500 \times 25 = 112{,}500 \text{ W} = 112.5 \text{ kW}$$ This represents the **wheel-side** power demand. Accounting for a typical EV drivetrain efficiency of 90%, the **battery-side** power draw would be: $$P_{batt} = \frac{112.5}{0.90} \approx 125 \text{ kW}$$ ### Part (c) — Grade Climbing at 15 m/s on 30% Slope For 30% grade: $\tan\alpha = 0.30$, so $\sin\alpha \approx 0.287$ and $\cos\alpha \approx 0.954$. **Rolling resistance (corrected for slope):** $$F_{rr} = 1500 \times 9.81 \times 0.012 \times 0.954 = 168.49 \text{ N}$$ **Aerodynamic drag at 15 m/s:** $$\begin{aligned} F_{ad} &= 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 0.28 \times 2.1 \times 15^2 \\ &= 0.3528 \times 225 \\ &= 79.38 \text{ N} \end{aligned}$$ **Hill climbing force:** $$F_{hc} = 1500 \times 9.81 \times 0.287 = 4223.21 \text{ N}$$ **Total resisting force:** $$F_{resist} = 168.49 + 79.38 + 4223.21 = 4471.08 \text{ N}$$ **Net accelerating force available:** $$F_{net} = 4500 - 4471.08 = 28.92 \text{ N}$$ **Resulting acceleration:** $$a = \frac{28.92}{1650} = 0.01753 \text{ m/s}^2$$ > **Conclusion:** The motor can barely maintain speed (near-zero acceleration) on a 30% grade at 15 m/s. The EV has **insufficient margin** to climb such a steep grade while still accelerating. --- ## 3.3 Analytical Comparison Matrix — ICE vs Hybrid vs Electric | Parameter | Conventional ICE | Hybrid (HEV) | Battery Electric (BEV) | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | Torque at 0 rpm | **0 (stalls)** | **High (motor assist)** | **Maximum (peak torque)** | | 0–100 km/h | 8–12 s | 6–9 s | **3–7 s** | | Power at top speed | Limited by ICE redline | Extended via motor | **High (single gear)** | | Acceleration consistency | Drops with gear shifts | Smooth (CVT/e-CVT) | **Smoothest (no shift)** | | Regen braking recovery | None | Partial (10–25%) | **High (20–40%)** | | Drivetrain inertia factor $\delta$ | 0.05–0.10 | 0.07–0.12 | **0.05–0.10** | > **Key Takeaway:** BEVs deliver **peak torque at zero rpm**, eliminating the launch delay inherent in ICE vehicles — this is the single biggest contributor to superior acceleration performance. # SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Vehicle Dynamics — Force Interaction Block Diagram This block diagram illustrates how the four resistance forces combine at the **wheel-road interface** to balance the **tractive force** delivered by the EV drivetrain. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Battery Pack
