# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

A **DC Motor Drive** is an integrated electromechanical power conversion system comprising a Direct Current (DC) machine, a power electronic converter (DC-DC chopper or rectifier), and a closed-loop controller, used to deliver variable speed and variable torque to a mechanical load. In the context of **Hybrid and Electric Vehicles (HEVs/EVs)**, a DC motor drive converts stored electrical energy from the battery pack into precisely controlled mechanical traction power at the wheels.

The mathematical operating region of any DC motor drive is governed by three foundational equations:

$$V_a = E_b + I_a R_a$$

$$E_b = K_e \cdot \phi \cdot \omega$$

$$T = K_t \cdot \phi \cdot I_a$$

Where:
- $V_a$ = Armature terminal voltage (Volts)
- $E_b$ = Back-EMF (Volts)
- $I_a$ = Armature current (Amperes)
- $R_a$ = Armature resistance (Ohms)
- $K_e$ = Voltage constant (V·s/rad)
- $K_t$ = Torque constant (N·m/A)
- $\phi$ = Flux per pole (Weber)
- $\omega$ = Angular speed (rad/s)
- $T$ = Electromagnetic torque (N·m)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Board Examiner Note:** In SI units, $K_e = K_t$. Examiners frequently award or deduct **2 marks** solely on this dimensional equivalence.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The Bicycle Dynamo in Reverse

Imagine a **bicycle dynamo** (a small DC generator). When you spin its wheel, it produces voltage — that is *back-EMF opposing rotation*. Now reverse the process: feed it DC current from a battery, and it spins a wheel. This is a DC motor.

A **DC motor drive** is essentially the same setup, but with a *throttle*. The accelerator pedal in an EV is not a mechanical cable; it is a **potentiometer** that sends a 0–5 V reference signal to a controller. The controller then regulates the battery voltage reaching the motor — just like opening or closing a water tap. More voltage → more speed; more current → more torque.

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuitive Summary:** A DC motor drive is the "throttle-to-wheel translator" of an electric vehicle. The battery supplies raw DC, the chopper/controller modulates it, and the motor converts it into rotary motion.

## 1.3 Standard Physical Constants & Performance Metrics

| Metric | Typical EV Traction Value |
|---|---|
| Specific Power (Power-to-weight) | **0.1 – 0.5 kW/kg** |
| Peak Efficiency | **85 – 92 %** |
| Base Speed | **1500 – 3000 rpm** |
| Constant Power Speed Range | **3 : 1 to 4 : 1** |
| Maximum Torque (per unit) | **2 – 3 × Rated Torque** |

# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Classification of DC Motors Used in EV/HEV Applications

DC motors used in traction are classified by **field winding connection**, which directly determines the torque-speed characteristic — the single most important property for vehicle propulsion.

### A. Separately Excited DC Motor (SEDM)
- Field winding is supplied from an **independent DC source**.
- Flux $\phi$ is controlled independently of armature current.
- **Application:** Historically used in electric forklifts, modern small EVs, and laboratory drives. Excellent for **regenerative braking** because $\phi$ can be reduced to push speed above base.

### B. Series DC Motor (SDM)
- Field winding connected in **series** with the armature.
- $\phi \propto I_a$ (until magnetic saturation).
- **Application:** Traditional choice for EVs due to enormous starting torque — exactly what a vehicle needs at standstill / hill climb.

### C. Shunt DC Motor
- Field winding in **parallel** with the armature.
- $\phi$ is approximately constant.
- **Application:** Rare in modern EVs (poor starting torque), but appears in auxiliary drives (cooling fans, pumps).

### D. Compound DC Motor
- Hybrid of series and shunt field.
- Used in **heavy traction locomotives** (diesel-electric locomotives like Indian Railways WAP-5, WAG-9 historically used compound DC traction motors before the transition to three-phase AC).

### E. Permanent Magnet DC Motor (PMDC)
- Field produced by **rare-earth permanent magnets** (NdFeB).
- Compact, high efficiency, no field copper losses.
- **Application:** Modern small EVs, e-bikes, golf carts, two-wheelers.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU High-Yield Point:** When asked *"Why are series DC motors preferred for traction?"*, the model answer must contain three keywords: **(1) High starting torque (∝ I²)**, **(2) Self-protection against overload**, **(3) Naturally suited for variable-speed traction loads.**

## 2.2 Why DC Motors in HEVs/EVs? The Engineering Trade-off

> [!NOTE]
> **Modern Reality Check:** Most 2024+ production EVs (Tesla Model 3, Hyundai Ioniq 5, Tata Nexon EV) use **3-phase AC induction** or **PMSM (Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor)** drives — *not* DC. However, DC drives remain in the KTU syllabus because (a) many low-speed EVs and two-wheelers in India still use BLDC/PMDC, (b) the pedagogical foundation of motor drives begins with DC machines, and (c) regenerative braking logic is conceptually identical.

| Feature | DC Motor Drive | AC Motor Drive |
|---|---|---|
| Controller complexity | Simple (1 quadrant chopper) | Complex (SVPWM, FOC) |
| Starting torque | Very high (series) | High (with vector control) |
| Maintenance | High (brushes, commutator) | Very low (brushless) |
| Efficiency at rated load | 85–90 % | 92–97 % |
| Cost (controller) | Low | Moderate–High |
| Suitability for HEV | Limited (small vehicles) | Industry standard |

## 2.3 Operating Quadrants of a DC Motor Drive

A complete drive must operate in **four quadrants** to support real driving:

| Quadrant | Speed $\omega$ | Torque $T$ | Driving Mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | + (Forward) | + (Forward) | Forward motoring (acceleration) |
| II | + (Forward) | − (Braking) | Forward regenerative braking |
| III | − (Reverse) | − (Reverse) | Reverse motoring |
| IV | − (Reverse) | + (Braking) | Reverse regenerative braking |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 14-Mark Favourite:** Questions on *"Explain the four-quadrant operation of a DC motor drive with chopper circuits"* are a **guaranteed appearance** in End Semester Examinations.

## 2.4 KTU Formula Cheat Sheet

| # | Equation | Physical Meaning | Typical Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $V_a = E_b + I_a R_a$ | Armature voltage equation (KVL) | All KTU numericals |
| 2 | $E_b = K_e \phi \omega$ | Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction | Speed calculation |
| 3 | $T = K_t \phi I_a$ | Lorentz force-based torque production | Torque/current calculation |
| 4 | $N = \dfrac{V_a - I_a R_a}{K_e \phi} \cdot \dfrac{60}{2\pi}$ | Speed in RPM | Speed regulation problems |
| 5 | $\omega = \dfrac{V_a - I_a R_a}{K_e \phi}$ | Speed in rad/s | Derivation base |
| 6 | $P_{developed} = T \cdot \omega = E_b \cdot I_a$ | Internal electromagnetic power | Power flow diagram |
| 7 | $P_{input} = V_a \cdot I_a$ | Electrical input power | Efficiency calculation |
| 8 | $\eta = \dfrac{E_b I_a}{V_a I_a} = 1 - \dfrac{I_a R_a}{V_a}$ | Efficiency expression | Efficiency problems |
| 9 | $\phi_{series} \propto I_a \Rightarrow T \propto I_a^2$ | Series motor torque law | Quadrant problems |
| 10 | $\dfrac{d\omega}{dT} = -\dfrac{R_a}{(K_e \phi)^2}$ | Slope of N-T characteristics | Stability analysis |

> [!WARNING]
> **Equation #10** is rarely taught in class but appears in KTU **Part C (14-mark) derivations**. Memorize it — it comes from differentiating $\omega = (V - I_a R_a) / K_e \phi$ and substituting $T = K_t \phi I_a$.

## 2.5 Real-World Utility in HEV/EV Engineering

1. **Traction Control**: A DC drive with closed-loop PI controller maintains exact wheel torque demanded by the driver.
2. **Regenerative Braking**: When the chopper is operated in boost mode, the motor acts as a generator, feeding current back to the battery — recovering **10–30 %** of kinetic energy.
3. **Battery Management Compatibility**: DC drives draw variable current but at varying voltage, allowing Battery Management Systems (BMS) to operate within the State-of-Charge (SOC) sweet spot.
4. **Auxiliary Loads**: Power windows, HVAC blowers, coolant pumps, and electronic power steering in many HEVs use small PMDC or BLDC drives.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation I — Speed Equation of a Separately Excited DC Motor (Starting from First Principles)

**Objective:** Derive the expression for angular speed $\omega$ in terms of $V_a$, $I_a$, $R_a$, $\phi$, and $K_e$.

### Step 1 — Apply Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to the armature loop
The armature circuit consists of the supply voltage $V_a$, the armature resistance $R_a$, the armature inductance $L_a$, and the induced back-EMF $E_b$.

$$V_a = I_a R_a + L_a \frac{dI_a}{dt} + E_b$$

### Step 2 — Assume steady-state operation
Under steady-state conditions, the current $I_a$ is no longer changing with time, hence $\dfrac{dI_a}{dt} = 0$. The transient inductance term vanishes.

$$V_a = I_a R_a + E_b$$

### Step 3 — Express back-EMF using Faraday's law
For a DC machine with $P$ poles, $Z$ total conductors, and $A$ parallel paths, the average back-EMF induced per conductor is the rate of cutting of flux. For a wave-wound armature ($A = 2$):

$$E_b = \frac{\phi Z N P}{60 A}$$

The combined machine constant $K_e$ is defined as $K_e = \dfrac{ZP}{60A}$, yielding:

$$E_b = K_e \cdot \phi \cdot N$$

where $N$ is in revolutions per minute (RPM).

### Step 4 — Convert RPM to angular speed in rad/s
By definition, $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi N}{60}$. Rearranging, $N = \dfrac{60 \omega}{2\pi}$. Substituting:

$$E_b = K_e \cdot \phi \cdot \frac{60 \omega}{2\pi} = \left(\frac{60 K_e}{2\pi}\right) \phi \omega$$

### Step 5 — Define a new constant $K_e'$ such that $E_b = K_e' \phi \omega$
Combining:

$$K_e' = \frac{60 K_e}{2\pi} = \frac{30 K_e}{\pi}$$

Therefore in SI units, $E_b = K_e' \phi \omega$. (For simplicity, most textbooks and KTU papers absorb this $30/\pi$ factor into the constant and write $E_b = K \phi \omega$.)

### Step 6 — Substitute $E_b$ back into the KVL equation

$$V_a = I_a R_a + K_e' \phi \omega$$

### Step 7 — Solve for $\omega$

$$K_e' \phi \omega = V_a - I_a R_a$$

$$\boxed{\omega = \frac{V_a - I_a R_a}{K_e' \phi}}$$

### Step 8 — Express in RPM form (preferred for KTU board answers)

$$\boxed{N = \frac{V_a - I_a R_a}{K_e \phi} \times \frac{60}{2\pi} = \frac{(V_a - I_a R_a) \times 60}{2 \pi K_e \phi}}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Conclusion:** The speed depends on **(a) applied voltage $V_a$**, **(b) armature current $I_a$ (i.e., load torque)**, **(c) flux $\phi$**, and **(d) machine constant $K_e$**. Two control strategies emerge from this single equation: **Armature Voltage Control** and **Flux Control** — both are KTU 14-mark favourites.

---

## 3.2 Derivation II — Torque Equation of a DC Motor

**Objective:** Derive $T = K_t \phi I_a$.

### Step 1 — Force on a single current-carrying conductor
A conductor of length $l$ carrying current $I$ in a magnetic field of flux density $B$ experiences a force:

$$F = B \cdot I \cdot l$$

### Step 2 — Express $B$ in terms of flux per pole
For a pole shoe of area $A_p$, the average flux density is $B = \phi / A_p$. Thus:

$$F = \frac{\phi}{A_p} \cdot I \cdot l$$

### Step 3 — Torque produced by a single conductor
If the conductor is at radius $r$ from the shaft:

$$F_{per\ cond} \cdot r = \frac{\phi \cdot I \cdot l \cdot r}{A_p}$$

### Step 4 — Total torque from all $Z$ conductors
Each conductor carries current $I_a / A$ (where $A$ is the number of parallel paths). Summing over all $Z$ conductors:

$$T = \frac{Z}{A} \cdot \frac{\phi \cdot I_a \cdot l \cdot r}{A_p}$$

### Step 5 — Define torque constant
The geometric terms $Z, l, r, A, A_p$ are constants of the machine. Group them as $K_t$:

$$K_t = \frac{Z \cdot l \cdot r}{A \cdot A_p}$$

### Step 6 — Final torque equation

$$\boxed{T = K_t \cdot \phi \cdot I_a}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> In **SI units**, the numerical value of $K_t$ equals that of $K_e'$ (the back-EMF constant in V·s/rad). This is not a coincidence — it follows directly from energy conservation ($P_{electrical} = P_{mechanical}$).

---

## 3.3 Derivation III — Torque-Speed Characteristic of a Separately Excited DC Motor

**Objective:** Derive the linear relationship $N$ vs $T$ that defines the motor's load line.

### Step 1 — Start from the speed equation
From Derivation I:

$$\omega = \frac{V_a - I_a R_a}{K_e' \phi}$$

### Step 2 — Express $I_a$ in terms of $T$ from Derivation II

$$I_a = \frac{T}{K_t \phi}$$

### Step 3 — Substitute into speed equation

$$\omega = \frac{V_a}{K_e' \phi} - \frac{R_a}{K_e' \phi} \cdot \frac{T}{K_t \phi}$$

### Step 4 — Use the SI identity $K_e' = K_t = K$

$$\omega = \frac{V_a}{K \phi} - \frac{R_a}{(K \phi)^2} \cdot T$$

### Step 5 — No-load speed ($T = 0$)

$$\omega_0 = \frac{V_a}{K \phi}$$

### Step 6 — Stall torque ($\omega = 0$)

$$T_{stall} = \frac{V_a \cdot K \phi}{R_a}$$

### Step 7 — Final linear characteristic

$$\boxed{\omega = \omega_0 \left( 1 - \frac{T}{T_{stall}} \right)}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Interpretation:** This is the equation of a **straight line** in the $\omega$–$T$ plane. It intercepts the $\omega$-axis at $\omega_0$ and the $T$-axis at $T_{stall}$. The slope $\dfrac{d\omega}{dT} = -\dfrac{R_a}{(K\phi)^2}$ is *negative* and very steep (high $K\phi$ → flatter curve, better speed regulation).

---

## 3.4 Derivation IV — Efficiency of a DC Motor Drive

### Step 1 — Electrical input power

$$P_{in} = V_a I_a$$

### Step 2 — Mechanical output power
Mechanical output = developed power − rotational losses (friction, windage, stray). At shaft:

$$P_{out} = T_{shaft} \cdot \omega$$

### Step 3 — Developed (air-gap) power
Air-gap power is the electromechanical conversion point:

$$P_{gap} = E_b I_a = T \cdot \omega$$

### Step 4 — Armature copper loss

$$P_{cu} = I_a^2 R_a$$

### Step 5 — Efficiency expression

$$\eta = \frac{E_b I_a}{V_a I_a} = \frac{E_b}{V_a} = \frac{V_a - I_a R_a}{V_a} = 1 - \frac{I_a R_a}{V_a}$$

### Step 6 — Condition for maximum efficiency
Differentiating with respect to $I_a$ and setting to zero gives:

$$\frac{d\eta}{dI_a} = -\frac{R_a}{V_a} = 0 \quad (\text{cannot be zero})$$

A more rigorous derivation considering variable armature voltage gives the **maximum efficiency condition**:

$$\boxed{E_b = \frac{V_a}{2} \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad I_a R_a = \frac{V_a}{2}}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Insight:** A DC motor (or any DC-DC converter) achieves **maximum efficiency at 50 % voltage drop across internal resistance** — a consequence of the square-law copper loss.

# SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Block Diagram — DC Motor Drive System in an EV

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    batt[Battery Pack DC Source] --> conv[Power Electronic Converter Chopper or DC-DC]
    conv --> ctrl[Controller ECU Level Signal]
    ctrl --> conv
    conv --> motor[DC Motor Armature + Field]
    motor --> shaft[Mechanical Shaft to Wheels]
    shaft --> load[Vehicle Load Variable]
    load --> fb[Tachogenerator Speed Feedback]
    fb --> ctrl
    motor --> fb2[Current Sensor Armature]
    fb2 --> ctrl
    motor -.-> regen[Regenerative Braking Path]
    regen -.-> batt
```

**Interpretation of the block diagram:**
- The **battery** (typically 48 V – 400 V Li-ion pack) supplies raw DC.
- The **chopper** is a high-frequency IGBT/MOSFET switch (e.g., 5–20 kHz) that modulates the average voltage.
- The **controller** is a microcontroller / DSP implementing a PI or fuzzy logic algorithm.
- **Tachogenerator** provides speed feedback (closed-loop).
- **Current sensor** provides torque-feedback (inner loop).
- **Regenerative path** returns energy to the battery during braking.

## 4.2 Schematic — Power Flow and Loss Diagram of a DC Motor

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    pin[Electrical Input Power V_a times I_a] --> pcu[Armature Copper Loss I_a squared R_a]
    pin --> pcore[Core Loss Hysteresis and Eddy Current]
    pcu --> pgap[Air Gap Power E_b times I_a]
    pcore --> pgap
    pgap --> pmec[Mechanical Power Developed T times omega]
    pmec --> pfric[Friction and Windage Loss]
    pmec --> pstray[Stray Load Loss]
    pfric --> pshaft[Shaft Output Power T_shaft times omega]
    pstray --> pshaft
```

## 4.3 Schematic — Four-Quadrant Operation of a DC Drive (Chopper-Based)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Q1[Quadrant I Forward Motoring]
        Q1F[T positive, omega positive]
    end
    subgraph Q2[Quadrant II Forward Braking]
        Q2F[T negative, omega positive]
    end
    subgraph Q3[Quadrant III Reverse Motoring]
        Q3F[T negative, omega negative]
    end
    subgraph Q4[Quadrant IV Reverse Braking]
        Q4F[T positive, omega negative]
    end
    Q1 -->|Driver releases accelerator| Q2
    Q2 -->|Reverse gear engaged| Q3
    Q3 -->|Reverse brake applied| Q4
    Q4 -->|Reset to forward| Q1
```

## 4.4 Functional Architecture — Speed and Torque Control Loops

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    ref[Reference Speed from Accelerator Pedal] --> sum1
    fb_speed[Tachogenerator Feedback] --> sum1
    sum1{Error e_omega} --> pi_outer[PI Controller Outer Loop]
    pi_outer --> i_ref[Torque Reference or Current Reference]
    i_ref --> sum2
    fb_cur[Current Sensor Feedback] --> sum2
    sum2{Error e_I} --> pi_inner[PI Controller Inner Loop]
    pi_inner --> pwm[PWM Generator]
    pwm --> chopper[IGBT Chopper]
    chopper --> motor[DC Motor]
    motor --> wheel[Vehicle Wheel]
    wheel --> fb_speed
    motor --> fb_cur
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Architectural Insight:** This is a **cascaded dual-loop PI structure** — the gold standard for DC drives. The **outer (speed) loop** is slow (bandwidth ~10 Hz) and computes the torque demand. The **inner (current) loop** is fast (bandwidth ~1 kHz) and computes the actual PWM duty cycle. KTU questions often ask you to justify *why* two loops are used — the answer is: **current must be limited to protect the chopper, motor windings, and battery from inrush**.

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 — [KTU University Exam - May 2024]
**Define back-EMF in a DC motor. Why is it called "back"?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
Back-EMF $E_b$ is the voltage induced in the armature conductors of a DC motor due to the rotation of the armature in the magnetic field (Faraday's law, 1 mark). It is governed by $E_b = K_e \phi \omega$ (1 mark). It is called "back" because, by Lenz's law, its polarity opposes the applied armature voltage $V_a$, thereby *opposing* the very current that produces the rotation (1 mark).

---

### Question 2 — [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]
**List any three advantages of separately excited DC motors over series DC motors for EV applications.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
1. **Independent control of flux and armature current** enables decoupled torque and speed control (1 mark).
2. **No risk of runaway speed** at no-load — unlike a series motor, a separately excited motor has a finite no-load speed $\omega_0 = V_a / K\phi$ (1 mark).
3. **Regenerative braking is straightforward** — by reducing $\phi$ below rated value, the motor acts as a generator over a wide speed range (1 mark).

---

## 5.2 Part B Question (14 Marks) — Module Internal Choice

### Question A — [KTU University Exam - Model Paper 2024]

**(a)** With the help of a neat block diagram, explain the main components of an **electric vehicle DC motor drive system**. Discuss the function of each block. **[7 Marks]**

**(b)** Derive the **speed equation** of a separately excited DC motor starting from Kirchhoff's Voltage Law. Hence, deduce the **no-load speed** and **stall torque** expressions. **[7 Marks]**

---

### Model Solution — Part (a) [7 Marks]

A DC motor drive system for an electric vehicle consists of **five major functional blocks**:

1. **Energy Source (Battery Pack)** — A high-voltage DC battery (e.g., 400 V Li-ion) acts as the primary energy reservoir. **(1 mark)**
2. **Power Electronic Converter (DC-DC Chopper)** — Uses IGBTs/MOSFETs to vary the average armature voltage. The **duty cycle** $\alpha$ of the chopper directly sets $V_a$. **(1.5 marks)**
3. **Controller (ECU / DSP)** — Implements the speed and current control algorithms (PI/Fuzzy). Receives accelerator pedal input (0–5 V) and tachogenerator feedback. **(1.5 marks)**
4. **DC Motor (Series / Separately Excited / PMDC)** — Converts regulated DC into rotary mechanical power. **(1 mark)**
5. **Sensors and Feedback Loop** — Tachogenerator (speed), current shunt (armature current), and sometimes Hall-effect position sensor. **(1 mark)**
6. **Auxiliary Path: Regenerative Braking** — During deceleration, the motor acts as a generator; the chopper is reconfigured to push current back into the battery. **(1 mark)**

---

### Model Solution — Part (b) [7 Marks]

**Step 1 — Write KVL for the armature circuit** (1 mark):

$$V_a = I_a R_a + L_a \frac{dI_a}{dt} + E_b$$

**Step 2 — Apply steady-state condition** (0.5 mark): $\dfrac{dI_a}{dt} = 0$, so:

$$V_a = I_a R_a + E_b$$

**Step 3 — Write back-EMF expression** (1 mark):

$$E_b = K_e \phi \omega$$

**Step 4 — Solve for $\omega$** (1 mark):

$$\omega = \frac{V_a - I_a R_a}{K_e \phi}$$

**Step 5 — Substitute $I_a = T / K_t \phi$** (1 mark):

$$\omega = \frac{V_a}{K \phi} - \frac{R_a}{(K \phi)^2} T$$

**Step 6 — Deduce no-load speed** at $T = 0$ (1 mark):

$$\omega_0 = \frac{V_a}{K \phi}$$

**Step 7 — Deduce stall torque** at $\omega = 0$ (1 mark):

$$T_{stall} = \frac{V_a \cdot K \phi}{R_a}$$

**Step 8 — Final boxed result and physical interpretation** (0.5 mark):

$$\boxed{N = \frac{(V_a - I_a R_a) \times 60}{2 \pi K_e \phi}}$$

The speed is directly proportional to $V_a$ and inversely proportional to $\phi$, which leads to two control strategies: **armature voltage control** (constant $\phi$, vary $V_a$) and **flux control** (constant $V_a$, vary $\phi$).

---

### Question B (Alternative Choice) — [KTU University Exam - Model Paper 2024]

**(a)** Explain the **four-quadrant operation** of a DC motor drive used in electric vehicles. Sketch the torque-speed characteristics in each quadrant. **[7 Marks]**

**(b)** A 220 V, 1500 rpm, 10 A separately excited DC motor has an armature resistance of 1 Ω. The field current is held constant. Calculate: (i) the no-load speed if the armature voltage is reduced to 180 V; (ii) the speed when the motor draws 8 A at 200 V armature voltage. **[7 Marks]**

---

### Model Solution — Part (a) [7 Marks]

A vehicle drive system must operate in **all four quadrants** of the torque-speed plane to support forward/reverse motion and motoring/braking modes (1 mark).

**Quadrant I — Forward Motoring** (2 marks): $\omega > 0$, $T > 0$. The chopper operates in step-down (buck) mode, supplying positive $V_a$ to drive the vehicle forward. Power flows from battery to motor (motoring mode).

**Quadrant II — Forward Braking (Regenerative)** (2 marks): $\omega > 0$, $T < 0$. When the accelerator is released, the vehicle's kinetic energy rotates the motor above no-load speed, making $E_b > V_a$. Current reverses; the chopper is reconfigured to boost the generated voltage above battery voltage, returning energy to the battery.

**Quadrant III — Reverse Motoring** (1 mark): $\omega < 0$, $T < 0$. Armature voltage polarity is reversed (H-bridge), causing reverse rotation. Used for reversing the vehicle.

**Quadrant IV — Reverse Braking** (1 mark): $\omega < 0$, $T > 0$. Regenerative braking in reverse direction, energy returned to the battery.

---

### Model Solution — Part (b) [7 Marks]

**Given Data:**
- Rated voltage $V_{rated} = 220$ V
- Rated speed $N_{rated} = 1500$ rpm
- Rated current $I_{rated} = 10$ A
- Armature resistance $R_a = 1$ Ω
- Field current is constant → $\phi$ is constant

**Step 1 — Find the back-EMF constant $K_e \phi$ at rated condition** (1 mark):

$$E_{b,rated} = V_a - I_a R_a = 220 - (10)(1) = 210 \text{ V}$$

$$K_e \phi = \frac{E_{b,rated} \cdot 60}{2 \pi N_{rated}} = \frac{210 \times 60}{2\pi \times 1500}$$

$$K_e \phi = \frac{12600}{9424.78} = 1.337 \text{ V·s/rad}$$

**Step 2 — Part (i): No-load speed at $V_a = 180$ V, $I_a \approx 0$** (2 marks):

At no-load, $I_a R_a \approx 0$, so $E_b \approx V_a$:

$$E_b = 180 \text{ V}$$

$$N_0 = \frac{180 \times 60}{2 \pi \times 1.337} = \frac{10800}{8.40} \approx 1285.7 \text{ rpm}$$

$$\boxed{N_0 \approx 1286 \text{ rpm}}$$

**Step 3 — Part (ii): Speed at $V_a = 200$ V, $I_a = 8$ A** (3 marks):

$$E_b = V_a - I_a R_a = 200 - (8)(1) = 192 \text{ V}$$

Using $K_e \phi$ from Step 1 (since $\phi$ is unchanged):

$$N = \frac{192 \times 60}{2\pi \times 1.337} = \frac{11520}{8.40} \approx 1371.4 \text{ rpm}$$

$$\boxed{N \approx 1371 \text{ rpm}}$$

**Step 4 — Verification by ratio method** (1 mark): Since $\phi$ is constant, $N \propto E_b$:

$$N_2 = N_{rated} \times \frac{E_{b2}}{E_{b,rated}} = 1500 \times \frac{192}{210} = 1500 \times 0.9143 \approx 1371.4 \text{ rpm} \checkmark$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfalls — Where Students Lose Marks:**
> 1. **Forgetting to convert RPM to rad/s** when substituting into $E_b = K \phi \omega$. KVL gives you $E_b$ in Volts, not $\omega$ — unit consistency is checked first. **(−1 to −2 marks)**
> 2. **Confusing $K_e$ and $K_t$ units** — write both side-by-side to avoid mistakes.
> 3. **Assuming $I_a = 0$ at no-load for a series motor** — valid only for separately excited/shunt motors. In series motors, no-load $I_a$ is small but not zero, and the motor may *run away*.
> 4. **In four-quadrant questions**, failing to mark power flow direction arrows. Examiners expect arrows showing motoring (P from battery → motor) and regenerative (P from motor → battery). **(−1 mark if missing)**
> 5. **Dropping the $60/(2\pi)$ conversion** in the final speed expression. The single most common KTU valuation deduction.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid-Revision Checklist for DC Motor Drives (Introduction):**

- **The Trinity of DC Motor Equations (must memorize):**
  - $V_a = I_a R_a + E_b$
  - $E_b = K_e \phi \omega$
  - $T = K_t \phi I_a$

- **In SI units, $K_e = K_t = K$ (numerically).** This is the single most-testable fact.

- **Two control strategies:** (1) **Armature voltage control** (vary $V_a$, constant $\phi$) — used below base speed; (2) **Flux control** (vary $\phi$, constant $V_a$) — used above base speed (field-weakening region).

- **No-load speed** of separately excited motor = $V_a / (K\phi)$. **Finite**, so no runaway risk.

- **Stall torque** = $V_a K \phi / R_a$. Very high because $R_a$ is small.

- **Series motor** torque $\propto I_a^2$ → **excellent starting torque** for traction. Runaway risk at no-load.

- **Four-quadrant operation** is essential for any EV drive.

- **Regenerative braking** is possible by making $E_b > V_a$ — current reverses, energy returns to battery.

- **Power flow:** $P_{in} = V_a I_a$ → $P_{cu} = I_a^2 R_a$ → $P_{gap} = E_b I_a = T \omega$ → $P_{rotational\ losses}$ → $P_{shaft}$.

- **Efficiency maximum** occurs when **armature copper loss = constant loss** (i.e., at ~50 % of no-load speed for a separately excited motor with constant loss).

- **Modern EV reality:** Most 2024 EVs use PMSM/AC induction, not DC. But DC drives are still used in **two-wheelers, e-rickshaws, golf carts, forklifts, and as a pedagogical foundation** for understanding all motor drives.

- **The DC motor drive is the "Hello World"** of electric vehicle propulsion — every advanced AC drive ultimately implements the same torque-speed-decoupling philosophy, just with more complex mathematics (Clarke/Park transforms, FOC).

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** OEEET722 - HYBRID AND ELECTRIC VEHICLES > - **Module:** Module 2 > - **Topic:** Induction Motor Drives: Introduction # MODULE 2 — INDUCTION MOTOR DRIVES: INTRODUCTION ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Definition — Induction Motor (IM) Drive for EV Application:** > An **Induction Motor Drive** is an electromechanical propulsion system in which a three-phase (or single-phase) AC induction machine—typically the **squirrel-cage rotor** type—is electronically commutated and torque-controlled by a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) / Voltage Source Inverter (VSI) to deliver the variable torque–speed characteristics demanded by the road-load profile of an Electric or Hybrid Electric Vehicle (HEV). The induction machine operates on the principle of **rotating magnetic field (RMF)** and **Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction**. A rotating stator MMF (magnetomotive force) cuts the short-circuited rotor conductors and induces currents in them (Lenz's law). The interaction between the induced rotor currents and the stator RMF produces the **Lorentz force ($F = BIL$)**, which manifests as electromagnetic torque ($T_e$) on the rotor. In an EV, the induction motor is *never* started direct-on-line (DOL). Instead, it is fed from a **DC-link inverter** that synthesises a sinusoidal PWM (SPWM) or SVPWM voltage whose **frequency ($f_s$) and voltage ($V_s$) are jointly varied** to maintain a constant air-gap flux ($\Phi$). This combined $V/f$ control scheme makes the IM a true "Variable Speed Drive" (VSD). **Key Standard Metrics used in EV-grade IM Drives:** - **Synchronous speed ($N_s$)** in **rpm** - **Slip ($s$)** — dimensionless, typically **0.01 to 0.05** for EV operation - **Per-phase supply frequency ($f_s$)** in **Hz (50/60 Hz base, varied 0–200 Hz in EV)** - **Air-gap flux density ($B_g$) ≈ 0.7 T to 0.9 T** in modern EV motors - **Number of poles ($P$)** — always an **even integer (2, 4, 6, 8)** in traction IM ### 1.2 Intuitive Analogy — "The Spinning Tornado of a Washing Machine" > [!NOTE] > **Conceptual Analogy — "The Invisible Whirlpool":** > Imagine a giant, invisible "tornado" of magnetism spinning inside the motor housing (this is the **stator's rotating magnetic field**). The rotor is like a small metal squirrel cage sitting in the middle of this tornado. The tornado *drags* the squirrel cage along with it — not because the wind pushes the bars directly, but because the changing magnetic field "induces" swirling currents in the closed-cage bars (like eddy currents), and these currents, trying to *oppose* the change (Lenz's law), get pulled along by the tornado. The rotor can never quite catch up with the tornado — this small "lag" is called **slip ($s$)**, and *without slip, there is no induced current, and hence no torque*. That is the essence of an induction motor! For an EV, imagine you are the *driver* (the VFD/inverter). You can change the speed of the tornado (by changing the frequency) and its strength (by changing the voltage). By adjusting both together, you keep the tornado's strength per unit area (the air-gap flux) **constant**, so the squirrel-cage rotor never loses its grip. This is the **$V/f$ control** strategy used in every Tesla Model S, X, 3 and Y. ### 1.3 Why Induction Motors in Electric Vehicles? > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Highlight — Tesla's Traction Motor Choice:** > Tesla Motors (under the technical leadership of **JB Straubel** and **Elon Musk**) famously chose **3-Phase AC Squirrel-Cage Induction Motors** for the **Tesla Roadster (2008), Model S (2012), Model X (2015)** and **Model 3 (2017)**. The deciding factors were: > 1. **No rare-earth permanent magnets** (unlike PMSM) — cheaper, geopolitically safer. > 2. **Rotor robustness** — rotor can withstand **> 18,000 RPM** without structural failure (no magnets to fly apart). > 3. **Excellent field-weakening** — natural constant-power region for high-speed cruising. > 4. **Liquid-cooling friendly** — uniform copper cage dissipates heat isotropically. > 5. **Lower cost per kW** than PMSM or SRM. --- # 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 Operational Block Decomposition The complete EV traction drive chain consists of **four** interacting subsystems. Understanding their handshakes is critical for KTU Module-2 answers: - **Step 1 — Battery Pack (DC Source):** A high-voltage Li-ion pack (typically **400 V** in EVs like Tata Nexon EV, **800 V** in Hyundai E-GMP, Porsche Taycan) provides the **DC link voltage ($V_{DC}$)**. - **Step 2 — DC-Link Capacitor Bank:** A large electrolytic/film capacitor ($C \approx 1$–$2$ mF) smooths the inverter-input current ripple and acts as an energy buffer during regenerative braking. - **Step 3 — Voltage Source Inverter (VSI):** Six IGBTs/MOSFETs arranged in three half-bridge legs produce a 3-phase PWM output. The **modulation index ($m_a$)** controls the fundamental RMS voltage, and the **modulation frequency ($f_{PWM}$)**, typically **5–20 kHz**, controls the stator electrical frequency. - **Step 4 — Three-Phase Induction Motor:** The stator windings receive variable-V, variable-f supply. The rotor (copper/aluminium squirrel cage) converts electromagnetic energy to mechanical torque ($T_e$) on the shaft. ### 2.2 The "Why" Behind Each Step - **Why DC link capacitor?** The inverter draws *pulsating* current from the battery. Without the capacitor, the battery would see AC ripples → premature degradation. - **Why vary V and f together?** The air-gap flux $\Phi \propto V / f$. If you increase $f$ alone, $\Phi$ drops → torque collapses. If you increase $V$ alone, $\Phi$ saturates the iron core → excessive magnetising current → overheating. Hence the constant $V/f$ rule in the *constant-torque region*. - **Why PWM at 5–20 kHz?** Above the audible range (20 Hz–20 kHz) it avoids acoustic noise; below ~20 kHz the switching losses in IGBTs are acceptable. ### 2.3 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet > [!NOTE] > **The following table is a CHEAT SHEET for Module 2 questions. Memorise each entry — it appears in almost every past KTU exam.** | # | Quantity | Formula | Units | Operating Condition | |---|----------|---------|-------|---------------------| | 1 | Synchronous speed | $N_s = \dfrac{120 \, f_s}{P}$ | **rpm** | Stator electrical frequency $f_s$ in Hz, $P$ = number of poles | | 2 | Synchronous angular speed | $\omega_s = \dfrac{2\pi f_s}{P/2} = \dfrac{4\pi f_s}{P}$ | **rad/s** | Equivalent mechanical rad/s of the rotating field | | 3 | Slip | $s = \dfrac{N_s - N_r}{N_s}$ | **dimensionless** | $s = 0$ at synchronous, $s = 1$ at standstill | | 4 | Rotor speed | $N_r = N_s (1 - s)$ | **rpm** | Actual mechanical shaft speed | | 5 | Rotor frequency | $f_r = s \cdot f_s$ | **Hz** | Frequency of induced rotor currents | | 6 | Air-gap flux (constant V/f) | $\Phi \propto \dfrac{V_s}{f_s}$ | **Wb** | Constant-torque region (base speed & below) | | 7 | Developed electromagnetic torque | $T_e = \dfrac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \dfrac{V_s^2 \cdot (R_r / s)}{(R_s + R_r / s)^2 + (X_s + X_r)^2}$ | **N·m** | The exact per-phase equivalent-circuit torque | | 8 | Starting torque (s = 1) | $T_{st} = \dfrac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \dfrac{V_s^2 \cdot R_r}{(R_s + R_r)^2 + (X_s + X_r)^2}$ | **N·m** | Plugging/launch condition of EV | | 9 | Maximum (pull-out) torque | $T_{max} = \dfrac{3}{2\omega_s} \cdot \dfrac{V_s^2}{R_s + \sqrt{R_s^2 + (X_s + X_r)^2}}$ | **N·m** | Slip at $T_{max}$: $s_{max} = \dfrac{R_r}{\sqrt{R_s^2 + (X_s + X_r)^2}}$ | | 10 | Mechanical output power | $P_{out} = T_e \cdot \omega_m$ | **W** | $\omega_m = (1-s)\omega_s$ is the rotor mechanical speed | | 11 | Air-gap power split | $P_{ag} : P_{cu,r} : P_{mech} = 1 : s : (1-s)$ | **W** | Fundamental power-flow identity (must memorise) | | 12 | Rotor copper loss | $P_{cu,r} = s \cdot P_{ag}$ | **W** | Slip × air-gap power | | 13 | Developed mechanical power | $P_{mech} = (1-s) P_{ag}$ | **W** | Air-gap power minus rotor copper loss | | 14 | EV traction force | $F_t = \dfrac{T_e \cdot \eta_{tr}}{r_w}$ | **N** | $\eta_{tr}$ = drivetrain eff., $r_w$ = wheel radius | | 15 | Vehicle dynamics (cruise) | $F_t = m g f_r + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho C_d A v^2$ | **N** | $f_r$ = rolling resistance coeff., $C_d$ = drag coeff. | > [!IMPORTANT] > **The identity $P_{ag} : P_{cu,r} : P_{mech} = 1 : s : (1-s)$** is the single most-asked relation in KTU ESE. It states that *for every 1 W of air-gap power crossing the air-gap, $s$ watts are dissipated as rotor copper heat, and $(1-s)$ watts emerge as useful mechanical shaft power*. Hence, an EV cruising at low slip ($s \approx 0.02$) wastes only **2 %** of air-gap power in the rotor — a key reason induction motors are highly efficient. ### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility - **Formula 14 → 15** is used by every OEM (Tesla, Tata Motors, Mahindra Electric) to size the motor for a vehicle target (0–100 km/h time, gradeability). - **Formula 9** ($T_{max}$) determines the "overload capability" — an EV IM can deliver **2–3× rated torque for 30 seconds** for overtaking bursts. - **Formula 11** justifies why EVs prefer multi-pole (P = 4 or 6) motors at **low base speeds** (~1500–3000 rpm), then use **reduction gears** (single or two-speed, like Porsche Taycan) to match wheel speed. --- # 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Derivation 1 — Synchronous Speed of Rotating Magnetic Field A three-phase winding distributed over $120°$ electrical in the stator slots, energised by a balanced 3-phase supply, produces a sinusoidal **MMF wave** that physically rotates in space. **Step A — Per-phase MMF expressions:** The three phase MMFs (assumed sinusoidally distributed in space with $P/2$ pole-pairs) are: $$\begin{aligned} F_A(\theta, t) &= F_{max} \cos(\theta) \cdot \cos(\omega_s t) \\[2mm] F_B(\theta, t) &= F_{max} \cos(\theta - 120°) \cdot \cos(\omega_s t - 120°) \\[2mm] F_C(\theta, t) &= F_{max} \cos(\theta - 240°) \cdot \cos(\omega_s t - 240°) \end{aligned}$$ **Step B — Apply the trigonometric product-to-sum identity** $\cos A \cos B = \tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(A-B) + \cos(A+B)]$: $$\begin{aligned} F_A(\theta, t) &= \tfrac{F_{max}}{2} [\cos(\theta - \omega_s t) + \cos(\theta + \omega_s t)] \\[2mm] F_B(\theta, t) &= \tfrac{F_{max}}{2} [\cos(\theta - \omega_s t) + \cos(\theta + \omega_s t - 240°)] \\[2mm] F_C(\theta, t) &= \tfrac{F_{max}}{2} [\cos(\theta - \omega_s t) + \cos(\theta + \omega_s t - 480°)] \end{aligned}$$ **Step C — Sum the three MMFs.** The forward-traveling waves (containing $\theta - \omega_s t$) **add in phase**, while the backward waves ($\theta + \omega_s t$) are **120° apart** and sum to zero: $$\begin{aligned} F_{total}(\theta, t) &= F_A + F_B + F_C \\[2mm] &= \tfrac{3 F_{max}}{2} \cos(\theta - \omega_s t) \end{aligned}$$ **Step D — Interpret the result.** The resultant is a single sinusoidal wave with constant amplitude $\tfrac{3 F_{max}}{2}$, whose peak occurs when $\theta - \omega_s t = 0$, i.e., at space-angle: $$\begin{aligned} \theta(t) = \omega_s t \end{aligned}$$ This means the peak of the MMF wave **rotates** in space at electrical angular speed $\omega_s$. Converting to mechanical RPM via $\omega_m = \omega_s / (P/2)$: $$\begin{aligned} \omega_m = \dfrac{2 \omega_s}{P} = \dfrac{2 \cdot 2\pi f_s}{P} = \dfrac{4\pi f_s}{P} \quad \Rightarrow \quad N_s = \dfrac{60 \cdot \omega_m}{2\pi} = \dfrac{120 f_s}{P} \end{aligned}$$ This is the **synchronous speed** — it is independent of load and depends *only* on supply frequency and pole count. --- ## 3.2 Derivation 2 — Electromagnetic Torque from the Per-Phase Equivalent Circuit The per-phase equivalent circuit of a 3-phase induction motor referred to the stator side yields the **air-gap power**: $$\begin{aligned} I_r' = \dfrac{V_s}{\sqrt{\left(R_s + \dfrac{R_r'}{s}\right)^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2}} \end{aligned}$$ **Step A — Air-gap power per phase** is the power dissipated in the rotor branch resistance $R_r'/s$: $$\begin{aligned} P_{ag,\phi} = (I_r')^2 \cdot \dfrac{R_r'}{s} \end{aligned}$$ **Step B — Total 3-phase air-gap power:** $$\begin{aligned} P_{ag} = 3 (I_r')^2 \cdot \dfrac{R_r'}{s} \end{aligned}$$ **Step C — Substitute $I_r'$ and multiply by 3:** $$\begin{aligned} P_{ag} = \dfrac{3 V_s^2 \, (R_r'/s)}{\left(R_s + \dfrac{R_r'}{s}\right)^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2} \end{aligned}$$ **Step D — Electromagnetic torque is air-gap power divided by synchronous mechanical angular speed** $\omega_s$: $$\begin{aligned} T_e = \dfrac{P_{ag}}{\omega_s} = \dfrac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \dfrac{V_s^2 \, (R_r'/s)}{\left(R_s + \dfrac{R_r'}{s}\right)^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2} \end{aligned}$$ **Step E — Slip at maximum torque.** Differentiate $T_e$ with respect to $s$ and set $dT_e/ds = 0$. After algebraic reduction (chain-rule applied to numerator and denominator), the result simplifies elegantly: $$\begin{aligned} s_{max} = \dfrac{R_r'}{\sqrt{R_s^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2}} \end{aligned}$$ **Step F — Substitute $s_{max}$ back into the torque equation** and simplify using $R_s \ll \sqrt{R_s^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2}$ (valid for typical EV motors where $R_s < 0.1 \, \vert X_s + X_r' \vert$): $$\begin{aligned} T_{max} \approx \dfrac{3}{2 \omega_s} \cdot \dfrac{V_s^2}{R_s + \sqrt{R_s^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2}} \end{aligned}$$ > [!IMPORTANT] > **Key Insight:** $T_{max}$ is **independent of rotor resistance $R_r'$**! This is why an EV designer cannot change $T_{max}$ by altering rotor bar material — but CAN change the **slip** $s_{max}$ at which it occurs. This is exploited in **deep-bar / double-cage rotors** to tailor the torque curve for traction. --- ## 3.3 Derivation 3 — The Power-Flow Identity $P_{ag} : P_{cu,r} : P_{mech} = 1 : s : (1-s)$ **Step A — Rotor copper loss** is by Joule heating in $R_r'$ at the *slip frequency* $f_r = s f_s$: $$\begin{aligned} P_{cu,r} = 3 (I_r')^2 R_r' \end{aligned}$$ **Step B — Air-gap power** (from Step C of Derivation 2): $$\begin{aligned} P_{ag} = 3 (I_r')^2 \cdot \dfrac{R_r'}{s} \end{aligned}$$ **Step C — Take the ratio** $P_{cu,r} / P_{ag}$: $$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{P_{cu,r}}{P_{ag}} = \dfrac{3 (I_r')^2 R_r'}{3 (I_r')^2 (R_r'/s)} = s \end{aligned}$$ **Step D — Hence** $P_{cu,r} = s \cdot P_{ag}$ — QED for one identity. **Step E — Mechanical power developed** is air-gap power minus rotor copper loss: $$\begin{aligned} P_{mech} = P_{ag} - P_{cu,r} = P_{ag} - s P_{ag} = (1 - s) P_{ag} \end{aligned}$$ **Step F — Final normalised identity:** $$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{P_{ag} : P_{cu,r} : P_{mech}}{P_{ag}} = 1 : s : (1-s) \end{aligned}$$ --- ## 3.4 Numerical Worked Example (Typical KTU Problem) > **Problem:** A 3-phase, 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor drives an EV. Full-load slip is 4 %. Stator copper loss = 300 W, rotor copper loss = 200 W, iron loss = 150 W, mechanical (friction + windage) loss = 100 W. Compute: (a) Air-gap power, (b) Shaft power, (c) Efficiency. **Solution:** Given $P_{cu,r} = 200$ W and $s = 0.04$. From the identity $P_{cu,r} = s \, P_{ag}$: $$\begin{aligned} P_{ag} = \dfrac{P_{cu,r}}{s} = \dfrac{200}{0.04} = 5000 \text{ W} = 5 \text{ kW} \end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned} P_{mech} = (1 - s) P_{ag} = (1 - 0.04)(5000) = 4800 \text{ W} \end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned} P_{shaft} = P_{mech} - P_{fw} = 4800 - 100 = 4700 \text{ W} \end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned} P_{input} = P_{shaft} + P_{cu,r} + P_{cu,s} + P_{iron} + P_{fw} = 4700 + 200 + 300 + 150 + 100 = 5450 \text{ W} \end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned} \eta = \dfrac{P_{shaft}}{P_{input}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{4700}{5450} \times 100\% \approx 86.24\% \end{aligned}$$ --- # 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Block Diagram — EV Induction Motor Drive Power Flow ```mermaid graph LR BAT[Battery Pack
400 V or 800 V DC] DC[DC Link Capacitor
1 to 2 mF] INV[Voltage Source Inverter
6 IGBT 3 Phase] CTRL[VFD Controller
V by f Strategy] IM[3 Phase Induction Motor
Squirrel Cage Rotor] GEAR[Reduction Gearbox
Single or 2 Speed] WH[EV Wheels] BAT --- DC DC --- INV CTRL -.fPWM.-> INV INV ==> IM IM --- GEAR GEAR --- WH INV -. Regenerative Braking .-> DC DC -. Charge Current .-> BAT style BAT fill:#fde2e4,stroke:#c1121f,color:#000 style DC fill:#fff1b8,stroke:#b08900,color:#000 style INV fill:#cddafd,stroke:#3a86ff,color:#000 style CTRL fill:#d8f3dc,stroke:#2d6a4f,color:#000 style IM fill:#ffd6a5,stroke:#e85d04,color:#000 style GEAR fill:#caffbf,stroke:#40916c,color:#000 style WH fill:#bdb2ff,stroke:#5a189a,color:#000 ``` **Reading the diagram:** Solid arrows = forward motoring power flow. Dashed arrows = control signals (low-power) and reverse regenerative-braking energy. The **double-arrow `==>`** marks the electromechanical energy conversion at the air-gap. --- ## 4.2 Torque–Speed Characteristic of EV Induction Motor Drive ```mermaid graph TB subgraph CONST_TORQUE["CONSTANT TORQUE REGION 0 to Base Speed"] direction LR T0[Starting Torque Tst] --> TR[Rated Torque Trated] end subgraph CONST_POWER["CONSTANT POWER REGION Base to Max Speed"] direction LR TR2[Rated Torque] --> TW[Weakened Field Torque] end N0[Nr = 0 Standstill] --> NB[Base Speed Nbase] --> NMAX[Max Speed Nmax] T0 -. s = 1 .- N0 TR -. rated slip .- NB TW -. field weakening .- NMAX style CONST_TORQUE fill:#ffd6a5,stroke:#e85d04,color:#000 style CONST_POWER fill:#caffbf,stroke:#40916c,color:#000 style T0 fill:#fff style TR fill:#fff style TW fill:#fff ``` **Interpretation:** - **0 → Base speed:** $V/f$ is held constant; flux is constant; torque is constant ≈ $T_{rated}$. This is the **launch & low-speed cruising region**. - **Base → Max speed:** $V$ is clamped at max (battery voltage limit); only $f$ increases; flux weakens as $\Phi \propto 1/f$; power $P = T \omega$ remains constant — hence the name **constant-power region**. This is the **highway cruising & overtaking region**. --- ## 4.3 Power-Flow Sankey-Style Architecture ```mermaid graph LR PIN[Input Electrical Power Pin] --> CSL[Stator Cu Loss] PIN --> IR[Iron Loss] CSL --> PAG[Air Gap Power Pag] IR --> PAG PAG --> CRL[Rotor Cu Loss s times Pag] PAG --> PMECH[Mechanical Power Developed] CRL --> THERMAL[Heat Dissipation] PMECH --> FWL[Friction and Windage] PMECH --> PSHAFT[Shaft Output Power] FWL --> THERMAL style PIN fill:#a2d2ff,stroke:#023e8a,color:#000 style PAG fill:#ffb703,stroke:#fb8500,color:#000 style PSHAFT fill:#80ed99,stroke:#38a169,color:#000 style THERMAL fill:#ffadad,stroke:#c1121f,color:#000 ``` --- # 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Q1. `[KTU University Exam — May 2024, Series-1]` **Why are three-phase squirrel-cage induction motors preferred over DC motors and PMSM for many modern Electric Vehicle applications? Mention any four reasons.** **Model Answer (3 marks):** 1. **No permanent magnets** → avoids rare-earth (NdFeB) supply-chain risks; reduces cost by ~30 % compared to PMSM. 2. **Rugged rotor construction** (cast aluminium / copper bars in solid iron laminations) → can sustain centrifugal stresses at **> 18,000 rpm**, far beyond what surface-mounted magnets can tolerate. 3. **Excellent field-weakening range** → natural constant-power region from base speed to 3–4× base speed enables single-gear highway cruising. 4. **Liquid-cooling friendly** → uniform isotropic copper cage dissipates heat; stator end-windings are easily jacket-cooled. *(1 mark for any 2 reasons, full marks for 4 well-explained reasons.)* ### Q2. `[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]` **Define "slip" in an induction motor. Why is slip essential for torque production?** **Model Answer (3 marks):** **Slip ($s$)** is defined as the relative difference between synchronous speed $N_s$ and actual rotor speed $N_r$, expressed as a fraction of $N_s$: $s = (N_s - N_r)/N_s$. Slip is **essential** because: - **At $s = 0$** the rotor rotates in synchronism with the stator RMF → no relative motion → no flux-cutting → no induced EMF (Faraday's law requires $d\Phi/dt \neq 0$) → no rotor current → **no torque**. - **At any $s > 0$**, the rotor conductors *cut* the RMF → induced EMF → induced current → force on conductors → **torque**. - Therefore torque is a function of $s$: $T_e \propto s$ at low slip (linear region) and $T_e \propto 1/s$ at high slip. *(2 marks for definition; 1 mark for the "why" explanation.)* --- ## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks — Internal Choice) ### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam — May 2024, Module 2, Set A]` **(a)** With a neat per-phase equivalent circuit, derive the expression for the electromagnetic torque developed by a 3-phase induction motor. Show that the slip at maximum torque is independent of stator voltage. **(7 marks)** **(b)** A 3-phase, 6-pole, 50 Hz induction motor has a full-load slip of 4 %. The rotor copper loss at full load is 600 W and the stator copper loss is 800 W. The friction and windage losses total 200 W. Compute: (i) Air-gap power, (ii) Shaft power, (iii) Mechanical power developed, (iv) Efficiency. **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution to Q-A(a) **Step 1:** Write the per-phase equivalent circuit referred to the stator (show $R_s$, $X_s$, magnetising branch $jX_m$, rotor branch $R_r'/s + jX_r'$). **(1 mark)** **Step 2:** Express the rotor-referred current from circuit: $$\begin{aligned} I_r' = \dfrac{V_s}{\left[\left(R_s + \dfrac{R_r'}{s}\right)^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2\right]^{1/2}} \end{aligned}$$ **Step 3:** Air-gap power per phase, $P_{ag,\phi} = (I_r')^2 \cdot R_r'/s$; total $P_{ag} = 3 (I_r')^2 R_r'/s$. **(1 mark)** **Step 4:** Electromagnetic torque, $T_e = P_{ag}/\omega_s$: $$\begin{aligned} T_e = \dfrac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \dfrac{V_s^2 \cdot (R_r'/s)}{\left(R_s + \dfrac{R_r'}{s}\right)^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2} \end{aligned}$$ **(2 marks for arriving at this final equation)** **Step 5:** Differentiate $T_e$ with respect to $s$, set $dT_e/ds = 0$. Using the quotient rule on numerator $N(s) = R_r'/s$ and denominator $D(s) = (R_s + R_r'/s)^2 + (X_s+X_r')^2$, after algebraic simplification: $$\begin{aligned} s_{max} = \dfrac{R_r'}{\sqrt{R_s^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2}} \end{aligned}$$ **(2 marks for derivation; $s_{max}$ is independent of $V_s$ — completing the proof.)** **Step 6:** The corresponding $T_{max}$ expression: $$\begin{aligned} T_{max} = \dfrac{3}{2\omega_s} \cdot \dfrac{V_s^2}{R_s + \sqrt{R_s^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2}} \end{aligned}$$ **(1 mark for stating the conclusion that $T_{max} \propto V_s^2$ but $s_{max}$ is $V_s$-independent.)** --- #### Model Solution to Q-A(b) Given: $P = 6$, $f = 50$ Hz, $s = 0.04$, $P_{cu,r} = 600$ W, $P_{cu,s} = 800$ W, $P_{fw} = 200$ W. **(i) Air-gap power** — using the identity $P_{cu,r} = s \cdot P_{ag}$: **(2 marks)** $$\begin{aligned} P_{ag} = \dfrac{P_{cu,r}}{s} = \dfrac{600}{0.04} = 15000 \text{ W} = 15 \text{ kW} \end{aligned}$$ **(ii) Shaft power** — $P_{shaft} = P_{mech} - P_{fw}$: $$\begin{aligned} P_{mech} &= (1 - s) P_{ag} = (1 - 0.04)(15000) = 14400 \text{ W} \\[2mm] P_{shaft} &= 14400 - 200 = 14200 \text{ W} = 14.2 \text{ kW} \quad \textbf{(2 marks)} \end{aligned}$$ **(iii) Mechanical power developed** = $P_{mech} = (1-s) P_{ag} = 14.4$ kW. **(1 mark)** **(iv) Efficiency** — Input power = $P_{shaft} + P_{cu,s} + P_{cu,r} + P_{fw}$: $$\begin{aligned} P_{in} &= 14200 + 800 + 600 + 200 = 15800 \text{ W} \\[2mm] \eta &= \dfrac{14200}{15800} \times 100\% \approx 89.87\% \quad \textbf{(2 marks)} \end{aligned}$$ --- ### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice** `[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Module 2, Set B]` **(a)** Explain with block diagram the role of a **Variable Frequency Drive (VFD)** in controlling a 3-phase induction motor used in an EV. Discuss the **$V/f$ control** strategy in detail. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Compare **Squirrel-Cage IM, PMSM and SRM** for EV application on the basis of (i) Power density, (ii) Efficiency, (iii) Cost, (iv) Cooling complexity, (v) Field-weakening capability, (vi) Reliability, (vii) Regenerative braking ability. **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution to Q-B(a) **Step 1 — Block Diagram (3 marks):** The VFD chain for an EV IM drive is: **Battery (DC)** → **DC-link Capacitor** → **Rectifier** (only if AC charging considered; otherwise direct DC link) → **VSI (3-phase IGBT inverter)** → **Induction Motor**. The **controller** senses rotor position (or estimates it via sensorless FOC), reads accelerator-pedal torque demand, and modulates inverter $f_{PWM}$ and $m_a$. **Step 2 — V/f Strategy (2 marks):** Below **base speed** ($\omega_{base}$), maintain $V/f = \text{constant}$ so that air-gap flux $\Phi$ stays at rated value. This yields **constant torque** capability. Typical V/f ratio for a 400 V, 100 Hz base is **4 V/Hz** (per-phase RMS line-neutral ≈ 230 V at 50 Hz). **Step 3 — Field Weakening (2 marks):** Above base speed, $V$ saturates at the battery maximum. Only $f$ rises → $\Phi \propto 1/f$ drops → torque falls as $1/f$, but power $T\omega \approx$ constant. **Key Equation (1 mark):** $$\begin{aligned} \Phi_{air-gap} = \dfrac{V_s}{4.44 \, f_s \, N_s \, k_w} \end{aligned}$$ where $k_w$ is the winding factor and $N_s$ is turns per phase. To keep $\Phi$ constant, $V_s / f_s$ must remain constant. --- #### Model Solution to Q-B(b) | Criterion | Squirrel-Cage IM | PMSM | SRM | |-----------|------------------|------|-----| | Power density | Medium (3–5 kW/kg) | High (5–7 kW/kg) | High (5–6 kW/kg) | | Peak efficiency | 92–95 % | 95–97 % | 92–94 % | | Cost per kW | **Low** (no magnets) | High (rare-earth magnets) | Medium | | Cooling complexity | **Easy** (uniform copper) | Hard (localised magnet heating) | Hard (rotor hot-spots) | | Field-weakening | **Excellent** (natural) | Limited by magnet flux linkage | Excellent (variable excitation) | | Reliability | **Very high** (rugged rotor) | Medium (demag at high T) | High | | Regen braking | Excellent (inverter-driven) | Excellent | Excellent | **(Award 1 mark per row for correct comparison with justification — sample 5–6 rows suffice for full 7 marks.)** > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:** > 1. **Confusing air-gap power with shaft power** — many students write $P_{shaft} = P_{ag} - P_{cu,r}$ and forget friction/windage. Deduct 1 mark. > 2. **Using $N_s = 120 f / P$ incorrectly** — remember $N_s$ is in **rpm**, not rad/s. For mechanical angular speed use $\omega_s = 2\pi N_s / 60$. > 3. **Forgetting to convert per-phase voltage** when using the torque equation — $V_s$ in the formula is the **phase (line-neutral) RMS voltage**, NOT the line-to-line. Many students substitute $V_{LL}$ directly. **Penalty: −1 mark.** > 4. **Slip must always be in DECIMAL (0.04)**, not percentage (4 %). The identity $P_{cu,r} = s P_{ag}$ uses dimensionless slip. > 5. **In $V/f$ control** — clearly state **TWO regions** (constant torque, constant power). Generic statements like "voltage and frequency are varied" fetch only partial marks. --- ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!IMPORTANT] > **Rapid Revision Checklist for Module 2 — Induction Motor Drives (Introduction)** - [ ] **Slip** $s = (N_s - N_r)/N_s$; at start $s = 1$; at synchronous $s = 0$; at EV cruise $s \approx 0.01$–$0.05$. - [ ] **Synchronous speed** $N_s = 120 f_s / P$ — depends ONLY on $f$ and pole count, not load. - [ ] **The golden identity** $P_{ag} : P_{cu,r} : P_{mech} = 1 : s : (1-s)$ — must be memorised verbatim. - [ ] **Rotor copper loss** $P_{cu,r} = s \cdot P_{ag}$ — low slip → low rotor heat → high efficiency. - [ ] **Air-gap flux** $\Phi \propto V/f$ — keep this constant in the constant-torque region (V/f control). - [ ] **Torque equation** $T_e = \dfrac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \dfrac{V_s^2 (R_r'/s)}{(R_s + R_r'/s)^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2}$. - [ ] **Slip at max torque** $s_{max} = R_r' / \sqrt{R_s^2 + (X_s + X_r')^2}$ — independent of $V_s$. - [ ] **Max torque** $T_{max} \propto V_s^2$ — but $s_{max}$ does not depend on $V_s$. - [ ] **Two operating regions in EV:** (i) Constant-torque ($V/f$ constant, 0 → base speed) for launch/grade; (ii) Constant-power (field-weakened, base → max speed) for cruise. - [ ] **Why IM in EVs:** no magnets, rugged rotor, low cost, high field-weakening range, excellent regen. - [ ] **VFD components:** DC link capacitor + VSI (6-IGBT) + PWM controller using $V/f$ or **Field-Oriented Control (FOC)**. - [ ] **Tesla application:** Model S/X/3/Y all use 3-phase AC squirrel-cage IMs (later versions moving to PMSM with carbon-wrapped rotor for higher specific power). - [ ] **Rotor frequencies** $f_r = s f_s$ — for an EV at $s = 0.03$ and $f_s = 100$ Hz, rotor currents oscillate at only **3 Hz** — enabling deep-bar rotor design. - [ ] **Permanent-magnet-free** advantage gives IM a strategic supply-chain edge as the world moves away from Chinese rare-earth monopoly. ---

topics.title: Speed Control of Induction Motor
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** OEEET722 - HYBRID AND ELECTRIC VEHICLES
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Speed Control of Induction Motor

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

A **Three-Phase Induction Motor (IM)** is a self-starting, robust, brushless AC machine whose rotor speed $N_r$ is fundamentally tied to the synchronous speed $N_s$ of the rotating stator magnetic field through the **slip (s)**. Because the rotor cannot physically reach synchronous speed (which would require zero induced rotor current and thus zero torque), **Speed Control of an Induction Motor** is the systematic manipulation of input electrical parameters — namely **voltage (V), frequency (f), and pole count (P)** — to deliberately alter the synchronous speed and operating slip, thereby commanding the mechanical output speed of the motor across a desired range.

Mathematically, this relationship is anchored by the **fundamental speed equation**:

$$N_s = \frac{120 \cdot f}{P} \quad \text{[in RPM]}$$

and the **slip relation**:

$$s = \frac{N_s - N_r}{N_s}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** In Hybrid and Electric Vehicle applications, induction motors are favored for their ruggedness, high power density, and absence of rare-earth magnets (unlike PMSMs). The dominant speed-control strategy in production EVs (e.g., Tesla Model S, Tata Nexon EV) is **Variable Voltage Variable Frequency (VVVF)** control, often combined with **Field-Oriented Control (FOC)**.

### 1.2 Intuitive Overview — The Bicycle Analogy

Imagine you are cycling on a stationary bicycle trainer connected to a generator:

- The **pedaling rate** = Stator supply frequency ($f$)
- The **gear ratio** = Number of magnetic poles ($P$)
- The **actual wheel rotation** = Rotor speed ($N_r$)
- The **lag of the wheel** = Slip ($s$)

To go faster, you have three choices: pedal quicker (**increase frequency**), shift to a smaller gear (**reduce poles**), or change the terrain resistance. Induction motor speed control works on identical principles — we modulate *how fast* the magnetic field rotates and *how strongly* the rotor chases it.

> [!NOTE]
> **Physical Constants & Units to Memorize:**
> - Synchronous speed $N_s$ → **RPM**
> - Supply frequency $f$ → **Hz**
> - Slip $s$ → **per unit (p.u.) or fraction**
> - Pole count $P$ → **integer (always even)**
> - Mechanical rotor speed $N_r$ → **RPM**

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Why Speed Control is Inherently Difficult in Induction Motors

Unlike DC motors where speed is a linear function of armature voltage, the AC induction motor presents a **non-linear, coupled electromagnetic system**. The torque produced depends on:

1. Stator flux $\Phi$
2. Slip frequency $sf$
3. Rotor time constant $\tau_r = L_r / R_r$

Because flux $\Phi \propto V/f$, any change in frequency must be accompanied by a proportional change in voltage to maintain **constant flux** and prevent magnetic saturation (over-fluxing) or torque collapse (under-fluxing).

### 2.2 Classification of Speed Control Methods (KTU-Exam Essential Taxonomy)

| Sl. No. | Category | Sub-Methods |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **From Stator Side** | (i) V/F Control (VVVF) |
| | | (ii) Variable Voltage Control |
| | | (iii) Pole Changing (PAM) |
| **B** | **From Rotor Side** | (iv) Rotor Resistance Control |
| | | (v) Slip Power Recovery (Kramer/Scherbius) |
| **C** | **Advanced Vector Methods** | (vi) Field-Oriented Control (FOC) |
| | | (vii) Direct Torque Control (DTC) |

### 2.3 Method 1 — V/F Control (VVVF) — **The Dominant EV Method**

**Operating Principle:** Maintain a constant **Volts-per-Hertz ratio** so that air-gap flux remains nominal across the entire speed range.

$$\frac{V}{f} = \text{constant}$$

**Operating Regions of V/F Drive:**

| Region | Speed Range | Control Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Constant Torque Region** (0 → Base Speed) | $0 < N < N_{base}$ | $V$ rises linearly with $f$; flux $\Phi$ held constant |
| **Constant Power Region** (Base → Critical Speed) | $N_{base} < N < N_{max}$ | $V$ held constant at rated; $f$ increased; flux weakens |
| **Constant Voltage / Series Region** | $N > N_{max}$ | Both limited by inverter ceiling; torque drops as $1/N^2$ |

> [!NOTE]
> **Why is V/F control critical for HEV/EV?**
> - The inverter (DC-AC) in an EV feeds the motor with synthesized sine waves whose amplitude and frequency are software-controlled.
> - During **city driving (low speed, high torque)**, the inverter operates in the **constant torque region**.
> - During **highway cruising (high speed, lower torque)**, the inverter pushes into the **field-weakening (constant power) region**.
> - This mimics an IC engine's torque curve, allowing **single-pedal driving feel** and **regenerative braking** integration.

### 2.4 Method 2 — Vector / Field-Oriented Control (FOC)

FOC transforms the 3-phase stator currents ($i_a, i_b, i_c$) into a **rotating 2-axis reference frame (d-q)** aligned with the rotor flux:

- $i_d$ (direct-axis current) → controls **flux**
- $i_q$ (quadrature-axis current) → controls **torque**

This **decouples** torque and flux, allowing the induction motor to be controlled with the same precision as a separately excited DC motor.

$$T_e = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{P}{2} \cdot \frac{L_m^2}{L_r} \cdot i_d \cdot i_q$$

### 2.5 Method 3 — Direct Torque Control (DTC)

DTC uses **hysteresis comparators** on stator flux and torque estimates to directly select inverter switching states from an **optimum switching table**. It offers:
- Faster torque response (~1 ms)
- No PWM modulator or coordinate transformations needed
- Higher torque ripple (a key EV trade-off)

### 2.6 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

| Symbol | Formula / Relation | Meaning & Units |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous Speed | $N_s = 120 f / P$ | Rotating field speed, **RPM** |
| Slip | $s = (N_s - N_r)/N_s$ | Fraction, dimensionless |
| Rotor Frequency | $f_r = s \cdot f$ | Frequency of rotor current, **Hz** |
| V/F Ratio | $V/f = k$ (constant) | Maintains rated flux |
| Air-Gap Flux | $\Phi \approx V / (4.44 \cdot f \cdot N \cdot k_w)$ | **Weber (Wb)** |
| Electromagnetic Torque | $T_e = \frac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \frac{s \cdot E_2^2 \cdot R_2}{R_2^2 + (s \cdot X_2)^2}$ | **N·m** |
| Slip at Max Torque | $s_{max} = R_2 / X_2$ | Independent of load |
| Maximum Torque | $T_{max} = \frac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \frac{E_2^2}{2 X_2}$ | **N·m**, constant in V/F mode |
| FOC Torque | $T_e = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{P}{2} \cdot \frac{L_m^2}{L_r} \cdot i_d \cdot i_q$ | **N·m** |
| EV Power Balance | $P_{mech} = T_e \cdot \omega_m$ | **Watts (W)** |
| EV Drive Power | $P_{batt} = P_{mech} / (\eta_{motor} \cdot \eta_{inv})$ | Includes inverter + motor losses |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **CRITICAL KTU Pitfall — Escape Velocity of V/F Method:**
> Notice in the torque formula that if you keep $V/f$ constant, then $E_2/f$ is constant and therefore $T_{max}$ becomes **independent of frequency** — this is precisely why V/F drives deliver **constant rated torque below base speed**.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation: Torque-Slip Characteristic of Induction Motor

Starting from the **per-phase equivalent circuit** (approximate, with rotor referred to stator), the air-gap power transferred to the rotor is:

$$P_{ag} = 3 \cdot I_2^{\prime 2} \cdot \frac{R_2^{\prime}}{s}$$

The mechanical power developed (air-gap power minus rotor copper loss) is:

$$P_m = 3 \cdot I_2^{\prime 2} \cdot R_2^{\prime} \cdot \frac{(1-s)}{s}$$

Since $P_m = T_e \cdot \omega_m$ and $\omega_m = \omega_s (1 - s)$ where $\omega_s = 2\pi f / (P/2)$:

$$T_e = \frac{P_m}{\omega_m} = \frac{3 \cdot I_2^{\prime 2} \cdot R_2^{\prime} / s}{\omega_s}$$

Substituting the rotor current from the equivalent circuit:

$$I_2^{\prime} = \frac{s \cdot V}{\sqrt{R_2^{\prime 2} + (s \cdot X_2^{\prime})^2}}$$

we obtain the **complete torque equation**:

$$T_e = \frac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \frac{s \cdot V^2 \cdot R_2^{\prime}}{R_2^{\prime 2} + (s \cdot X_2^{\prime})^2}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Logic Transition:** The numerator contains $s \cdot V^2 \cdot R_2^{\prime}$ — this explains *why voltage control works* (torque scales as $V^2$ at low slip). The denominator $(R_2^{\prime 2} + (s \cdot X_2^{\prime})^2)$ grows rapidly at high slip, causing torque to drop after $s_{max}$.

### 3.2 Derivation: Slip at Maximum Torque ($s_{max}$)

To find the slip where $T_e$ is maximum, we apply $dT_e/ds = 0$.

Let $K = \dfrac{3 V^2 R_2^{\prime}}{\omega_s}$ (a constant for a given V/f pair), so:

$$T_e = K \cdot \frac{s}{R_2^{\prime 2} + s^2 X_2^{\prime 2}}$$

Differentiating with respect to $s$:

$$\frac{dT_e}{ds} = K \cdot \frac{(R_2^{\prime 2} + s^2 X_2^{\prime 2}) - s \cdot (2 s X_2^{\prime 2})}{(R_2^{\prime 2} + s^2 X_2^{\prime 2})^2}$$

Setting the numerator to zero:

$$R_2^{\prime 2} + s^2 X_2^{\prime 2} - 2 s^2 X_2^{\prime 2} = 0$$

$$R_2^{\prime 2} = s^2 X_2^{\prime 2}$$

$$\boxed{s_{max} = \frac{R_2^{\prime}}{X_2^{\prime}}}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical Engineering Insight:** $s_{max}$ depends **only on the rotor circuit parameters** — not on supply voltage. This means a V/F drive can shift the operating slip freely without altering the *location* of peak torque on the slip axis.

### 3.3 Derivation: Condition for Constant Torque in V/F Control

We want to show that when $V/f$ = constant, $T_{max}$ is independent of $f$.

The maximum torque expression (substituting $s_{max}$ back into $T_e$):

$$T_{max} = \frac{3}{\omega_s} \cdot \frac{E_2^{\prime 2}}{2 X_2^{\prime}}$$

Since $X_2^{\prime} = 2\pi f L_2^{\prime}$, dividing both $E_2^{\prime 2}$ and $X_2^{\prime}$ by $f$:

$$T_{max} = \frac{3}{(2\pi f / (P/2))} \cdot \frac{E_2^{\prime 2}}{2 \cdot 2\pi f L_2^{\prime}} = \text{constant when } \frac{E_2^{\prime}}{f} = \text{constant}$$

In the linear magnetic region, $E_2^{\prime} \approx V$, hence:

$$\boxed{\frac{V}{f} = \text{constant} \implies T_{max} = \text{constant (below base speed)}}$$

### 3.4 Derivation: FOC Torque Equation from d-q Model

The induction motor stator voltage equations in the synchronous reference frame are:

$$v_{ds} = R_s i_{ds} + \frac{d\lambda_{ds}}{dt} - \omega_e \lambda_{qs}$$

$$v_{qs} = R_s i_{qs} + \frac{d\lambda_{qs}}{dt} + \omega_e \lambda_{ds}$$

with flux linkages:

$$\lambda_{ds} = L_s i_{ds} + L_m i_{dr}, \quad \lambda_{qs} = L_s i_{qs} + L_m i_{qr}$$

$$\lambda_{dr} = L_m i_{ds} + L_r i_{dr}, \quad \lambda_{qr} = L_m i_{qs} + L_r i_{qr}$$

In the **rotor-flux-oriented frame**, by definition $\lambda_{qr} = 0$ and $\lambda_{dr} = \lambda_r$. Solving:

$$i_{dr} = \frac{\lambda_r - L_m i_{ds}}{L_r}, \quad i_{qr} = - \frac{L_m}{L_r} i_{qs}$$

The electromagnetic torque in the d-q frame is:

$$T_e = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{P}{2} \cdot L_m (i_{qs} i_{dr} - i_{ds} i_{qr})$$

Substituting $i_{dr}$ and $i_{qr}$:

$$T_e = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{P}{2} \cdot \frac{L_m}{L_r} (i_{qs} \lambda_r - i_{ds} \cdot 0) \cdot \text{(rearrangement gives)}$$

$$\boxed{T_e = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{P}{2} \cdot \frac{L_m^2}{L_r} \cdot i_{ds} \cdot i_{qs}}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Logic of Decoupling:** With $i_{ds}$ controlling flux and $i_{qs}$ controlling torque independently, the AC induction motor is reduced — *in software* — to a linear DC-machine-like control system.

### 3.5 Worked Numerical Example (KTU Numerical Style)

**Problem:** A 3-phase, 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor runs at 1440 RPM on full load. Calculate (a) slip, (b) rotor frequency, (c) rotor copper loss as a percentage of input if mechanical losses are 5% of input.

**Solution:**

(a) Synchronous speed:

$$N_s = \frac{120 \cdot 50}{4} = 1500 \text{ RPM}$$

Slip:

$$s = \frac{1500 - 1440}{1500} = \frac{60}{1500} = 0.04 \text{ p.u. (or 4\%)}$$

(b) Rotor frequency:

$$f_r = s \cdot f = 0.04 \cdot 50 = 2 \text{ Hz}$$

(c) Mechanical power developed: $P_m = (1 - s) P_{ag}$. Let input $P_{in} = 1.0$ p.u.

Rotor copper loss: $P_{rcu} = s \cdot P_{ag}$. Mechanical output: $P_{out} = P_m - P_{mech,loss}$.

Using $P_{ag}/P_{in} = 1/(1 - s_{total})$ and mechanical losses = 0.05 p.u., solving yields **rotor copper loss ≈ 4.2% of input**.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall:** Students often confuse $P_m$ (mechanical power developed) with $P_{out}$ (shaft output). Remember: $P_m = (1-s) P_{ag}$ and $P_{out} = P_m - P_{rotational\ losses}$.

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Block-Level Functional Architecture of EV Induction Motor Drive

```mermaid
flowchart TD

    J --> D
    H --> K[Gearbox Single Speed Reducer]
    K --> L[Wheels EV Drivetrain]

```

### 4.4 Comparative Selection Map for EV Motor Control

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[Induction Motor Speed Control in EV] --> A1[Scalar V/F]
    Q --> A2[Vector FOC]
    Q --> A3[DTC]

    A2 --> B2[High performance most EVs Tesla Tata]

    B3 --> C3[Robust parameter independent]
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Diagram Interpretation:** The block diagrams map the **functional flow** of signal, control, and power paths in a production EV. Notice the closed feedback loop from the **resolver/encoder** back to the FOC algorithm — this is what enables the precise torque vectoring that gives modern EVs their instant acceleration feel.

---

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
*State the fundamental relationship between synchronous speed, supply frequency, and number of poles in a three-phase induction motor. Why is speed control of an induction motor considered more complex than that of a DC motor?*

**Model Answer:**
The synchronous speed of the rotating magnetic field is given by $N_s = 120 f / P$. Speed is directly proportional to supply frequency $f$ and inversely proportional to pole count $P$. Induction motor speed control is inherently complex because the rotor speed depends on slip, and torque is a **non-linear function** of both voltage and frequency. Unlike a DC motor where flux and torque are independently controllable via separate field and armature circuits, in an AC induction motor these quantities are **magnetically coupled**, requiring sophisticated electronic control (V/F, FOC, or DTC) to achieve decoupled control. **[3 marks]**

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – June 2024]**
*What is meant by "constant V/F ratio" in induction motor speed control? State its significance in electric vehicle applications.*

**Model Answer:**
The constant V/F ratio refers to maintaining $V/f = \text{constant}$ so that the air-gap flux $\Phi$ remains at its rated value. Since $\Phi \propto V/f$, holding this ratio constant prevents **flux weakening** (which reduces torque) and **flux strengthening** (which saturates the core). In EV applications, V/F control is essential because the inverter synthesizes variable voltage and frequency from the DC bus; maintaining constant flux delivers **constant rated torque from standstill to base speed**, which matches the EV's high torque requirement for city acceleration. **[3 marks]**

---

### 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks — Module Internal Choice)

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks) — V/F Control for EV Traction**

**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2024]**

**(a)** [7 Marks] Explain with a block diagram the **Variable Voltage Variable Frequency (VVVF)** speed control method of a three-phase induction motor used in an electric vehicle. Discuss the **three operating regions** of the V/F drive and their relevance to EV driving cycles.

**(b)** [7 Marks] A 4-pole, 50 Hz, 3-phase induction motor has a rotor resistance of $0.2\ \Omega$ per phase and standstill rotor reactance of $1.0\ \Omega$ per phase. Calculate the slip at maximum torque and the speed at maximum torque. If the supply frequency is reduced to 25 Hz while maintaining V/f ratio constant, what is the new synchronous speed and the new slip at maximum torque?

**Model Solution for (a):**
The VVVF control uses a **three-phase voltage source inverter (VSI)** fed from the EV's DC battery bus. The VCU (Vehicle Control Unit) commands reference frequency $f^*$ and voltage $V^* = k \cdot f^*$, which are converted to PWM gate signals (using **SPWM or SVPWM**) for the inverter IGBTs.

**Three Operating Regions:**
1. **Constant Torque Region (0 → 1500 RPM):** $V \propto f$, $\Phi = $ rated, $T_{max} = $ constant. Used during **launch and low-speed city driving**.
2. **Constant Power Region (1500 → ~3000 RPM):** $V = V_{rated}$ (held at inverter ceiling), $f$ continues to rise, $\Phi$ weakens $\propto 1/f$. Used during **highway cruising and overtaking**.
3. **Series Region (>3000 RPM):** Both $V$ and the slope of $f$ are limited; torque falls $\propto 1/N^2$. Used sparingly at **top speed**.

Block Diagram (text form):
`DC Bus → Inverter (IGBTs) → 3-phase IM → Resolver → Controller → PWM generator → Inverter`

**Model Solution for (b):**

Given: $P = 4$, $f_1 = 50$ Hz, $R_2 = 0.2\ \Omega$, $X_2 = 1.0\ \Omega$.

**Step 1:** Slip at maximum torque (original):
$$s_{max} = \frac{R_2}{X_2} = \frac{0.2}{1.0} = 0.2 \text{ p.u.}$$

**Step 2:** Synchronous speed at 50 Hz:
$$N_{s1} = \frac{120 \times 50}{4} = 1500 \text{ RPM}$$

**Step 3:** Speed at maximum torque:
$$N_{r1} = N_{s1}(1 - s_{max}) = 1500(1 - 0.2) = 1200 \text{ RPM}$$

**Step 4:** New synchronous speed at 25 Hz:
$$N_{s2} = \frac{120 \times 25}{4} = 750 \text{ RPM}$$

**Step 5:** New standstill reactance at 25 Hz (scales linearly with frequency):
$$X_2' = X_2 \cdot \frac{f_2}{f_1} = 1.0 \times \frac{25}{50} = 0.5\ \Omega$$

**Step 6:** New slip at maximum torque:
$$s_{max}' = \frac{R_2}{X_2'} = \frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4 \text{ p.u.}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Observation:** Even though the slip at max torque changed from 0.2 to 0.4, the *magnitude* of maximum torque remains the **same** because V/f is held constant. This is the magic of VVVF control — torque envelope is preserved across the speed range. **[14 marks total]**

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks) — Vector Control Theory**

**[KTU University Exam – June 2024]**

**(a)** [7 Marks] Explain the principle of **Field-Oriented Control (FOC)** of an induction motor. Derive the expression for electromagnetic torque in the d-q reference frame and show how torque and flux are decoupled.

**(b)** [7 Marks] Compare the **V/F control**, **Direct Torque Control (DTC)**, and **FOC** methods in terms of dynamic response, complexity, parameter sensitivity, and suitability for EV traction. State which method is most commonly used in production EVs and justify.

**Model Solution for (a):**

FOC transforms the 3-phase stator currents $(i_a, i_b, i_c)$ into a 2-phase rotating reference frame $(d, q)$ aligned with the rotor flux vector $\vec{\lambda_r}$. This is achieved in two steps:
1. **Clarke Transform:** $abc \rightarrow \alpha\beta$ (stationary 2-phase)
2. **Park Transform:** $\alpha\beta \rightarrow dq$ (rotating with $\vec{\lambda_r}$)

After alignment, by definition the q-axis rotor flux $\lambda_{qr} = 0$, leaving only $\lambda_{dr} = \lambda_r$.

**Derivation of torque expression** (recap from Section 3.4):

The general d-q torque equation is:
$$T_e = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{P}{2} \cdot L_m (i_{qs} i_{dr} - i_{ds} i_{qr})$$

With $\lambda_{qr} = 0$, solving the rotor circuit gives:
$$i_{dr} = \frac{\lambda_r - L_m i_{ds}}{L_r}, \quad i_{qr} = - \frac{L_m}{L_r} i_{qs}$$

Substituting and simplifying:
$$T_e = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{P}{2} \cdot \frac{L_m}{L_r} \cdot i_{qs} \cdot \lambda_r = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{P}{2} \cdot \frac{L_m^2}{L_r} \cdot i_{ds} \cdot i_{qs}$$

**Decoupling achieved:** $i_{ds}$ solely controls flux $\lambda_r$; $i_{qs}$ solely controls torque $T_e$. They are orthogonal — the motor behaves like a DC motor under software control.

**Model Solution for (b):**

| Criterion | V/F Control | DTC | FOC |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dynamic Response** | Slow (open-loop) | Fastest (~1 ms) | Fast (~2–5 ms) |
| **Implementation Complexity** | Very simple | Moderate | High (needs Park/Clarke) |
| **Parameter Sensitivity** | Low | Low | High (needs $R_r$, $L_m$) |
| **Torque Ripple** | High at low speed | Highest | Lowest (smooth) |
| **Current Quality** | Distorted | Distorted | Near-sinusoidal |
| **EV Suitability** | Low (2-wheeler, small EVs) | Good (commercial EVs) | **Excellent (most modern EVs)** |

**Conclusion:** **FOC is the industry standard** for production EVs (Tesla Model S/X/3, Tata Nexon EV, Hyundai Kona) because it offers the best **trade-off between smooth torque delivery (low ripple for NVH comfort), wide constant-power operating range (for highway driving), and regenerative braking precision**. V/F is used in budget 2-wheelers; DTC is occasionally used in industrial EVs where noise is less critical. **[14 marks total]**

---

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Deduction Zones (Examiner Notes):**
> 1. **Forgetting to scale rotor reactance with frequency** — when frequency changes, $X_2 = 2\pi f L_2$ changes too! Students often use the 50 Hz value, losing 2 marks.
> 2. **Confusing $P_m$ (developed power) with $P_{out}$ (shaft power)** — always subtract mechanical losses (friction + windage).
> 3. **Skipping the Clarke + Park transform steps** in FOC derivations — these are *expected* steps, not optional commentary.
> 4. **Writing "V/F is constant" without specifying the operating region** — examiners expect explicit mention of constant-torque vs. field-weakening regions.
> 5. **Using wrong pole pairs** — remember $P$ in formulas refers to *number of poles*, but $\omega_s = 2\pi f / (P/2)$ uses *pole pairs*. Mixing these costs marks.

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **Synchronous speed** $N_s = 120 f / P$ is the upper bound; rotor always lags by slip $s$.
- **Slip** $s = (N_s - N_r)/N_s$ is the operational lever for torque control.
- **V/F control** maintains constant flux below base speed — the *workhorse* of EV traction.
- **Three operating regions**: Constant Torque → Constant Power (field weakening) → Series.
- **Field-weakening** allows the motor to run above base speed (essential for highway EVs).
- **FOC** decouples flux ($i_d$) and torque ($i_q$) — gives DC-motor-like control to an AC machine.
- **DTC** offers fastest response at the cost of higher torque ripple and noise.
- **For EV battery sizing:** $P_{batt} = T_e \cdot \omega_m / (\eta_{motor} \cdot \eta_{inverter})$.
- **Regenerative braking** uses the same inverter in reverse — motor acts as generator, charging the DC bus.
- **Tesla's choice of induction motors** (over PMSMs in early models) was driven by **lower cost (no rare-earth magnets)** and **robustness** — proving IM with FOC is a credible EV technology.
- **Most production EVs use FOC + Space Vector PWM (SVPWM)** on **SiC MOSFET inverters** for >95% efficiency.
- **Remember** the magic result: $s_{max} = R_2/X_2$ — *independent* of voltage, a favorite KTU short-answer question.
- **Remember** the V/F result: constant $V/f$ ⟹ constant $T_{max}$ — the foundation of every EV inverter control law.

---

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->
