<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Battery — Formal KTU 2024 Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Battery (Electrochemical Energy Storage Device):** A battery is a **galvanic (voltaic) cell** or an assembly of such cells that converts stored **chemical energy** into **electrical energy** through spontaneous redox (reduction–oxidation) reactions. In the context of **Hybrid and Electric Vehicles (HEVs/EVs)**, a battery functions as the **primary on-board Energy Storage System (ESS)**, supplying electrical power to the traction motor, auxiliary loads, and regenerative braking recovery circuits.

A battery is rated by its **nominal voltage (V)**, **capacity (Ah)**, **energy content (Wh or kWh)**, and **C-rate**, all of which must be tightly matched to the vehicle's power-train demand profile.

---

### 1.2 Intuitive Analogy — "The Water Tank Model"

> [!NOTE]
> **Conceptual Analogy:** Imagine a water tank connected to a tap.
> - The **size of the tank** = **Capacity (Ah)** — how much charge it can hold.
> - The **water pressure** = **Voltage (V)** — how forcefully the charge is delivered.
> - The **total water you can spray** = **Energy (Wh = V × Ah)** — the actual useful work.
> - **How fast you open the tap** = **C-rate** — the speed of discharge.
> - **Sediment buildup over time** = **Internal resistance rise / State of Health (SOH) loss** with ageing.
> - **Scale inside the tank** = **State of Charge (SOC) indicator**.

A bigger tank with higher pressure = more energy. Opening the tap wider (higher C-rate) drains it faster and stresses the system more. This is exactly how a **Traction Battery Pack** behaves in an EV.

---

### 1.3 Types of Batteries (HEV/EV Relevant)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> KTU 2024 Module 3 mandates study of the following battery chemistries used in modern vehicles:

| Category | Examples | Key Trait |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| **Lead-Acid (Pb-acid)** | SLI, VRLA, AGM | Mature, cheap, low energy density |
| **Nickel-Metal Hydride (NiMH)** | Toyota Prius Gen 1–3 packs | Reliable, moderate energy density |
| **Lithium-Ion (Li-ion) family** | LFP, NMC, NCA, LTO | High energy & power density |
| **Solid-State Batteries** | Sulfide / Oxide / Polymer electrolytes | Next-gen, non-flammable |
| **Sodium-Ion / Zinc-Air** | Emerging chemistries | Low-cost alternatives |

The **Lithium-ion family** dominates contemporary EV traction packs because of superior **specific energy (Wh/kg)** and **cycle life**.

---

### 1.4 Core Battery Parameters — Quick Glossary

> [!NOTE]
> **Essential Parameter Vocabulary (KTU Board-Exam Favourite):**

- **Nominal Voltage (Vₙ):** The reference operating voltage of a single cell.
- **Open-Circuit Voltage (OCV):** Terminal voltage when no load is connected.
- **Terminal Voltage (Vₜ):** Voltage under load — always less than OCV due to internal resistance drop.
- **Capacity (C, Ah):** Total charge a battery can deliver; 1 Ah = 3600 Coulombs.
- **Energy (E, Wh):** Total work extractable = Vₙ × C.
- **C-rate:** Discharge/charge current normalised to rated capacity.
- **State of Charge (SOC):** Present charge level as a percentage of full charge.
- **Depth of Discharge (DOD):** Complement of SOC; charge used so far.
- **State of Health (SOH):** Current maximum capacity ÷ rated capacity, expressed as a percentage.
- **Internal Resistance (Rᵢ):** Opposition to current flow inside the cell (mΩ level).
- **Cycle Life:** Number of complete charge–discharge cycles before capacity fades to 80 % of rated value.
- **Specific Energy (Wh/kg):** Energy per unit mass.
- **Energy Density (Wh/L):** Energy per unit volume.
- **Specific Power (W/kg):** Power-delivery capability per unit mass.

---

### 1.5 Units of Battery Energy Storage

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Standard SI & Practical Units used in EV Industry:**

- **Charge:** Coulomb (C), Ampere-hour (Ah), where **1 Ah = 3600 C**.
- **Energy:** Joule (J), Watt-hour (Wh), kilowatt-hour (kWh), where **1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ**.
- **Power:** Watt (W), kilowatt (kW).
- **Energy Density (Gravimetric):** Wh/kg.
- **Energy Density (Volumetric):** Wh/L.
- **Specific Power:** W/kg.
- **Operating Temperature:** °C or K.
- **Self-Discharge Rate:** % per month.

A typical EV traction pack stores between **30 kWh (small EV)** to **100+ kWh (long-range EV)**. The 1 kWh benchmark is sometimes used as a **rule-of-thumb unit cost reference**.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Why Different Battery Types Exist — The Engineering Trade-off

Batteries are not "one-size-fits-all." Each chemistry represents a compromise along four engineering axes:

1. **Energy Density** — How far can the vehicle go on a full charge?
2. **Power Density** — How fast can it accelerate / accept regen braking?
3. **Cycle Life** — How long before replacement?
4. **Safety / Cost** — Thermal runaway risk and $ per kWh.

> [!NOTE]
> **Why the EV industry moved from Pb-acid → NiMH → Li-ion:**
> Energy density increased from ~**35 Wh/kg (Pb-acid)** → ~**80 Wh/kg (NiMH)** → ~**150–250 Wh/kg (Li-ion NMC)**. This directly translated to **longer driving range** without increasing pack weight.

---

### 2.2 Comparison of Major EV Battery Chemistries

| Chemistry | Nominal V (V) | Specific Energy (Wh/kg) | Cycle Life | EV Application |
|-----------|---------------|--------------------------|------------|----------------|
| Lead-Acid (VRLA) | 2.0 | 30–40 | 300–500 | 12 V aux, mild-hybrid |
| NiMH | 1.2 | 60–90 | 1000+ | Toyota Prius (Gen 1–3) |
| Li-ion LFP | 3.2 | 90–160 | 2000–5000 | BYD, e-buses, entry EVs |
| Li-ion NMC | 3.7 | 150–220 | 1000–2000 | Hyundai, Kia, VW, MG |
| Li-ion NCA | 3.6 | 200–260 | 500–1000 | Tesla (legacy) |
| Li-Titanate LTO | 2.4 | 60–80 | 10000+ | Ultra-fast charging EVs |
| Solid-State (emerging) | ~3.7 | 300–500 (target) | TBD | 2027+ production EVs |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Memory Trick — "LFP is Safe, NMC is Normal, NCA is Niche, LTO is Long-life, Solid is the Star."**

---

### 2.3 Detailed Battery Parameter Analysis

#### A. Voltage Parameters
- **Electromotive Force (EMF / OCV):** Determined by Nernst equation based on electrolyte concentration and electrode chemistry.
- **Terminal Voltage:** Vₜ = OCV − I × Rᵢ (during discharge).
- **Cut-off Voltage:** Manufacturer-defined minimum allowed Vₜ; discharging below it permanently damages the cell.

#### B. Capacity
- **Theoretical Capacity** = (n × F) / (3600 × M), where n = electrons transferred, F = Faraday constant, M = molar mass of active material.
- **Practical Capacity < Theoretical** because of side reactions, inactive mass, and electrolyte depletion.

#### C. Internal Resistance
- **Ohmic part (RΩ):** Electrode + electrolyte + contact resistance.
- **Charge-transfer part (Rct):** From electrochemical reaction kinetics.
- **Diffusion part (Wd):** From mass-transport limitations.
- **Total Rᵢ = RΩ + Rct + Wd** — rises as SOC drops and as the cell ages.

#### D. Self-Discharge
All batteries lose charge when idle. Rate: ~**3–20 % per month** depending on chemistry and temperature.

#### E. Efficiency
- **Coulombic Efficiency (ηC)** = (Charge out ÷ Charge in) × 100 %.
- **Energy Efficiency (ηE)** = (Energy out ÷ Energy in) × 100 %.
- Li-ion: ηC > 99 %, ηE ≈ 90–95 %.

---

### 2.4 Capacity Rate (C-Rate) — The Heart of EV Powertrain Sizing

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **C-Rate Definition (KTU Board Definition):**
> The **C-rate** is the **discharge or charge current** of a battery expressed as a **multiple of its rated capacity**. A **1C rate** means the current that would **fully discharge the battery in 1 hour**. An **nC rate** means the current that would **fully discharge the battery in (1/n) hours**.

**Mathematical Statement:**

$$C\text{-rate} = \dfrac{I_{\text{discharge}}}{C_{\text{rated}}}$$

where $I_{\text{discharge}}$ is in Amperes and $C_{\text{rated}}$ is in Ampere-hours (Ah).

**Inverse relationship with discharge time:**

$$t_{\text{discharge}} = \dfrac{C_{\text{rated}}}{I} = \dfrac{1}{C\text{-rate}} \text{ (hours)}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Real EV Example — Tesla Model 3 LR Pack:**
> Capacity ≈ **75 kWh** at ~**350 V nominal** → pack Ah ≈ 214 Ah.
> Peak discharge current during launch ≈ **1500 A** → C-rate ≈ 1500 / 214 ≈ **7C**.
> This means the pack is designed to deliver its full energy in just **~8.5 minutes** at peak power. A normal driving C-rate is around **0.3C–0.5C**.

---

### 2.5 Units of Battery Energy Storage — Conversion Hierarchy

$$1 \text{ kWh} = 1000 \text{ Wh} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ J} = 3.6 \text{ MJ}$$

$$1 \text{ Ah} \times V_{\text{nominal}} = 1 \text{ Wh (at that voltage)}$$

$$E_{\text{stored}} = V_{\text{nominal}} \times C_{\text{Ah}} \quad [\text{Wh}]$$

$$E_{\text{stored}} = \dfrac{V_{\text{nominal}} \times C_{\text{Ah}}}{1000} \quad [\text{kWh}]$$

---

### 2.6 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet (Exam Cheat Sheet)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **All equations you must memorise for Module-3 KTU Board Exam:**

| # | Formula | Description | Units |
|---|---------|-------------|-------|
| 1 | $E = V \times C$ | Energy stored | Wh |
| 2 | $E = V \times I \times t$ | Energy from power × time | Wh |
| 3 | $P = V \times I$ | Instantaneous power | W |
| 4 | $E = P \times t$ | Energy = power × time | Wh |
| 5 | $C\text{-rate} = I / C_{\text{rated}}$ | C-rate definition | dimensionless |
| 6 | $t = 1 / C\text{-rate}$ | Discharge time at constant C-rate | hours |
| 7 | $I = C_{\text{rated}} \times C\text{-rate}$ | Current from C-rate | A |
| 8 | $SOC = (C_{\text{remaining}} / C_{\text{rated}}) \times 100$ | State of Charge | % |
| 9 | $DOD = 100 - SOC$ | Depth of Discharge | % |
| 10 | $SOH = (C_{\text{max,present}} / C_{\text{rated,new}}) \times 100$ | State of Health | % |
| 11 | $Q = I \times t$ | Charge delivered | Ah |
| 12 | $E_{\text{specific}} = E / m$ | Specific energy | Wh/kg |
| 13 | $P_{\text{specific}} = P / m$ | Specific power | W/kg |
| 14 | $V_t = OCV - I \cdot R_i$ | Terminal voltage under load | V |
| 15 | $\eta_E = (E_{out} / E_{in}) \times 100$ | Energy efficiency | % |
| 16 | $E_{\text{kinetic}} = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ | Regen braking recoverable energy | J |
| 17 | $R_{\text{total}} = R_\Omega + R_{ct} + W_d$ | Internal resistance components | Ω |
| 18 | $1 \text{ kWh} = 3.6 \text{ MJ} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$ | Energy unit conversion | — |

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Utility:** In EV design, equations 1–7 are used during **battery pack sizing**; equations 8–10 drive the **BMS (Battery Management System)** firmware; equations 12–13 dictate **vehicle range and acceleration performance**; equation 16 links **regenerative braking energy recovery** to motor-controller design.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation 1 — Relationship Between C-Rate and Discharge Time

> [!NOTE]
> **Starting Premise:** C-rate is the current that would discharge a fully charged cell in exactly one hour.

**Step 1:** By definition, the **rated capacity** of a battery is the charge it can deliver over 1 hour at its rated discharge current.

$$C_{\text{rated}} = I_{\text{1C}} \times 1 \text{ hour}$$

This is a direct application of the fundamental charge equation:

$$Q = I \times t \quad \Rightarrow \quad I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$$

**Step 2:** Substituting the rated capacity in Ampere-hours and the discharge time of 1 hour:

$$I_{\text{1C}} = \dfrac{C_{\text{rated}}}{1 \text{ h}} = C_{\text{rated}} \quad \text{[in Amperes, when C is in Ah]}$$

**Step 3:** For a generic C-rate of value $n$ (e.g., 2C, 0.5C, 5C), the discharge current is:

$$I_{nC} = n \times I_{\text{1C}} = n \times C_{\text{rated}}$$

**Step 4:** The discharge time $t$ at this current equals the rated capacity divided by the discharge current:

$$t = \dfrac{C_{\text{rated}}}{I_{nC}}$$

**Step 5:** Substitute $I_{nC} = n \times C_{\text{rated}}$:

$$t = \dfrac{C_{\text{rated}}}{n \times C_{\text{rated}}}$$

**Step 6:** Cancel $C_{\text{rated}}$ from numerator and denominator:

$$\boxed{\,t = \dfrac{1}{n} \text{ hours}\,}$$

**Interpretation Table:**

| C-rate (n) | Discharge Current (I = nC) | Discharge Time (t) |
|------------|----------------------------|--------------------|
| 0.2C | 0.2 × C_rated | 5 h |
| 0.5C | 0.5 × C_rated | 2 h |
| 1C | 1 × C_rated | 1 h |
| 2C | 2 × C_rated | 30 min |
| 5C | 5 × C_rated | 12 min |
| 10C | 10 × C_rated | 6 min |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Exam Tip:** Always show Step 3–Step 6 explicitly. Marks are awarded for **substitution and cancellation** steps, not just the final box.

---

### 3.2 Derivation 2 — Energy Stored vs Capacity vs C-rate

**Step 1:** The total energy stored in a battery is the integral of instantaneous power over the discharge time:

$$E = \int_{0}^{t} P(t) \, dt$$

**Step 2:** For a battery operating at (approximately) constant terminal voltage $V$ and constant current $I$:

$$E = V \times I \times t$$

**Step 3:** But $I \times t = Q$, the charge delivered. If the battery is fully discharged:

$$Q = C_{\text{rated}} \quad \text{[in Ah]}$$

**Step 4:** Substituting:

$$E = V \times C_{\text{rated}}$$

**Step 5:** If the discharge is only partial (DOD = x, where $0 \le x \le 1$):

$$E_{\text{usable}} = x \times V \times C_{\text{rated}}$$

**Step 6:** In SI units (Joules), recognising $1 \text{ V} \times 1 \text{ Ah} = 3600 \text{ J}$:

$$E_{\text{Joules}} = V \times C_{\text{rated}} \times 3600$$

**Step 7:** To convert to kWh, divide by 1000:

$$\boxed{\,E_{\text{kWh}} = \dfrac{V \times C_{\text{rated}}}{1000}\,}$$

**Verification Example (Numerical):**
- A 400 V, 100 Ah pack → E = 400 × 100 / 1000 = **40 kWh**. ✓
- A 350 V, 214 Ah pack (Tesla Model 3) → E = 350 × 214 / 1000 ≈ **74.9 kWh**. ✓

---

### 3.3 Derivation 3 — Power Delivered at a Given C-rate

**Step 1:** Instantaneous power delivered by the battery:

$$P = V_{\text{terminal}} \times I$$

**Step 2:** Substituting $I = n \times C_{\text{rated}}$:

$$P = V_{\text{terminal}} \times n \times C_{\text{rated}}$$

**Step 3:** Using $V \times C_{\text{rated}} = E$ (rated energy in Wh):

$$P = n \times E_{\text{rated,Wh}}$$

**Step 4:** To get power in kW:

$$\boxed{\,P_{\text{kW}} = n \times E_{\text{rated,kWh}}\,}$$

**Interpretation:** A battery with **75 kWh** rated energy discharged at **2C** delivers:
- $P = 2 \times 75 = 150$ kW of peak power.

This is the equation used by EV manufacturers to **advertise peak motor power** from the battery pack.

---

### 3.4 Derivation 4 — Peukert's Law (Capacity Fading at High C-rate)

> [!NOTE]
> **Background:** A real battery delivers **less usable capacity** at high discharge currents than its rated value. This is captured empirically by **Peukert's Law (1897)**.

**Step 1:** Empirical statement of Peukert's Law:

$$t = H \times \left( \dfrac{C_{\text{rated}}}{I \times H} \right)^{n}$$

where:
- $t$ = actual discharge time (hours)
- $H$ = rated discharge time (hours, typically 20 h for lead-acid)
- $C_{\text{rated}}$ = rated capacity (Ah)
- $I$ = actual discharge current (A)
- $n$ = Peukert's exponent (1.0 < n < 1.5; typically ~1.2 for lead-acid, ~1.05 for Li-ion)

**Step 2:** Simplify by setting $H = 1$ (i.e., rate relative to 1C):

$$t = \left( \dfrac{C_{\text{rated}}}{I} \right)^{n}$$

**Step 3:** The effective capacity delivered is $C_{\text{eff}} = I \times t$:

$$C_{\text{eff}} = I \times \left( \dfrac{C_{\text{rated}}}{I} \right)^{n} = I^{1-n} \times C_{\text{rated}}^{n}$$

**Step 4:** Take logarithms to linearise (useful for experimental data fitting):

$$\log(t) = n \cdot \log(C_{\text{rated}}) - n \cdot \log(I) + \log(H)$$

**Step 5:** Example — a 100 Ah lead-acid battery with n = 1.25:
- At 5 A discharge (0.05C) → t = (100/5)^1.25 = 20^1.25 ≈ 47.7 h → C_eff ≈ 238 Ah (effective).
- At 50 A discharge (0.5C) → t = (100/50)^1.25 = 2^1.25 ≈ 2.38 h → C_eff ≈ 119 Ah.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Significance:** Peukert's Law is why EV packs specify a **maximum continuous C-rate** (typically 1C–2C) and a **peak C-rate** (3C–10C) separately. Operating at very high C-rates continuously causes irreversible capacity loss.

---

### 3.5 Derivation 5 — Regenerative Braking Energy Recovery Efficiency

**Step 1:** Kinetic energy of a moving vehicle of mass $m$ at speed $v$:

$$E_{\text{kinetic}} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$$

**Step 2:** Convert speed from km/h to m/s: $v_{\text{m/s}} = v_{\text{km/h}} \times \dfrac{5}{18}$

$$E_{\text{kinetic}} = \dfrac{1}{2} m \left( v_{\text{km/h}} \times \dfrac{5}{18} \right)^2$$

**Step 3:** Regenerative system recovers only a fraction $\eta_{\text{regen}}$ (typically 0.6–0.8) and battery charge acceptance is $\eta_{\text{chg}}$ (~0.9 for Li-ion):

$$E_{\text{recovered}} = \eta_{\text{regen}} \times \eta_{\text{chg}} \times E_{\text{kinetic}}$$

**Step 4:** Add the **C-rate check** to ensure battery can absorb the regen current:

$$I_{\text{regen}} = \dfrac{P_{\text{regen}}}{V_{\text{bus}}} = \dfrac{F_{\text{brake}} \times v}{V_{\text{bus}}}$$

The regen C-rate is $I_{\text{regen}} / C_{\text{rated}}$, which must be within the battery's **maximum charge C-rate limit** (typically 1C–2C for Li-ion NMC, up to 5C for LTO).

**Numerical Example (KTU-style):**
- $m = 1500$ kg, $v = 60$ km/h = 16.67 m/s, $\eta_{\text{regen}} = 0.7$, $\eta_{\text{chg}} = 0.9$.
- $E_{\text{kinetic}} = 0.5 \times 1500 \times (16.67)^2 = 0.5 \times 1500 \times 277.9 = 208{,}425$ J ≈ **57.9 Wh**.
- $E_{\text{recovered}} = 0.7 \times 0.9 \times 57.9 = 36.5$ Wh per braking event.

## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short-Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Style]**

---

**Q1. Define the term C-rate with a suitable example.** `[3 Marks]`

**Model Answer:**

> [!NOTE]
> The **C-rate** of a battery is the **discharge or charge current** expressed as a **multiple of its rated capacity** (in Ah). Mathematically, $\text{C-rate} = I / C_{\text{rated}}$, where $I$ is the current in Amperes and $C_{\text{rated}}$ is the rated capacity in Ampere-hours. It is **dimensionless**.
>
> **Example:** A battery rated at **50 Ah** discharged at **25 A** is operating at a C-rate of $25 / 50 = 0.5\text{C}$. The discharge time at this rate is $t = 1 / 0.5 = 2$ hours. *(3 marks: 1 for definition, 1 for formula, 1 for numerical example.)*

---

**Q2. List any six important battery parameters used to characterise EV traction batteries.** `[3 Marks]`

**Model Answer:**

> [!NOTE]
> Six important battery parameters for EV traction batteries are:
> 1. **Nominal Voltage (Vₙ)** — Reference operating voltage per cell.
> 2. **Capacity (C, Ah)** — Total charge deliverable.
> 3. **Energy (E, Wh or kWh)** — Total work extractable = V × C.
> 4. **Specific Energy (Wh/kg)** — Energy per unit mass, governs range.
> 5. **C-rate** — Normalised charge/discharge current.
> 6. **State of Charge (SOC, %)** — Present charge level as a percentage of full charge.
>
> *(Other acceptable parameters: Internal Resistance, Cycle Life, SOH, DOD, Self-Discharge Rate, Power Density.)* *(3 marks: 0.5 mark per parameter.)*

---

### 5.2 Part B — Long-Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, with Internal Choice)

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 / Model Paper Style]**

---

#### QUESTION A (14 Marks)

**(a)** Classify and explain the **different types of batteries** used in Electric and Hybrid Electric Vehicles, with a focus on **Lead-Acid, NiMH, and Li-ion** chemistries. Compare their **specific energy, cycle life, and cost**. `[7 Marks]`

**(b)** Define the following parameters in detail: **C-rate, State of Charge (SOC), Depth of Discharge (DOD), State of Health (SOH), and Internal Resistance**. Show how SOC and DOD are mathematically related. `[7 Marks]`

---

#### MODEL SOLUTION — Question A

**(a) Battery Types for EV/HEV:**

> [!NOTE]
> **1. Lead-Acid Batteries (Pb-acid):** The oldest rechargeable battery technology. Two varieties — **SLI (Starting, Lighting, Ignition)** and **VRLA (Valve-Regulated Lead-Acid, including AGM)**. Used in conventional 12 V auxiliary systems and in some mild-hybrid 48 V architectures. Specific energy ~**30–40 Wh/kg**, cycle life ~**300–500 cycles**, cost ~**$100–150/kWh**. Pros: cheap, recyclable, robust. Cons: low energy density, sulphation if left discharged, contains toxic lead. *(2 marks)*

> [!NOTE]
> **2. Nickel-Metal Hydride (NiMH):** Dominated first-generation HEVs, notably the **Toyota Prius (1997–2015)**. Specific energy ~**60–90 Wh/kg**, cycle life ~**1000+ cycles**, cost ~**$250–300/kWh**. Pros: safe, tolerant to overcharge, good power density. Cons: memory effect (mild), self-discharge higher than Li-ion, contains nickel (expensive). *(2 marks)*

> [!NOTE]
> **3. Lithium-Ion Family (Li-ion):** Current standard for all modern EVs. Sub-variants:
> - **LFP (LiFePO₄):** ~3.2 V nominal, 90–160 Wh/kg, safest, 2000–5000 cycles, used in BYD and entry-level EVs.
> - **NMC (Li-Ni-Mn-Co-O₂):** ~3.7 V nominal, 150–220 Wh/kg, 1000–2000 cycles, used in Hyundai, Kia, VW.
> - **NCA (Li-Ni-Co-Al-O₂):** ~3.6 V nominal, 200–260 Wh/kg, used in Tesla legacy packs.
> - **LTO (Li₄Ti₅O₁₂):** ~2.4 V nominal, 60–80 Wh/kg, 10000+ cycles, ultra-fast charging.
>
> Cost: ~**$120–140/kWh** (2024 industry benchmark). Pros: highest energy density, low self-discharge, no memory effect. Cons: requires BMS, thermal runaway risk if abused. *(3 marks)*

**Comparison Table (within the 7-mark sub-part):**

| Chemistry | Specific Energy (Wh/kg) | Cycle Life | Relative Cost |
|-----------|--------------------------|------------|---------------|
| Pb-acid | 30–40 | 300–500 | Lowest |
| NiMH | 60–90 | 1000+ | Medium |
| Li-ion (LFP) | 90–160 | 2000–5000 | Low–Medium |
| Li-ion (NMC) | 150–220 | 1000–2000 | Medium–High |
| Li-ion (NCA) | 200–260 | 500–1000 | High |

---

**(b) Battery Parameter Definitions:**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **1. C-rate:** Defined as the discharge (or charge) current divided by the rated capacity: $\text{C-rate} = I / C_{\text{rated}}$. A 1C rate discharges the battery in 1 hour; a 2C rate in 30 minutes; a 0.5C rate in 2 hours. Dimensionless. *(1.5 marks)*

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **2. State of Charge (SOC):** The ratio of **remaining capacity** to **rated capacity**, expressed as a percentage:
> $$SOC = \dfrac{C_{\text{remaining}}}{C_{\text{rated}}} \times 100\%$$
> SOC = 100 % when fully charged; SOC = 0 % at cut-off voltage. *(1.5 marks)*

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **3. Depth of Discharge (DOD):** The percentage of rated capacity that has been **discharged**:
> $$DOD = \dfrac{C_{\text{discharged}}}{C_{\text{rated}}} \times 100\%$$
> *(1 mark)*

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **4. State of Health (SOH):** Ratio of **present maximum capacity** to **rated new capacity**:
> $$SOH = \dfrac{C_{\text{max,present}}}{C_{\text{rated,new}}} \times 100\%$$
> A battery is considered end-of-life when SOH ≤ 80 %. *(1.5 marks)*

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **5. Internal Resistance (Rᵢ):** Opposition to current flow inside the cell; composed of **ohmic (RΩ)**, **charge-transfer (Rct)**, and **diffusion (Wd)** components. Rises with age, low SOC, and low temperature. Affects terminal voltage: $V_t = OCV - I \cdot R_i$. *(1.5 marks)*

**SOC–DOD Relationship:**
$$SOC + DOD = 100\%$$
$$\boxed{\,SOC = 100\% - DOD\,}$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Do not confuse SOH with SOC.** SOH measures ageing (capacity fade over years); SOC measures instantaneous charge level.
> 2. **Internal resistance is temperature-dependent** — stating only the formula $V_t = OCV - IR_i$ without mentioning the temperature variation is considered incomplete and loses 1 mark.
> 3. **C-rate is dimensionless**, not in "per hour." Writing "C-rate = 1/h" is a common wrong answer that costs 0.5–1 mark.
> 4. In the comparison table, ensure you mention **cycle life** alongside specific energy and cost — examiners specifically check for it.

---

#### QUESTION B (14 Marks) — *Internal Choice Alternative*

**(a)** A **Li-ion traction battery** is rated at **200 Ah** and **3.7 V nominal voltage**. Calculate:
- (i) The **total rated energy** in kWh and MJ. `[2 Marks]`
- (ii) The **discharge current and time** if discharged at a **C/5 rate**. `[2 Marks]`
- (iii) The **peak power** delivered if the battery is momentarily discharged at **5C rate**. `[3 Marks]`

**(b)** Explain the **units of battery energy storage** (Wh, kWh, Ah, MJ) and show how they interconvert. Discuss why **specific energy (Wh/kg)** and **energy density (Wh/L)** are the most important metrics for EV designers. `[7 Marks]`

---

#### MODEL SOLUTION — Question B

**(a) Numerical Solution:**

**Given:** $C_{\text{rated}} = 200 \text{ Ah}$, $V_n = 3.7 \text{ V}$.

**(i) Rated Energy in kWh and MJ:**

$$E_{\text{Wh}} = V_n \times C_{\text{rated}} = 3.7 \times 200 = 740 \text{ Wh}$$

$$E_{\text{kWh}} = \dfrac{740}{1000} = 0.74 \text{ kWh}$$

$$E_{\text{MJ}} = 0.74 \times 3.6 = 2.664 \text{ MJ}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Answer:** $E = 0.74$ kWh = $2.664$ MJ. *(2 marks: 1 for kWh, 1 for MJ, with explicit conversion shown.)*

**(ii) Discharge Current and Time at C/5 rate:**

$$n = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2\text{C}$$

$$I = n \times C_{\text{rated}} = 0.2 \times 200 = 40 \text{ A}$$

$$t = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{0.2} = 5 \text{ hours}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Answer:** $I = 40$ A, $t = 5$ h. *(2 marks: 1 for current, 1 for time, both with units.)*

**(iii) Peak Power at 5C rate:**

$$I_{\text{peak}} = 5 \times 200 = 1000 \text{ A}$$

$$P_{\text{peak}} = V_n \times I_{\text{peak}} = 3.7 \times 1000 = 3700 \text{ W} = 3.7 \text{ kW}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Answer:** $P_{\text{peak}} = 3.7$ kW. *(3 marks: 1 for current calculation, 1 for power formula, 1 for final numerical answer with unit.)*

---

**(b) Units of Battery Energy Storage:**

> [!NOTE]
> **1. Coulomb (C):** SI unit of electric charge. $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A} \times 1 \text{ s}$. Not commonly used in EV context because batteries store thousands of Coulombs. *(1 mark)*

> [!NOTE]
> **2. Ampere-hour (Ah):** $1 \text{ Ah} = 3600 \text{ C}$. Practical unit for battery **capacity**, because it directly tells us how long the battery can deliver a known current. A 200 Ah battery can supply 200 A for 1 hour, or 50 A for 4 hours, etc. *(1 mark)*

> [!NOTE]
> **3. Watt-hour (Wh):** $1 \text{ Wh} = 3600 \text{ J}$. The product of voltage and capacity: $E = V \times C$. This is the **true measure of energy** because it accounts for the voltage at which charge is delivered. Two batteries of the same Ah rating but different voltages store different energy. *(1.5 marks)*

> [!NOTE]
> **4. Kilowatt-hour (kWh):** $1 \text{ kWh} = 1000 \text{ Wh} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ J} = 3.6 \text{ MJ}$. Industry standard for EV pack sizing. Typical EV: 30 kWh (small) to 100+ kWh (long range). *(1 mark)*

> [!NOTE]
> **5. Megajoule (MJ):** $1 \text{ MJ} = 10^6 \text{ J} = 0.2778 \text{ kWh}$. Used in scientific literature and for comparing regenerative braking energy recovery. *(0.5 mark)*

**Conversion chain:**
$$1 \text{ Ah} \times V[\text{V}] = 1 \text{ Wh} \quad \Rightarrow \quad 1000 \text{ Wh} = 1 \text{ kWh} = 3.6 \text{ MJ}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **6. Why Specific Energy and Energy Density Matter for EVs:**
> - **Specific Energy (Wh/kg)** governs the **driving range** of the EV. A higher specific energy means **lighter battery for the same range**, which further reduces the vehicle mass, creating a virtuous cycle.
> - **Energy Density (Wh/L)** governs the **pack packaging** — how much physical space the battery occupies. Critical for vehicle design because a bulky pack reduces passenger/cargo space.
> - Together, they determine whether an EV can practically achieve 400+ km range without exceeding weight and volume budgets. *(2 marks)*

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Part B Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Unit conversion errors are the #1 cause of lost marks.** Always write $1 \text{ kWh} = 3.6 \text{ MJ}$ explicitly before substituting. Do not assume the examiner will infer it.
> 2. In part (a)(iii), students often forget to **convert W to kW** at the end — losing 0.5 mark.
> 3. In part (b), do not list units without **explanations**. Listing "Wh, kWh, Ah, MJ" without converting or justifying why they are used is a 0–1 mark answer.
> 4. The relationship $1 \text{ Ah} \times V = 1 \text{ Wh}$ is a **must-state**; examiners specifically check this.

---

### 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist for Module 3 — Types of Battery, Battery Parameters, Units, C-rate**

- ☐ **Battery** = electrochemical device converting chemical energy to electrical energy; rated by **V × Ah = Wh**.
- ☐ **Five key EV battery chemistries** to remember: **Pb-acid, NiMH, LFP, NMC, NCA**. Add LTO and Solid-State for advanced answers.
- ☐ **Li-ion NMC** is the current industry standard for traction packs due to high specific energy (**150–220 Wh/kg**) and reasonable cycle life.
- ☐ **Specific energy** of Pb-acid ≈ **30–40 Wh/kg**; NiMH ≈ **60–90 Wh/kg**; Li-ion NMC ≈ **150–220 Wh/kg**.
- ☐ **Battery parameters** (must-know list): **Nominal Voltage, OCV, Terminal Voltage, Capacity, Energy, C-rate, SOC, DOD, SOH, Internal Resistance, Cycle Life, Specific Energy, Energy Density, Specific Power, Self-Discharge, Efficiency**.
- ☐ **C-rate formula:** $n = I / C_{\text{rated}}$ (dimensionless). Discharge time $t = 1/n$ hours.
- ☐ **At 1C**, a fully charged battery is exhausted in **exactly 1 hour**.
- ☐ **At 5C**, discharge time = **12 minutes** (high stress).
- ☐ **At 0.2C (C/5)**, discharge time = **5 hours** (gentle, longer life).
- ☐ **Energy** = $V_n \times C_{\text{rated}}$ in Wh; divide by 1000 for kWh; multiply by 3.6 for MJ.
- ☐ **Power** at C-rate $n$ = $n \times E_{\text{rated,kWh}}$ kW.
- ☐ **Peak regen C-rate** of typical Li-ion = **1C–2C continuous, 5C peak**; LTO can accept up to **10C**.
- ☐ **SOC + DOD = 100 %**; **SOH ≤ 80 %** = end-of-life.
- ☐ **Internal resistance** $R_i$ causes voltage drop: $V_t = OCV - I R_i$.
- ☐ **Peukert's Law** (advanced): $t = H (C / I H)^n$; high C-rate reduces effective capacity.
- ☐ **EV pack sizing** example: 400 V × 100 Ah = 40 kWh; 350 V × 214 Ah ≈ 75 kWh (Tesla Model 3 LR).
- ☐ **Rule of thumb:** 1 kWh ≈ 5–7 km of EV range (varies with vehicle efficiency).
- ☐ **Conversion constants:** $1 \text{ Ah} = 3600 \text{ C}$; $1 \text{ kWh} = 3.6 \text{ MJ}$.
- ☐ **Energy in regen braking:** $E = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ — link this to C-rate to verify BMS acceptance.

# SECTION 1 — Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Cell Voltage (V)

**Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology):**
Cell Voltage is the electric potential difference developed between the positive and negative terminals of an electrochemical cell due to the difference in electrochemical potential of the two electrodes. It is expressed in **Volts (V)** and is a fundamental performance metric for any battery used in Electric Vehicles (EVs) and Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEVs).

Three distinct voltage levels are defined in KTU board examinations:

| Term | Symbol | Definition |
|------|--------|------------|
| **Nominal Voltage** | $V_{nom}$ | The "rated" or reference voltage assigned by the manufacturer (e.g., 3.7 V for Li-ion NMC) |
| **Open-Circuit Voltage (OCV)** | $V_{oc}$ | The terminal voltage when no load is connected (steady-state) |
| **Terminal Voltage** | $V_t$ | The voltage actually delivered to the load under current draw |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Board Note:** In a discharging cell under load, $V_t < V_{oc}$ because of internal voltage drops across internal resistance.

### Conceptual Analogy — The "Water Tap" Model
Imagine a water tank placed on a rooftop. The **height of the tank** represents the **cell voltage** (pressure pushing electrons out). A taller tank pushes water (current) out with greater force. But if the connecting pipe is narrow (high internal resistance), the actual water flow at the tap (terminal voltage) will be less than the tank's potential pressure (OCV). The tap water pressure is the **terminal voltage**, the tank pressure is the **OCV**, and the narrow pipe is the **internal resistance**.

---

## 1.2 Specific Energy (Wh/kg)

**Formal Definition:**
Specific Energy is the amount of electrical energy a battery can deliver per unit mass. It is measured in **Watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg)** and is the single most important metric that determines the **driving range** of an electric vehicle.

$$E_{sp} = \frac{E_{stored}}{m_{cell}} = \frac{V_{nom} \times C_{Ah}}{m_{cell}} \quad \text{[Wh/kg]}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Why Specific Energy matters in EVs:** A higher specific energy means a lighter battery pack for the same range. Tesla's 4680 cells (~300 Wh/kg) give far more range than older LFP packs (~160 Wh/kg) of the same mass.

### Conceptual Analogy — The "Fuel Tank" Analogy
Think of specific energy as the **energy content of fuel per liter**. Diesel has more energy per liter than petrol (≈ 35.8 MJ/L vs 32 MJ/L) — similarly, Li-S batteries (~500 Wh/kg theoretical) have more "fuel" per kilogram than lead-acid (~40 Wh/kg). A Tesla carrying Li-ion cells carries less "dead weight" than an old e-rickshaw carrying lead-acid.

---

## 1.3 Cycle Life

**Formal Definition:**
Cycle Life is the **number of complete charge-discharge cycles** a battery can deliver before its usable capacity drops to a defined end-of-life threshold, conventionally **80% of its initial rated capacity** (KTU 2024 reference standard).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Standard Definition:** A "cycle" = one full charge + one full discharge = one Depth-of-Discharge (DoD) of 100%.

### Conceptual Analogy — The "Shoe Sole" Analogy
A shoe's sole wears out with every step (cycle). Light usage (shallow DoD, low current) gives many steps before the sole tears. Heavy running (deep DoD, high C-rate) wears it out fast. Different chemistries have different "sole thicknesses" — LiFePO₄ is like a thick rubber hiking boot (3000+ cycles), while NMC is like a thin racing shoe (~1000 cycles).

---

## 1.4 Self-Discharge

**Formal Definition:**
Self-Discharge is the **irreversible loss of stored charge** in a battery when it is left idle (no external load connected), caused by internal parasitic chemical reactions and internal leakage currents. It is typically expressed as a **percentage of capacity lost per month (%/month)** at a reference temperature of **25 °C**.

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Board Tip:** Self-discharge is NOT the same as coulombic inefficiency. Self-discharge occurs even at rest, while coulombic inefficiency occurs only during active cycling.

### Conceptual Analogy — The "Leaking Water Bottle"
Imagine a sealed water bottle left in a cupboard. Even closed, tiny amounts evaporate through microscopic pores. A NiMH cell "leaks" ~30% of its charge per month (high self-discharge), while a Li-ion cell loses only ~2–3% per month. Storing at cool temperatures (refrigerator) slows the "evaporation."

---

## 1.5 Static Battery Equivalent Circuit Model

**Formal Definition:**
A Static Battery Equivalent Circuit Model is a **lumped-parameter electrical network** (composed of voltage sources, resistors, and capacitors) that mathematically reproduces the **steady-state I–V behavior** of a battery. The most widely used static models in KTU 2024 syllabus are:

1. **Ideal Voltage Source Model** — $V_t = V_{oc}$
2. **R-Internal (R-int) Model** — $V_t = V_{oc} - I \cdot R_{int}$
3. **Thevenin Model** — $V_{oc}$ in series with $R_{int}$ and one parallel RC network ($R_{ct} \parallel C_{dl}$) representing transient diffusion and charge-transfer effects.
4. **N-th Order RC Model** — multiple RC branches for higher accuracy.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **"Static" means the model parameters are assumed constant** for a given State-of-Charge (SoC) and temperature — no time-varying ODEs are solved in the static case. (Dynamic models add Warburg diffusion elements.)

### Conceptual Analogy — The "Battery as a Plumbing System"
The OCV is the water tank pressure. $R_{int}$ is the narrow pipe (ohmic drop). The RC network (parallel capacitor + resistor) represents the **elastic bladder inside the tank** — when current suddenly flows, the bladder flexes (capacitor charges), causing a transient voltage dip that recovers slowly (resistor bleeding off the charge).

---

## 1.6 Series-Parallel Battery Pack Equivalent Circuits

**Formal Definition:**
An EV battery pack is constructed by connecting many individual cells in **series** (to raise voltage) and **parallel** (to raise capacity). The series-parallel equivalent circuit is the electrical network that represents this combination using an aggregated OCV, equivalent resistance, and equivalent capacitance.

- **S cells in series** → pack voltage = $S \times V_{cell}$, capacity unchanged.
- **P cells in parallel** → capacity = $P \times C_{cell}$, voltage unchanged.
- **S-P hybrid** → pack rated as **S-series × P-parallel (SxP)** configuration.

### Conceptual Analogy — The "Battery as a Building"
Imagine stacking batteries like floors of a building. Floors in **series** raise the total "height" (voltage). Within each floor, multiple batteries placed **side-by-side in parallel** widen the floor (capacity). A typical Tesla Model 3 pack is **96s46p** (96 series, 46 parallel) — 96 floors tall, with 46 batteries per floor.

# SECTION 2 — Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Cell Voltage — Deep Analysis

The thermodynamic equilibrium voltage of a cell is governed by the **Nernst Equation**:

$$V_{oc} = V^{\circ} + \frac{RT}{nF} \ln\left(\frac{a_{\text{anode}}}{a_{\text{cathode}}}\right)$$

where:
- $V^{\circ}$ = standard electrode potential
- $R$ = universal gas constant = **8.314 J/(mol·K)**
- $T$ = absolute temperature (K)
- $n$ = number of electrons transferred per reaction
- $F$ = Faraday's constant = **96,485 C/mol**
- $a$ = activity of the chemical species

**Under load (terminal voltage):**

$$V_t = V_{oc} - I \cdot R_{int}$$

**Why is the voltage not constant during discharge?**
- **Activation overvoltage** ($V_{act}$) — needed to drive charge-transfer kinetics at electrodes.
- **Ohmic overvoltage** ($V_{ohm} = IR_{int}$) — drop across electrolyte, current collectors, electrodes.
- **Concentration overvoltage** ($V_{conc}$) — due to mass-transport limitations of ions.

$$V_t = V_{oc} - V_{act} - V_{ohm} - V_{conc}$$

---

## 2.2 Specific Energy — Deep Analysis

Specific energy can be expressed volumetrically or gravimetrically:

| Metric | Formula | Unit | Used For |
|--------|---------|------|----------|
| **Gravimetric Specific Energy** | $E_{sp} = \dfrac{V_{nom} \cdot C_{Ah}}{m}$ | Wh/kg | Vehicle range per mass |
| **Volumetric Energy Density** | $E_{vol} = \dfrac{V_{nom} \cdot C_{Ah}}{V_{cell}}$ | Wh/L | Pack packaging |

**Relationship to Specific Power:**
- **Specific Power** $P_{sp} = \dfrac{V \cdot I}{m}$ in W/kg
- **Energy-to-Power Ratio** (Ragone plot) determines application:
  - **High $E_{sp}$, low $P_{sp}$** → long-range EVs (e.g., NMC, LFP)
  - **Low $E_{sp}$, high $P_{sp}$** → acceleration, hybrid mode (e.g., NMC + supercapacitor hybrids)

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Exam Tip:** A common question: "Why can't we use lead-acid batteries in modern EVs?" Answer: low specific energy (~40 Wh/kg) — too heavy for range.

---

## 2.3 Cycle Life — Deep Analysis

**Mathematical definition:**
$$N_{cycles} = \text{Number of cycles until } C_{actual}(N) = 0.8 \times C_{rated}$$

**Empirical degradation model (KTU 2024):**
$$Q(N) = Q_0 \cdot \left(1 - k \cdot N^{0.5}\right)$$

where $k$ is a degradation constant dependent on chemistry, DoD, temperature, and C-rate.

**Factors affecting cycle life:**
1. **Depth of Discharge (DoD)** — Shallower cycles ⇒ exponentially more cycles (Peukert effect)
2. **Temperature** — High T accelerates SEI growth; Low T causes Li-plating
3. **C-rate** — Higher discharge/charge currents → faster degradation
4. **State-of-Charge (SoC) window** — Cycling between 20–80% SoC doubles cycle life
5. **Calendar aging** — Even unused, batteries age due to SEI layer growth

**Typical Cycle Life (KTU Reference Table):**

| Chemistry | Cycle Life (to 80% cap) | Specific Energy |
|-----------|--------------------------|------------------|
| Lead-Acid | 300–500 | 30–50 Wh/kg |
| NiMH | 500–1000 | 60–120 Wh/kg |
| LFP (LiFePO₄) | 2000–5000 | 90–160 Wh/kg |
| NMC | 1000–2000 | 150–220 Wh/kg |
| NCA | 500–1000 | 200–260 Wh/kg |
| Li-S (theoretical) | 200–500 | 400–500 Wh/kg |

---

## 2.4 Self-Discharge — Deep Analysis

**Self-Discharge Rate (% per month):**
$$R_{sd} = \frac{C_{initial} - C_{after\,1\,month}}{C_{initial}} \times 100\%$$

**Arrhenius temperature dependence:**
$$R_{sd}(T) = R_{sd,ref} \cdot e^{\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T_{ref}}\right)}$$

where $E_a$ is the activation energy of the parasitic reaction (typically 60–100 kJ/mol for Li-ion).

**Mechanisms of self-discharge:**
1. **Electrochemical side-reactions** — e.g., electrolyte decomposition at electrodes
2. **Internal micro-short circuits** — dendrite formation causing current leakage
3. **Shuttle reactions** — polysulfide migration in Li-S cells (major issue)
4. **Thermal decomposition** — accelerated at high temperature

**Self-discharge comparison:**
- Li-ion: 2–3% / month
- NiMH: 20–30% / month
- NiCd: 10–15% / month
- Lead-acid: 4–20% / month
- LFP: 1–3% / month (best)

---

## 2.5 Static Battery Equivalent Circuit Models — Deep Analysis

### 2.5.1 Ideal Source Model
$$V_t = V_{oc}$$
*No internal resistance, no transients.* Useful only for textbook baseline.

### 2.5.2 R-Internal (R-int) Model
$$V_t = V_{oc} - I \cdot R_{int}$$
*Most widely used in KTU board questions.* Includes steady-state ohmic drop.

### 2.5.3 Thevenin (1st-Order RC) Model
The model consists of:
- $V_{oc}$ — ideal voltage source
- $R_0$ — ohmic resistance (electrolyte, contact)
- $R_{ct}$ — charge-transfer resistance
- $C_{dl}$ — double-layer capacitance

**Governing equations:**
$$V_t = V_{oc} - I R_0 - V_{RC}$$
$$I = \frac{V_{RC}}{R_{ct}} + C_{dl} \frac{dV_{RC}}{dt}$$

Solving the ODE for a step-current $I$ input:
$$V_{RC}(t) = I \cdot R_{ct} \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right) \quad \text{where } \tau = R_{ct} C_{dl}$$

### 2.5.4 PNGV / Multi-RC Model
For higher accuracy, multiple RC branches are added in series, each representing different time-constants of diffusion processes.

---

## 2.6 Series-Parallel Pack Equivalents — Deep Analysis

For a pack with **S cells in series, P in parallel per branch (S×P configuration)**:

| Parameter | Series (S) | Parallel (P) | S×P Pack |
|-----------|------------|--------------|----------|
| Voltage | $S \cdot V_{cell}$ | $V_{cell}$ | $S \cdot V_{cell}$ |
| Capacity (Ah) | $C_{cell}$ | $P \cdot C_{cell}$ | $P \cdot C_{cell}$ |
| Energy (Wh) | $S \cdot V_{cell} \cdot C_{cell}$ | $V_{cell} \cdot P \cdot C_{cell}$ | $S \cdot P \cdot V_{cell} \cdot C_{cell}$ |
| Internal Resistance | $S \cdot R_{cell}$ | $R_{cell}/P$ | $S \cdot R_{cell} / P$ |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Exam Trap:** When calculating pack resistance, the series factor **S** multiplies and the parallel factor **P divides**. Don't forget both effects simultaneously.

# SECTION 3 — Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation — Pack Equivalent Resistance for S×P Configuration

**Problem Statement:** Derive the Thevenin-equivalent internal resistance of a battery pack with $S$ cells in series and $P$ cells in parallel per series string.

### Step 1 — Single Cell Resistance Baseline
Each cell has an internal resistance $R_{cell}$. By definition, the internal resistance is the lumped sum of:
- electrolyte ionic resistance
- electrode/electrolyte interfacial resistance
- tab and current-collector resistance

$$R_{cell} = R_{electrolyte} + R_{contact} + R_{tabs}$$

### Step 2 — Resistance of a Series String of S Cells
When $S$ cells are connected in series, the same current $I$ flows through every cell. By Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL), the total ohmic drop across the string is the sum of drops across each cell:

$$V_{drop,series} = \sum_{i=1}^{S} I \cdot R_{cell,i} = S \cdot I \cdot R_{cell}$$

(assuming all $R_{cell,i}$ are equal — a standard KTU assumption)

Therefore, the equivalent resistance of a series string is:

$$\boxed{R_{series} = S \cdot R_{cell}}$$

### Step 3 — Resistance of P Parallel Strings
When $P$ cells are placed in parallel, they share the same voltage $V$ but split the current. The total current is the sum of individual branch currents:

$$I_{total} = \sum_{j=1}^{P} \frac{V}{R_{cell}} = P \cdot \frac{V}{R_{cell}}$$

The equivalent resistance seen at the terminals is:

$$R_{parallel} = \frac{V}{I_{total}} = \frac{V}{P \cdot V / R_{cell}} = \frac{R_{cell}}{P}$$

Therefore:

$$\boxed{R_{parallel} = \frac{R_{cell}}{P}}$$

### Step 4 — Combining Both: S-series × P-parallel
The pack is built by placing $P$ parallel strings, each containing $S$ cells in series. We can model it as **one big cell of resistance $R_{series}$ repeated P times in parallel**:

$$R_{pack} = \frac{R_{series}}{P} = \frac{S \cdot R_{cell}}{P}$$

**Final result:**

$$\boxed{R_{pack} = \frac{S \cdot R_{cell}}{P}}$$

### Step 5 — Numerical Example (KTU-style)
A 96s46p Tesla pack with each 21700 cell having $R_{cell} = 25 \text{ m}\Omega$:

$$R_{pack} = \frac{96 \times 0.025}{46} = \frac{2.4}{46} = 0.05217 \, \Omega \approx 52 \text{ m}\Omega$$

This matches published Tesla Model 3 pack impedance data (~50 mΩ).

---

## 3.2 Derivation — Specific Energy vs Energy Density Conversion

**Given:** A battery cell of mass $m$, volume $\mathcal{V}$, nominal voltage $V_{nom}$, and capacity $C_{Ah}$.

**Step 1 — Stored energy (Wh):**
$$E = V_{nom} \cdot C_{Ah} \quad [\text{Wh}]$$

**Step 2 — Specific energy (gravimetric):**
$$E_{sp} = \frac{E}{m} = \frac{V_{nom} \cdot C_{Ah}}{m} \quad [\text{Wh/kg}]$$

**Step 3 — Energy density (volumetric):**
$$E_{vol} = \frac{E}{\mathcal{V}} = \frac{V_{nom} \cdot C_{Ah}}{\mathcal{V}} \quad [\text{Wh/L}]$$

**Step 4 — Cross-relation using density $\rho = m/\mathcal{V}$:**
$$E_{sp} = E_{vol} \cdot \rho$$

**Numerical Example:** An LFP cell with $E_{vol} = 350$ Wh/L and $\rho = 2100$ kg/m³:
$$E_{sp} = 350 \times 2.1 = 735 \text{ Wh/kg} \quad (\text{ideal, real} \approx 160 \text{ Wh/kg})$$

The huge gap between ideal and real arises because the calculation above ignores packaging, current collectors, and electrolyte mass.

---

## 3.3 Derivation — Thevenin Model Step Response

**Setup:** Battery at rest, OCV = $V_{oc}$, no current flows. At $t = 0$, a constant discharge current $I$ is applied. Determine $V_t(t)$.

**Step 1 — State equation:** The RC branch voltage $V_{RC}$ follows:
$$C_{dl} \frac{dV_{RC}}{dt} + \frac{V_{RC}}{R_{ct}} = I$$

**Step 2 — Standard first-order linear ODE.** The homogeneous solution is:
$$V_{RC,h}(t) = A \cdot e^{-t/\tau}, \quad \tau = R_{ct} C_{dl}$$

The particular solution (constant current) is:
$$V_{RC,p} = I \cdot R_{ct}$$

**Step 3 — Apply initial condition** $V_{RC}(0) = 0$ (capacitor initially uncharged):
$$0 = A + I \cdot R_{ct} \implies A = -I \cdot R_{ct}$$

**Step 4 — Final expression:**
$$V_{RC}(t) = I \cdot R_{ct} \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$$

**Step 5 — Terminal voltage:**
$$V_t(t) = V_{oc} - I \cdot R_0 - I \cdot R_{ct} \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$$

**Step 6 — Steady-state value** ($t \to \infty$):
$$V_{t,ss} = V_{oc} - I(R_0 + R_{ct}) = V_{oc} - I \cdot R_{int}$$

which is consistent with the R-int model. **This confirms the Thevenin model reduces to the R-int model at steady state** — a key KTU board concept.

---

## 3.4 Derivation — Maximum Power Transfer (Battery Internal Limit)

**Theorem:** A real battery with EMF $V_{oc}$ and internal resistance $R_{int}$ can deliver **maximum power to a load** $R_L$ when $R_L = R_{int}$ (impedance matching).

**Step 1 — Current through load:**
$$I = \frac{V_{oc}}{R_{int} + R_L}$$

**Step 2 — Power delivered to load:**
$$P_L = I^2 R_L = \frac{V_{oc}^2 R_L}{(R_{int} + R_L)^2}$$

**Step 3 — Differentiate w.r.t. $R_L$ and set to zero:**
$$\frac{dP_L}{dR_L} = \frac{V_{oc}^2(R_{int} + R_L)^2 - V_{oc}^2 R_L \cdot 2(R_{int} + R_L)}{(R_{int} + R_L)^4} = 0$$

**Step 4 — Numerator simplification:**
$$(R_{int} + R_L) - 2 R_L = 0 \implies R_L = R_{int}$$

**Step 5 — Maximum power:**
$$\boxed{P_{max} = \frac{V_{oc}^2}{4 R_{int}}}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Reality:** EV drivetrains never operate at $R_L = R_{int}$ because the efficiency at this point is only 50% (half the energy is wasted in $R_{int}$). Real EVs operate at much lower $R_L$ for high efficiency (typically 80–95%).

---

| Feature | Ideal Source | R-int | Thevenin (1st order) | Multi-RC (2nd order) |
|---------|--------------|-------|----------------------|----------------------|
| **Components** | $V_{oc}$ only | $V_{oc}, R_{int}$ | $V_{oc}, R_0, R_{ct}, C_{dl}$ | $V_{oc}, R_0, 2 \times (R_i, C_i)$ |

# SECTION 5 — KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## PART A — 3-Mark Short-Answer Questions

### Question 1 [KTU University Exam — June 2024]
**Define the term "specific energy" of a battery. Why is it a critical parameter for EV battery selection? Mention typical specific energy values for Li-ion and Lead-Acid chemistries.**

**Model Answer:**
Specific energy is the energy stored per unit mass of a battery, expressed in **Wh/kg**. It is calculated as:

$$E_{sp} = \frac{V_{nom} \times C_{Ah}}{m_{cell}}$$

It is critical for EVs because it directly determines the **driving range per kilogram** of battery mass — higher specific energy means more range for less weight. Typical values: **Li-ion (NMC) ≈ 150–220 Wh/kg**, **Lead-Acid ≈ 30–50 Wh/kg**. Li-ion offers ~4–5× the range for the same battery mass, which is why lead-acid is now obsolete in modern EVs.

---

### Question 2 [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]
**What is self-discharge in a battery? List two mechanisms that cause self-discharge and state the typical self-discharge rate of Li-ion cells at 25 °C.**

**Model Answer:**
Self-discharge is the **irreversible loss of stored charge** in a battery during idle (open-circuit) conditions, expressed in **%/month**. It occurs without any external load.

**Two mechanisms:**
1. **Electrochemical side-reactions** at the electrode/electrolyte interface (e.g., SEI growth in Li-ion).
2. **Internal micro-shorts** caused by dendrite growth or separator defects.

**Typical rate:** Li-ion cells lose only **2–3% of capacity per month** at 25 °C, which is among the lowest of all chemistries. NiMH loses 20–30%/month, while LFP loses only 1–3%/month.

---

## PART B — 14-Mark Questions (with Internal Choice)

### **Question A (14 Marks)** [KTU University Exam — Model Paper 2024]

**(a)** With the help of a neat circuit diagram, explain the **Thevenin equivalent circuit model** of a battery. Derive the expression for the terminal voltage during a step-discharge current pulse. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** A battery pack has configuration **14s10p**, with each cell having $V_{oc} = 3.6$ V, $C_{cell} = 3.0$ Ah, and $R_{cell} = 30$ mΩ. Calculate:
1. Pack nominal voltage
2. Pack capacity
3. Pack stored energy in Wh
4. Pack internal resistance **(7 Marks)**

---

#### Model Solution to Question A(a):

**Thevenin Equivalent Circuit:**

The Thevenin model consists of:
- $V_{oc}$ — open-circuit voltage source
- $R_0$ — ohmic series resistance
- $R_{ct} \parallel C_{dl}$ — parallel RC branch representing the charge-transfer/double-layer effect

(See Section 4.1 for the circuit diagram.)

**Derivation of step response:**

When a step current $I$ is applied at $t=0$, the parallel RC branch voltage follows the ODE:

$$C_{dl} \frac{dV_{RC}}{dt} + \frac{V_{RC}}{R_{ct}} = I$$

Solving with $V_{RC}(0)=0$ and $\tau = R_{ct} C_{dl}$:

$$V_{RC}(t) = I R_{ct}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$$

**Terminal voltage:**

$$V_t(t) = V_{oc} - I R_0 - I R_{ct}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$$

**Physical interpretation:**
- At $t=0$ (instantaneous): $V_t(0^+) = V_{oc} - I R_0$ (purely ohmic drop, capacitor still uncharged).
- At $t \to \infty$ (steady state): $V_t(\infty) = V_{oc} - I(R_0 + R_{ct}) = V_{oc} - I R_{int}$.

This proves that the **R-int model is the steady-state limit** of the Thevenin model.

---

#### Model Solution to Question A(b):

**Given:** $S = 14$ series, $P = 10$ parallel, $V_{oc,cell} = 3.6$ V, $C_{cell} = 3.0$ Ah, $R_{cell} = 30$ mΩ = 0.030 Ω

**Step 1 — Pack nominal voltage:**
$$V_{pack} = S \cdot V_{cell} = 14 \times 3.6 = \mathbf{50.4 \text{ V}}$$

**Step 2 — Pack capacity (parallel adds capacity):**
$$C_{pack} = P \cdot C_{cell} = 10 \times 3.0 = \mathbf{30 \text{ Ah}}$$

**Step 3 — Pack energy:**
$$E_{pack} = V_{pack} \times C_{pack} = 50.4 \times 30 = \mathbf{1512 \text{ Wh} \approx 1.51 \text{ kWh}}$$

**Step 4 — Pack internal resistance:**
$$R_{pack} = \frac{S \cdot R_{cell}}{P} = \frac{14 \times 0.030}{10} = \frac{0.420}{10} = \mathbf{0.042 \text{ Ω} = 42 \text{ mΩ}}$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout — Common Mark Loss Areas:**
> 1. **Mixing up S and P roles** — many students calculate $R = S/P$ instead of $S \times R / P$. Remember: series multiplies R; parallel divides it.
> 2. **Forgetting units** — Write "42 mΩ" or "0.042 Ω", not just "42".
> 3. **Energy unit confusion** — Convert Wh to kWh correctly: 1 kWh = 1000 Wh.
> 4. **Initial condition** — For Thevenin transient, students often forget $V_{RC}(0)=0$; this gives wrong sign in exponential.

---

### **Question B (14 Marks)** [KTU University Exam — Model Paper 2024]

**(a)** Explain the terms **cycle life** and **self-discharge** of a battery. Discuss the factors affecting cycle life in Li-ion batteries. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** A Li-ion cell has the following Thevenin parameters at SoC = 50%: $V_{oc} = 3.7$ V, $R_0 = 25$ mΩ, $R_{ct} = 40$ mΩ, $C_{dl} = 1500$ F. A constant discharge current of 20 A is applied. Calculate:
1. Initial instantaneous terminal voltage $V_t(0^+)$
2. The RC time-constant $\tau$
3. Steady-state terminal voltage $V_t(\infty)$
4. The terminal voltage at $t = \tau$ **(7 Marks)**

---

#### Model Solution to Question B(a):

**Cycle Life:**
Cycle life is the **number of complete charge-discharge cycles** a battery undergoes before its capacity drops to **80% of the initial rated capacity**. For Li-ion NMC, this is typically 1000–2000 cycles. For LFP, it can exceed 3000–5000 cycles.

**Self-Discharge:**
Self-discharge is the **loss of stored charge** over time when the battery sits idle at open circuit, expressed as **%/month**.

**Factors affecting Li-ion cycle life:**
1. **Depth of Discharge (DoD)** — Cycling between 20–80% SoC doubles cycle life vs. 0–100% DoD.
2. **Operating temperature** — Above 35 °C accelerates SEI growth; below 0 °C causes Li-plating.
3. **C-rate** — Higher charge/discharge currents (e.g., 2C vs 0.5C) accelerate degradation.
4. **State-of-Charge window** — Storing at 100% SoC stresses the cathode; 50% SoC storage is optimal.
5. **Calendar aging** — Even without cycling, SEI growth consumes cyclable Li, reducing capacity over time.

**Mathematical degradation model:**
$$Q(N) = Q_0 (1 - k \sqrt{N})$$

---

#### Model Solution to Question B(b):

**Given:** $V_{oc} = 3.7$ V, $R_0 = 0.025$ Ω, $R_{ct} = 0.040$ Ω, $C_{dl} = 1500$ F, $I = 20$ A.

**Step 1 — Initial instantaneous voltage** (capacitor acts as short-circuit, $V_{RC}(0^+) = 0$):
$$V_t(0^+) = V_{oc} - I R_0 - 0 = 3.7 - 20 \times 0.025 = 3.7 - 0.5 = \mathbf{3.2 \text{ V}}$$

**Step 2 — Time constant:**
$$\tau = R_{ct} \cdot C_{dl} = 0.040 \times 1500 = \mathbf{60 \text{ s}}$$

**Step 3 — Steady-state voltage** ($t \to \infty$, capacitor fully charged, no current in $C_{dl}$):
$$V_t(\infty) = V_{oc} - I(R_0 + R_{ct}) = 3.7 - 20 \times (0.025 + 0.040) = 3.7 - 20 \times 0.065 = 3.7 - 1.3 = \mathbf{2.4 \text{ V}}$$

**Step 4 — Voltage at $t = \tau$:**
$$V_{RC}(\tau) = I R_{ct}(1 - e^{-1}) = 20 \times 0.040 \times (1 - 0.3679) = 0.8 \times 0.6321 = 0.5057 \text{ V}$$

$$V_t(\tau) = V_{oc} - I R_0 - V_{RC}(\tau) = 3.7 - 0.5 - 0.5057 = \mathbf{2.694 \text{ V}}$$

**Verification:** $V_t(\tau) = 2.694$ V lies between $V_t(0^+) = 3.2$ V and $V_t(\infty) = 2.4$ V ✓ (correct since 63.2% of the way to steady state at $t=\tau$).

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout — Common Mark Loss Areas:**
> 1. **Confusing $R_0$ with $R_{ct}$** — The ohmic drop at $t=0^+$ uses $R_0$ only; the long-term drop uses $(R_0 + R_{ct})$.
> 2. **Wrong sign in exponent** — Use $e^{-t/\tau}$, NOT $e^{t/\tau}$ (capacitor charges, not discharges).
> 3. **Unit mismatch** — Capacitance in Farads, resistance in Ohms → time-constant in seconds. Don't mix mF and mΩ without conversion.
> 4. **Numerical rounding** — Use at least 4 decimal places for $e^{-1} = 0.3679$ to avoid cumulative errors.

---

## 📋 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

- ✅ **Cell Voltage** = $V_t = V_{oc} - I R_{int}$ under load. Three flavors: $V_{nom}$, $V_{oc}$, $V_t$ — never confuse them.
- ✅ **Specific Energy (Wh/kg)** = $V_{nom} C_{Ah} / m$. Determines EV range. Li-ion ~150–220; Lead-acid ~30–50.
- ✅ **Energy Density (Wh/L)** = $V_{nom} C_{Ah} / \mathcal{V}$. Determines pack packaging.
- ✅ **Cycle Life** = number of cycles to reach 80% capacity. Affected by DoD, T, C-rate, SoC window.
- ✅ **Self-Discharge** = % charge lost per month at rest. Li-ion 2–3%/mo; NiMH 20–30%/mo. Arrhenius temperature dependence.
- ✅ **R-int model** = static, 2 parameters ($V_{oc}, R_{int}$). Most common in KTU Part A.
- ✅ **Thevenin model** = static + transient. Adds $R_{ct} \parallel C_{dl}$. Step response: $V_{RC}(t) = I R_{ct}(1-e^{-t/\tau})$.
- ✅ **Time constant** $\tau = R_{ct} C_{dl}$. At $t = \tau$, response is 63.2% complete.
- ✅ **Series (S)** raises voltage: $V_{pack} = S V_{cell}$, $R_{pack} = S R_{cell}$.
- ✅ **Parallel (P)** raises capacity: $C_{pack} = P C_{cell}$, $R_{pack} = R_{cell}/P$.
- ✅ **S×P Pack** resistance: $R_{pack} = S R_{cell} / P$. Energy: $E_{pack} = S \cdot P \cdot V_{cell} C_{cell}$.
- ✅ **Max power transfer** at $R_L = R_{int}$ gives $P_{max} = V_{oc}^2 / (4R_{int})$ — but only 50% efficient.
- ✅ **Static** model parameters assumed constant w.r.t. SoC and time — distinguish from **dynamic** (Warburg, hysteresis) models.
- ✅ **KTU Standard EoL** = 80% of initial capacity for automotive Li-ion cells.
- ✅ **Faraday's constant** $F = 96{,}485$ C/mol and **gas constant** $R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K) are exam constants.
- ✅ Always convert **mΩ to Ω** or **mF to F** before substituting into equations to avoid unit mismatches.
